10165-across-the-zodiac-the-story-of-a-w:
Percy Greg's Across the Zodiac, the story of a wrecked record deciphered, translated, and edited by its finder, tells of a voyage to Mars. It opens with shipwreck and outward bound, then the untravelled deep and a new world.

Later chapters describe the new world's language, laws, and life. There are an official visit, escort duty, a faith and its founder, manners and customs, woman and wedlock, a country drive, a river journey, and the children of light. Greg writes early science fiction with earnest detail. Readers get a Victorian Mars, imagined whole, from its laws to its loves.
11247-the-exploits-of-brigadier-gerard:
Arthur Conan Doyle's Brigadier Gerard stories follow a boastful French cavalry officer of the Napoleonic wars, retelling his adventures in old age to admiring listeners. Eight episodes carry him to the Castle of Gloom, against the brothers of Ajaccio, into kings' courts. Into a game played for a kingdom, with a medal and a brush with the Devil along the way. Gerard's vanity is the joke, but his courage is real.

Conan Doyle wrote Gerard as a comic counterpart to Holmes: a narrator who cannot see his own absurdity. The stories move briskly and rely on Gerard's voice for their charm. They remain among the most entertaining Napoleonic tales in English, lighter than the author's historical novels but just as vivid.
11988-the-human-chord:
Algernon Blackwood's 1910 novel The Human Chord is dedicated to those who hear. It opens with a boy whose imagination is so vivid that his inventions come to feel real to him. He gives everything real names, and his inner playgrounds dwarf his father's hay-fields and lawns.

Blackwood, a master of supernatural fiction, builds the novel around sound, music, and the idea that a chord, rightly sounded, might open doors between worlds. Plains without horizon and seas deeper than any estate's fields give the boy's inner life its scale. The novel treats imagination not as escape but as a form of perception with real consequences.
12135-the-art-of-fencing-or-the-use-of-t:
Andrew Mahon, professor of the small sword in Dublin, translated this fencing manual from the French of Monsieur L Abbat in 1734. L Abbat taught at the Academy of Toulouse, and Mahon praised his rules for their nicety, exactness, and agreement with reason.

The book teaches the small sword as a gentleman art: guard positions, thrusts, parries, ripostes, volts, and the seizing of an enemy blade, with chapters on measure, timing, and footwork. Mahon addresses both proficient fencers and beginners, hoping to lay a regular foundation for future masters. The manual now serves historians of dueling and sport, showing how eighteenth-century gentlemen learned to fight with a point rather than an edge.
12663-the-phantom-herd:
B. M. Bower's 1916 western novel centres on Luck Lindsay, a film maker trying to shoot a cattle picture with Native actors. When his company reaches the range, old range hands, a small-town doctor, and rival picture men all pull the shoot in different ways. Cattle drives, storms, and a drifting herd keep the plot moving at a brisk pace.

At its heart the book sets the old West against the new film West, with real cowboys asked to play at being cowboys for the camera. Luck must hold his cast, his backers, and his story together while the range itself refuses to behave. The novel blends humour, romance, and outdoor action in the author's familiar Flying U manner.
13245-the-charm-of-oxford:
J. Wells, warden of Wadham College, published The Charm of Oxford in 1920, second revised edition 1921, illustrated by W. G. Blackall. Wells quotes the line home of lost causes as Oxford's blame, and mother of movements as her boast, in the same walls welcoming leaders of the age to be. Plates show Christ Church, quads, and libraries.

Wells tells how Merton's Mob Quad was saved by a narrow majority, after reformers sought to pull it down for modern buildings. A young fellow, G. C. Brodrick, forced a second vote, and the quad survived, though the grove was cut and a fine view spoiled. Brasenose, in the center by Radcliffe Square, gets its own chapter. The book is a loving, learned guide to Oxford's colleges.
13438-a-king-s-comrade-a-story-of-old-he:
Charles W. Whistler's story of old Hereford follows Wilfrid, a king's comrade in the days of Danes, Mercians, and Northumbrian kings. Wilfrid keeps a promise and swims in Portland, meets Ecgbert the Atheling, speaks with Ethelbert the king, and travels with him toward Offa's court at Sutton.

Queen Quendritha weaves plots, Marshal Gymbert loses his good name, and Ethelbert goes to his rest as earthquake and terror shake the palace. Thanes debate whether to die with their king or flee while time remains. Whistler builds the tale from early English history, with loyalty, treachery, and a young man's oath at its heart.
13674-chronicle-and-romance-froissart-ma:
A Harvard Classics volume from 1910, edited by Charles W. Eliot, that joins three kinds of old English writing under one cover. It opens with Froissart's chronicles in Lord Berners' translation, continues with Malory's Holy Grail from Caxton's Morte d'Arthur, and closes with William Harrison's description of Elizabethan England from Holinshed's chronicles.

Froissart gives battles such as Crecy and Poitiers and risings such as Wat Tyler's rebellion, told with colour and detail. Malory follows knights in search of the Grail, and Harrison sets out how English people lived, ate, dressed, and governed themselves. Together the three parts give a vivid cross-section of medieval and Tudor England, from war to daily life.
13803-making-his-way-or-frank-courtney-s:
Horatio Alger Jr. wrote Making His Way, the story of Frank Courtney's struggle upward. Frank loses his mother, faces a will, and finds himself disinherited. He leaves home, seeks work in New York, and meets Erastus Tarbox of Newark. Adventures in Wall Street, a capture, and a school friend's help mark his rise.

Alger's formula holds: honesty, hard work, and a lucky break reward the hero. Mark, a rival, yields to temptation and gets into trouble. Frank's grief at his mother's bedside gives the tale feeling. The novel belongs to Alger's long series for boys. It shows American ideals of self-help in popular form.
14486-the-thunder-bird:
B. M. Bower's 1919 western novel follows Johnny Jewel, a young Montana ranch hand who takes to flying just as airplanes reach the range. His nickname comes from the machine he learns to fly.

Johnny owes a debt of honor, chases Mary V across ranch country, crashes, recovers, and flies again, while old Sudden and other Flying U folk watch with amusement and worry. The plot runs through Mexico and back, mixing ranch work with stunt flying. Bower blends the cowboy tale with the new air age, and Johnny's pluck carries the story.
14755-father-stafford:
Anthony Hope's 1895 novel follows Father Stafford, a priest whose change of habits unsettles friends, rivals and a whole circle of English society. Around him move Eugene Lane and his guests, Sir Roderick Ayre, Mr. Morewood and Lady Claudia, each with a claim, a grievance or a romance in play.

Feuds, vigils, a retreat and a battle at Baden punctuate a plot of love, pride and good intentions gone astray. Three gentlemen act for the best and still make matters worse, while Lady Claudia grows vexed with mankind in general. Hope keeps the comedy light and the dialogue quick, but the questions underneath are serious: duty, conscience and what a man owes the people who trust him.
14893-prince-jan-st-bernard:
Forrestine C. Hooker tells the life of Prince Jan, a Saint Bernard, from the hospice dogs and the land of snow to a new world and a land of no snow. Jan learns to hate, meets the pound, a muzzle and a journey to the land of make-believe, before visiting the home of the sunbonnet babies.

Shorty, the poundmaster's problem, voices of the hospice dogs and a fireside story follow, with an unforgotten trail leading to a decision. Jan's duty, as the frontispiece puts it, is to save lives and be worthy of his ancestors. Illustrated by Lynn Bogue Hunt and dedicated to the author's father, a brigadier general, the book is a dog story with a moral spine.
15568-the-law-and-the-word:
T. Troward, late divisional judge in the Punjab, wrote this New Thought work, first published in May 1917, with Robert M. McBride in New York. This printing is the eighth, of June 1937. Troward, author of the Edinburgh Lectures on Mental Science, was honorary member of the Medico-Legal Society of New York and first vice-president of the International New Thought Alliance.

Eight chapters move from facts in nature and psychic experience to man's place in the creative order and the law of wholeness. The soul of the subject, the promises, death and immortality, and transferring the burden follow. A short appreciation of Troward opens the book, asking how one knows a friend. Troward argues that mind shapes life through a spiritual law, and that burdens pass to a higher power. The book is a classic of early New Thought philosophy.
15608-in-the-days-of-poor-richard:
Irving Bacheller published this historical novel in Indianapolis in 1922, with Bobbs-Merrill, illustrated by John Wolcott Adams. It is dedicated to Albert J. Beveridge, discerning student of prophets, heroes, and founders of democracy. A frontispiece shows young John Irons and Margaret Hare in the forest.

Book one follows the Horse Valley adventure, sowing the dragon's teeth, a journey to Philadelphia, a crossing, and Jack seeing London and the great philosopher. Lovers, a dawn, an appointment and challenge, and a departure follow. Book two brings ferment, service under the commander in chief, Boston jail, and the first Fourth of July. Bacheller sets a young man's growth against the Revolution, with Franklin's Poor Richard spirit as a guide.
15671-a-splendid-hazard:
A romantic adventure novel by Harold MacGrath, issued in 1910 with pictures by Howard Chandler Christy. The action opens in Paris, where Fitzgerald broods on Waterloo and the romance of a great battle. MacGrath, a popular writer of light adventure, builds his tale on daring, disguise, and high stakes. Grosset and Dunlap issued the book for readers who liked a brisk, gallant plot.

Fitzgerald is drawn into a scheme that sends the party sailing, scheming, and crossing purposes across Europe. A duke, an admiral, and a woman who knows too much all press on the plot. Chapters move from a plaster statuette and pirates to old scandals and the pines of Aitone. The end exposes the dream for what it was, leaving the hazard splendid but costly.
15822-the-faithful-steward:
A prize essay on giving by the Reverend Sereno D. Clark, on systematic beneficence as part of Christian character. A committee offered two hundred and fifty dollars for the best treatise on giving a set share of income to benevolent ends. From one hundred and seventy-two manuscripts, the judges picked four, and Clark's stood among the best. The essay argues that giving should be planned, not left to impulse.

Clark urges Christians to set aside a fixed portion of income, regularly and cheerfully, for good works. Stated giving, he holds, trains the heart and steadies the church's work. Examples and scripture back his plea. The essay still speaks to readers who ask how faith should shape money: give first, give by rule, and let generosity become habit.
15947-the-pleasures-of-england-lectures-:
A set of Oxford lectures by John Ruskin, Slade Professor of Fine Art in his second tenure. John Wiley and Sons issued them in New York in 1888. Ruskin, honorary student of Christ Church, treats English history as a series of pleasures. Four lectures carry the argument from early Saxon days to Elizabeth.

The pleasures of learning run from Bertha to Osburga, and of faith from Alfred to the Confessor. Deed follows from Alfred to Coeur de Lion, and fancy from Coeur de Lion to Elizabeth. Ruskin writes with fire for art, faith, and brave action. The lectures still stir readers who love England: history told as praise, not as mere dates.
16255-dickey-downy-the-autobiography-of-:
Virginia Sharpe Patterson's Dickey Downy, published in Philadelphia in 1899 by the American Baptist Publication Society, tells a bird's life in his own voice. An introduction by Congressman John F. Lacey and drawings by Elizabeth M. Hallowell support the tale, dedicated to the author's children Laura, Virgie, and Robert George. Chapters run from the orchard and Dickey's meditations through cousins, a parrot at a party, a winter in the South, and a prison.

Hunters, a new home, an ill-mannered child, two slaves of fashion, a country school, and Polly's farewell complete the story. Patterson teaches kindness to animals through humor and adventure. Young readers who love birds will enjoy this gentle, old-fashioned autobiography.
1644-the-adventures-of-gerard:
Etienne Gerard, a swaggering brigadier of hussars in Napoleon's armies, tells his own war stories in these linked tales by A. Conan Doyle. Doyle frames them as drawn from French memoirs of the period. Gerard narrates campaigns in Spain and elsewhere with the boastful charm of a man who never doubts his own courage.

Each episode drops Gerard into a tight spot — a message to carry, a rival to outface, a retreat to survive — and lets his vanity collide with real danger. Readers get a soldier's-eye view of the Napoleonic wars, told with humor, and a portrait of French military pride that is affectionate rather than solemn.
16963-the-golden-bird:
Maria Thompson Daviess's 1918 novel opens with a young woman who finds she needs money fast, not love. Polly, left poor, weighs a quick match to Matthew Berry against her pride and her hopes. Farm scenes, lambs, kin, and small-town talk fill the early chapters, and a fine bird of the title soon becomes the hinge of her plans.

The story mixes humor, sentiment, and plain talk about want, work, and marriage in the rural South. Polly's frank voice carries the book as she learns that quick cash can cost more than it pays. Readers who like warm, old-style romance with a plucky heroine will enjoy its mix of farm life and heart trouble.
17297-british-highways-and-byways-from-a:
Thomas D. Murphy recorded a five-thousand-mile summer motor tour of England, Wales, and Scotland in this 1908 Boston volume, with colour plates and maps. He states plainly that he did not mean to write a guidebook, though his notes on roads, towns, and country places can serve one. The trip runs from London to Canterbury, the Midlands, the Welsh border, Land's End, Wales, the Highlands, and Yorkshire.

Chapters pause at border towns, cathedral cities, Cromwell country, and the haunts of Milton and Penn, alongside out-of-the-way stops a rail traveller might miss. Readers get an early motoring view of Britain, when cars were still new and country roads set the pace. It suits anyone curious about how the island looked from the driver's seat a century ago.
17456-the-romance-of-a-christmas-card:
Kate Douglas Wiggin wrote this Christmas story, published in Boston and New York in 1916 by Houghton Mifflin Company, with pictures by Alice Ercle Hunt. Copyright had first been held in 1915 by the Butterick Publishing Company. The story opens on Christmas Eve, a Saturday night, when Mrs. Larrabee, the Beulah minister's wife, opens the door of the study where her husband is at work.

A Christmas card sets the romance in motion, linking the minister's household to wider lives and older memories. Readers get a gentle, sentimental holiday tale from the author of Rebecca of Sunnybrook Farm. The book suits family Christmas reading and admirers of Wiggin's warm, domestic fiction.
17769-the-house-by-the-church-yard:
J. Sheridan Le Fanu, author of Uncle Silas, wrote this novel, published in Dublin in 1904 by James Duffy and Company and in New York by Macmillan. Its contents open with a prologue of village chat, then the rector's night walk to his church and the nameless coffin. Mr. Mervyn in his inn and the fair green of Palmerstown follow.

How the Royal Artillery figures in the tale comes next, in a village world of soldiers, clergy, and secrets. Readers get a long Irish mystery novel, rich in local talk and slow-building dread, from a master of the form. The book suits readers of Le Fanu and of Victorian sensation fiction.
18022-betty-at-fort-blizzard:
Molly Elliot Seawell wrote Betty at Fort Blizzard in 1916, printed in Philadelphia by Lippincott. The book first ran in serial form as Colonel Fortescue's Betty, and it is dedicated to Eleanor T. Wood, a gentle lady whose path through life is radiant.

Betty takes a new role at a western fort, where pretty maids, gamecocks, letters, and soldiers' enlistments stir hearts. Chapters run from good-bye sweetheart to love the conqueror and the reveille. Seawell writes bright, old-style romance with a military air. It is a cheerful girls' book of fort life, full of flirtation, pride, and loyal love.
18248-lucy-raymond-or-the-children-s-wat:
The author of Katie Johnstone's Cross wrote this children's story, published at Toronto by James Campbell and Son. Lucy Raymond, or The Children's Watchword, follows Lucy and her circle through home scenes, Sundays, and small trials. The Toronto edition presents a moral tale for young readers, in the plain style of nineteenth-century Sunday school fiction.

Chapters run from Miss Preston's last Sunday and Lucy's home, through strawberrying, a mission, temptations, and partings, to new experiences, a start in life, ambition, and friendship. Later chapters bring an unexpected recognition, the flower fadeth, darkness and light, and home again. Readers get a gentle story of growing up, where watchfulness, kindness, and faith guide children through parting and return.
18991-the-late-miss-hollingford:
Rosa Mulholland, Lady Gilbert, wrote this novella, first published years earlier in All the Year Round. It had never been republished in England when this edition appeared. It had been translated into French and Italian, and Charles Dickens had chosen it as a companion piece for his own No Thoroughfare in the Tauchnitz series. Dickens admired Mulholland's tales.

The story follows Rachel, whose return to her mother fronts the illustrated edition, and the tangle of affection, duty, and misunderstanding around a household. Mulholland writes with warmth and a storyteller's pace. Readers get a short Victorian tale of family feeling, praised in its day by the leading novelist of the age, and readable in a single sitting.
19015-jane-allen-right-guard:
Edith Bancroft wrote this 1918 school story about Jane Allen, who earns the right guard spot on her team. The book follows Jane and her friends at school, where games, study, and dormitory life mix with plots and misunderstandings. Jane is proud and slow to complain of unfair treatment.

Her friends Judith, Ethel, and Adrienne hold a council of war when bad news arrives and Mrs. Weatherbee seems set against Jane. Loyalty, pluck, and team spirit carry the girls through. Young readers get a warm school tale of sport, friendship, and standing firm without making a fuss.
19402-frank-merriwell-s-reward:
Burt L. Standish wrote this 1900 boys' book, Frank Merriwell's Reward, in the long Merriwell series for Street and Smith. Frank, captain of his picked nine, faces a runaway automobile, a ball team, and a summer of schoolboy honour. Harry Rattleton, Bart Hodge, Jack Diamond, and Dismal Jones crowd the opening.

Dunstan Kirk asks Frank to let Badger pitch against Abernathy's Hartford nine, hoping that honour from one who is not Badger's friend will brace him out of despondency. Frank drums thoughtfully and agrees it may be done. Readers get a brisk school story of sport, loyalty, and second chances.
19665-my-lady-of-the-chinese-courtyard:
A writer on China was once asked why so little was written about Chinese women. He answered that one never hears about them. My Lady of the Chinese Courtyard answers that silence. It presents the life of a Chinese lady from inside her courtyard home. The book came to Western readers as letters and intimate domestic scenes.

Domestic writing of this kind gave foreign readers a rare view. Women's lives in old China were mostly hidden from print. A courtyard view shows family rank, ritual, and daily care up close. It also shows the limits of what an outsider could see. The book survives as a window into a closed world, opened a crack.
19902-the-affectionate-shepherd:
Richard Barnfield published The Affectionate Shepherd in 1594. It is a pastoral poem of a shepherd's love, among England's earliest such works. This edition's notes trace Barnfield's other writings. They list his lament for Lady Pecunia and The Encomium of Lady Pecunia. Copies sit in the British Museum and the Ashmolean. The scholarship around the poem is part of this volume's matter.

Barnfield was a contemporary and admirer of Shakespeare. Some once credited his sonnets to Shakespeare himself. The Affectionate Shepherd sings Daphnis's longing in rich pastoral dress. Its homoerotic frankness startled later centuries of editors. The poem holds a real place in Elizabethan literature. This old edition shows scholars recovering it.
19904-the-noble-lord:
Percival Wilde wrote The Noble Lord as a comedy in one act. Its stage business opens with a drenched handkerchief. The hero draws it from a hip pocket, wetter than his hands. He throws it away with vexation. Then he kneels by an unconscious girl and lays his ear over her heart. He looks quizzical, then rather timid. Wilde packs a rescue, a mystery, and a romance into minutes.

One-act plays fed vaudeville bills and amateur stages alike. Wilde was a master of the short form. A lord, a girl, and a wet evening supply his machinery. Timing matters more than scenery in such pieces. The Noble Lord shows his economy at work. It is theater built for one set and quick laughs.
2032-martin-pippin-in-the-apple-orchard:
Eleanor Farjeon tells a fairy tale for grown readers, in which Martin Pippin, a wandering minstrel, visits an apple orchard where six young women wait for news of their lovers. He tells them stories, one for each maid, to pass the time. Farjeon wrote Martin Pippin in 1921, when fairy tales for adults were finding a new audience.

The tales inside the tale mix wit, romance, and fancy, and the orchard itself becomes a place of talk and longing. Farjeon, praised for a rare gift of fancy, writes prose that is musical, gentle, and quietly wise. The six maidens each hear a tale fitted to her lover, so the book becomes a set of stories within a story.
20423-joyous-gard:
Joyous Gard takes its name and spirit from the Arthurian legends of Sir Lancelot. Its pages draw on the old romance of the Round Table. One passage retells the end of Lancelot's life, when a bishop finds him at peace.

The bishop explains his mirth: Lancelot was with him, with more angels than he ever saw men upon one day. So, the old story says, it was well with that great knight at the last. Around such scenes the book builds quiet essays on courage, joy, and the well-kept life, using the legends as a mirror.
20862-jerry-s-reward:
Jefferson Square, one short block in Gaminsville, holds a convent and a dumping common. Evelyn Snead Barnett sets Jerry's Reward, from 1900, in that tight world. A high brick wall guards the Convent of the Good Shepherd on its large lot.

Jerry, a street boy of the square, stands at the tale's warm centre. Kind deeds and their just reward shape the plot in classic form. Barnett wrote tales that found grace in rough city corners. This one shows her touch: slum scenes drawn with care, and a boy whose good heart earns more than coin by the close.
2123-the-crime-of-sylvestre-bonnard:
Anatole France tells, in diary form, of Sylvestre Bonnard, an old scholar whose quiet life by the Seine is broken by a crime of the heart. On Christmas Eve 1849 he sits by his fire, with his cat Hamilcar curled before the andirons. France wrote the novel in diary form, a shape that suits an old scholar's daily thoughts.

Bonnard's love of books, a young girl in need, and a manuscript lead him to break rules for kindness. France writes with gentle irony, and the novel charms as a portrait of learning softened by human feeling. Hamilcar the cat, curled by the fire, gives the opening its domestic warmth.
21328-the-parables-of-our-lord:
The Reverend William Arnot published this study of the parables of Jesus in London in 1874 with T. Nelson and Sons. Arnot also wrote Laws from Heaven for Life on Earth, a study of Proverbs, and Roots and Fruits of the Christian Life. His parables book works through the stories Jesus told, one by one.

Arnot writes for ordinary Christian readers rather than scholars, opening each parable's setting, meaning, and use in daily life. The seed, the soils, the lost sheep, and the talents become lessons in faith and conduct. His preface looks back warmly on the Reformers and Puritans as models of plain, serious Bible teaching for the home.
21448-the-african-trader-or-the-adventur:
Harry Bayford loses his father and his ease at the start of W. H. G. Kingston's The African Trader. Harry was born in Jamaica, where his father was a West India merchant, and schooled in England. Business losses break the father's health, and he dies.

Rather than burden his sisters, Harry ships on a trading vessel bound for Africa. Yellow fever kills much of the crew, and fire takes the ship on the way home. Harry and an African seaman escape on a raft, only to be picked up by a slave trader. A Royal Navy warship then gives chase, with lives in the balance.
22232-the-carved-cupboard:
Amy Le Feuvre, author of Teddy's Button and Probable Sons, published The Carved Cupboard in 1899. Le Feuvre wrote religious tales for children that sold in the millions. Her story opens with a supplanter and four verses, then moves to a country home. Clare, one of her girls, toys with her spoon at tea, listening with half her mind while her thoughts wander elsewhere.

A carved cupboard, nicknamed Bluebeard's cupboard in one chapter, holds the family's secret. Sealed directions in an envelope hang over the plot like a will. Le Feuvre mixes mystery with her usual lessons of faith and patience. The book is a fair piece of her gentle, popular art.
22536-jane-austen-her-life-and-letters-a:
William Austen-Leigh wrote Jane Austen: Her Life and Letters as a family record. He was the novelist's great-nephew, working with family papers. New documents became available for this fuller account of her life.

Miss Jane Austen, granddaughter of Admiral Charles Austen, allowed generous access. Miss Margaret Bellas, great-granddaughter of James Austen, did the same kindly. Their family documents exceeded what the earlier Memoir could use. Austen-Leigh traces the Austens and their Walters kin in Kent. Lincolnshire branches of the family enter the record as well. Letters carry much of Jane Austen's own quick, funny voice. Readers get the novelist's quiet life told by those who kept her papers.
22595-at-the-point-of-the-sword:
Herbert Hayens wrote At the Point of the Sword, a boys' adventure story set in old Peru. The catalog record gives no year. Hayens wrote many tales for young readers. Here he opens by teaching before he entertains. Peru, he explains, was once called the Land of the Sun, because its native people worshipped the sun.

The background runs to Cuzco, the great Inca city, and to Manco Capac, counted the first of the Inca emperors. Against that storied past of empire and conquest, the young hero's adventures play out. Boys of the era got history folded into their thrills. Modern readers get both a period adventure and a glimpse of how empire was romanticized for children.
22792-perils-and-captivity-comprising-th:
Perils and Captivity gathers true accounts of shipwreck and suffering, centered on the Picard family, French emigrants wrecked on the African coast in the disaster of the frigate Medusa. The catalog record names no author and gives no year. The Medusa's wreck in 1816, and the raft that became a byword for horror, shocked all Europe.

The narrative praises one young sufferer's amiable and girlish simplicity, which renders her story particularly engaging. It also reflects, with English satisfaction, that such disaster could not have befallen a British crew. The blame falls on the leaders' selfishness, aboard both ship and raft. That, the book argues, made the affair so serious. The volume belongs to the literature of maritime disaster, half testimony and half moral lesson, that the nineteenth century devoured.
2286-devil-s-ford:
Bret Harte's Devil's Ford returns to the mining country, where a river crossing gives the story its name and its dangers. Partners, rivals, and a woman of uncertain past cross paths at the ford, and old debts come due in Harte's familiar mix of humor and sudden feeling. The California setting does much of the work, with water, dust, and camp life vividly drawn.

The novella's strength lies in its characters: men who bluff, women who endure, and a community quick to judge. Harte keeps the plot tight and the ending bittersweet. It is a solid, compact example of his later western fiction.
22867-meeting-of-the-board:
Boardroom worry fills Meeting of the Board, a story of business under pressure. Walter, its central figure, sits with reports waiting on his desk. The promotion-draw reports and the expected dividend reports trouble him most. A shop steward goads him, annoying but tolerable. A man named Torkleson is a different matter.

The story stays close to office ground, where labor trouble and money trouble meet. Walter's weariness gives the piece its tone, a manager ground down between workers below and owners above. Nothing here needs a battlefield or a storm. The drama is fluorescent and familiar. Readers who enjoy workplace fiction from the industrial age will find a sharp little specimen, complete with period detail.
23376-a-terrible-coward:
George Manville Fenn set this short tale in a small Cornish fishing village, where boys and young men prove themselves by a risky dive from a rock. One young hero has not yet dared the feat, and a rival, vexed at his delay, plays a cruel trick that nearly drowns him.

Events soon turn the tables, and the supposed coward shows true nerve while his tormentor shows his own fear. Fenn packs the tale with close calls, sea spray, and quick turns, in the style that keeps young readers asking how the hero will get out next. The moral is plain and fair: courage is not loud talk or a dare, but steadiness when real danger comes.
24270-tom-gerrard:
Louis Becke wrote this Australian story, published by T. Fisher Unwin in 1904 and dedicated to Alrema. It opens with Tom Gerrard on horseback meeting a small, ill-clad girl of about ten gathering pippies on the sand. She is Mary Incubus, who roasts the shellfish with Jim in the stockman's kitchen when auntie is abed, under the eye of Mrs. Elizabeth Westonley.

Gerrard knows the name at once: he is Uncle Tom, the cattleman of the Northern Territory, come two thousand miles from Cape York to see his kin. Mary's mother was Gerrard's sister, also named Mary. Readers get a tale of the Australian bush, family found again, and a cattleman's long ride home.
24375-wizard:
Larry M. Harris wrote this science fiction story for Astounding Science Fiction in May 1960. Its frame comes from a short history of the Masquerade, the protection by which telepaths hid from non-telepaths. That protection was not fully formed until the late seventeenth century, though hidden telepath groups existed long before. One such group, in the Offenburg district, then in Prussia, began about 1594. It won a signal triumph eleven years later, possibly the only one of its kind until the Masquerade dissolved in 2103.

The tale opens with Jonas coming over a hill whistling, happy in a job with a slight and unavoidable risk, this time more than slight, even possibly fatal and painful. He stands at the crest, hands on hips, looking down at Speyer baking in May sun. Readers get a tale of hidden telepaths, old Europe, and a wizard's risky errand.
2444-oxford:
Andrew Lang's Oxford is a loving portrait of the university city: its colleges, its history, its dons, and its undergraduates. The book walks readers through quadrangles and libraries, recalling famous scholars and the traditions that shaped them. Lang, himself an Oxford man, writes with wit and affection.

The volume captures Oxford before the modern age, when its rituals still ruled student life. Its charm lies in anecdote and atmosphere. Readers who love universities will enjoy this nostalgic guide. Lang's Oxford recalls the dons and undergraduates of his own student years.
24551-oxford:
F. D. How described Oxford in this volume of the Beautiful England series, pictured by E. W. Haslehurst and published at Boston by Dana Estes. Its plates show Magdalen Bridge and Tower, Magdalen College from the Cherwell, Oxford from Headington Hill, the Martyrs' Memorial, and the college barges at Folly Bridge.

Later pictures take in Fisher Row and the remains of Oxford Castle, Worcester College gardens, the Clarendon Building, Christ Church, and Brasenose with the Radcliffe Library. How's text guides readers through colleges, streets, and river scenes. The book gives a charming, well-illustrated portrait of the university city.
24584-man-overboard:
F. Marion Crawford published this sea story at New York and London in 1903, with illustrations. Its title comes from the oldest cry at sea: a man has fallen overboard. Crawford, author of The Upper Berth and The Witch of Prague, builds his tale around a ship, its crew, and a sudden act of violence.

One picture shows a man letting go of a knife, its point stuck in the deck, while another shows wet, shining arms reaching from the water. The story moves between deck and sea, with suspense and a touch of the uncanny. Readers who enjoy Crawford's tales of mystery will find this short novel taut and atmospheric.
25037-war-and-the-weird:
Forbes Phillips and R. Thurston Hopkins's 1916 volume, from Simpkin, Marshall, gathers essays and sketches on war and the weird. Chapters take up the uncanny under fire, war the revealer, the soul's boundary line, the spiritual entity, angels, fellowship with the unseen, and the white comrade. Five sketches follow: Ombos, De Gamelyn traditions, the mills of God, a spy's story, and through the furnace.

The opening voice belongs to a six foot officer of the Royal Field Artillery, wounded at Mons. He never studied spiritualism, preferring sport, yet cannot dismiss experiences brought under his nose again and again. He dreamt on the march to Mons that he could not sit his horse; next day a wound inside his right knee stopped his riding for a week or two. Later, amid the conflict's marvellous tangles, a speaker tells Margot he would not take back one minute of those great days.
2515-stepping-heavenward:
Mrs. E. Prentiss wrote this novel as the journal of Katherine, called Katy, who begins writing at sixteen in January 1831. Katy is lively, quick tempered, and full of good resolves that fade by noon, and her diary records school days, family prayers, and her wish to grow into a better person.

Over the years Katy marries Ernest, keeps house, raises a child, and faces illness and loss, still measuring herself against her faith. Prentiss writes in a warm, plain voice, and the journal form lets readers watch a whole life of small steps. The book endures as a gentle portrait of a woman learning patience, love, and trust day by day.
26677-athelstane-ford:
Allen Upward published this adventure novel with C. Arthur Pearson at London in 1899. Its narrator, Athelstane Ford, flees his father's house at Brandon, gazes across Breydon Water to Yarmouth at sunset, and follows his cousin Rupert to seek treasure in the East Indies. He promises hardships, battles, love and jealousy, a trusted man turned enemy, and treasure found in a Hindoo king's palace.

Chapters run from a tavern of the Three-Decker and a king's ship to the siege of Gheriah, the Company's service, a spy, captivity, and the Black Hole. Sabat Jung arrives, a battle is fought in the dark, Meer Jaffier swears his oath, and Plassy and retribution follow. Ford returns home at last, in a Georgian tale of India, rivalry, and revenge.
26851-tom-brown-at-oxford:
Thomas Hughes wrote this sequel to Tom Brown's School Days, first serialized in Macmillan's Magazine and published in book form in 1861. Where the earlier novel followed Tom at Rugby from age eleven to sixteen, this one sends him to Oxford. He follows a three-year program of lectures and reading on his own with a tutor. Students in residence are up, or have come up; students who leave have gone down.

The chapters sketch Oxford life in the 1840s at St. Ambrose's College: a row on the river, a breakfast at Drysdale's, the boat club and its budget, Hardy the servitor, fishing with Drysdale and Blake, and an explosion. Muscular Christianity gets a chapter, as do the captain's notions, the first bump, a storm that brews and breaks, and the village of Englebourn. Tom's friendships, above all with Hardy, carry the story.
27661-master-of-the-vineyard:
Myrtle Reed published this novel with G. P. Putnam's Sons in New York and London in 1910, copyrighted under her married name, Myrtle Reed McCullough. She dedicates it to all who have loved in vain, and an illustration shows a woman gazing across the valley where the vineyard lay.

Chapters run from The Hill of the Muses and Brown Alpaca through The Crystal Ball, April's Sun, and The House of the Broken Heart, to More Stately Mansions. Later come Whom God Hath Joined, A Spring Day, The Hour of the Turning Night, The Stain of the Rose, The Inlaid Box, and The Last Tryst. Reed, known for Lavender and Old Lace, writes a romance of love and loss.
27962-one-snowy-night-long-ago-at-oxford:
Emily Sarah Holt wrote One Snowy Night, a historical tale of the first persecution of Christians by Christians in England, as its preface explains. The story follows Gerhardt, who left Germany to bring the pure Gospel back to England, and was cast out and slain, unlike Boniface, welcomed as a saint in Germany.

The novel opens at Saint Maudlin's Well with a tired mother calling for her boys Flemild, Romund, and Haimet, in a plain household of dark wool and linen. Holt writes as a convinced Protestant, insisting that the Bible, not the Church, is paramount. The tale blends domestic detail with martyrdom.
2878-the-disguising-at-hertford:
John Lydgate wrote The Disguising at Hertford around 1427 as a verse entertainment, preserved in a single manuscript owned by Trinity College, Cambridge. The edition notes that the medieval thorn character has been changed to modern th, and that the original punctuation, mostly slashes, has been replaced sparingly with commas and full stops. Superscript marks and mid-script dots have likewise been regularized.

The play itself gives wives a comic voice, as they claim mastery by prescription and long title of succession from wife to wife. They promise to set their husbands' lives in great noise and beg their sovereign lord to defend them. The text offers a rare glimpse of fifteenth-century court revels, with medieval spelling and humor intact beneath the editor's tidying.
2893-the-wizard:
H. Rider Haggard's The Wizard tells of a missionary named Owen who carries his faith into an African kingdom ruled by custom and a powerful wizard called Hokosa. Haggard dedicates the volume to Nada Burnham, the child who died of war hardship at Buluwayo in 1896, and calls the tale one of victorious faith. Owen works at a translation of St. John in his hut when Hokosa enters to bargain.

The wizard proposes that the two men pool their magic and rule the land together, confessing that Owen is too strong for him. Their contest becomes a test of rival powers, with conversion, fear, and loyalty at stake. The story shows Haggard's late interest in faith as a force equal to any army, told with his usual pace.
29579-watchbird:
Robert Sheckley's short tale opens among six watchbird makers, blue with expensive cigar smoke, waiting on a government man. Gelsen, one of the makers, recalls telling his chief engineer Macintyre that a new day was coming and Watchbird was the answer. The makers call themselves, wryly, members of a very exclusive firm of salvation, since only a certified government contract lets one save the human race.

Watchbirds are meant to bring peace on Earth by figuring out angles, a strange, hopeful, and ominous idea. Sheckley turns the millennium into a sales pitch with a sting. Fans of Sheckley will enjoy a short, sly satire on peace machines, profit, and the men who sell salvation.
30383-spies-die-hard:
Arnold Marmor sets a Martian espionage story around Harry Horn, thirty-four, five feet eleven, one hundred seventy-two pounds, wanted dead or alive for ten thousand credits. A telecaster flashes his photo while a voice names him a spy for Earth, and Lynn Brickel snaps off the humming machine in disbelief.

Horn had ranked high in the Martian Security Police as one of Lazar's top men, yet now he stands exposed. Brickel wonders why she was not told and whether trust in her is fading. She had helped McLean and Sanderson escape from Mars, and a hum at her door deepens the puzzle. Marmor builds a fast chase tale of double agents, bounties, and shifting loyalties.
32208-the-star-lord:
Boyd Ellanby's short story, printed in Imagination in June 1953, sends a ship on a voyage with a secret danger. The cover line says some aboard saw a first voyage as a joy trip, others as a fresh start, while danger stayed known to the captain alone. The Star Lord waits, poised for her maiden voyage, a gigantic spindle still cradled in scaffoldings, towering against the sky of Satellite Y.

Passengers come aboard while Captain Josiah Evans checks his officers' reports. The ship is ready for space. Nothing more can be done until takeoff, so Evans walks to his cabin with slow steps, closes the door, and sinks into his chair. Privacy, he feels, is the greatest luxury. He reaches for the post-bag delivered by the rocket ferry from Earth. Readers get a space-emigration tale. A captain carries a danger his passengers do not suspect.
32697-the-sword:
Frank Quattrocchi tells of George Harrison, an engineer called back from vacation on Balboa Island. He must report to Intersolar Spaceport in Los Angeles. A huge object is racing toward Earth at several times the speed of light. It has signaled in perfect Intersolar Convention code, though nothing so fast is known in the solar system.

Harrison has three days to decode the strangest message ever sent to Earth. Newsmen crowd the port, and officials fear panic. The tale turns on a sword, a weapons expert's knowledge, and a Bible. Through them Harrison works out what the visitors want, and what their arrival will cost.
32897-young-wallingford:
George Randolph Chester's 1910 novel follows Wix Wallingford, a sharp young man who starts to think for himself. He soon learns how easy money can be made, and how fast it can slip away. Early chapters show him taking a hand in schemes, chasing the easiest way to wealth, and testing his wits against older, harder players. Chester, already known for tales of clever rogues, keeps the tone brisk and comic.

The novel's fun lies in watching Wix grow from a small-time trickster into someone who must reckon with the costs of his own cleverness. Illustrations by F. R. Gruger and Henry Raleigh add period flavor to the business deals and street scenes. It is an American success story with a wink, fond of its hero's nerve while never quite letting him off the hook.
32985-a-modern-wizard:
Rodrigues Ottolengui's 1894 novel, A Modern Wizard, turns on a courtroom struggle over a man whose powers look like magic and may be crime. Its early chapters follow a lawyer and his client, an investigator named Jack Barnes, a wizard's trick, and a surrender by Dr. Medjora, before the case moves into prosecution and defense, damaging testimony, and closing arguments. The structure is that of a trial novel, with each side building its case in turn.

Ottolengui, already known for tales of crime and evidence, uses the trial to test how far science, suggestion, and showmanship can explain the uncanny. The wizard at the center remains a puzzle: fraud, hypnotist, or something stranger. Readers who enjoy Victorian detective fiction with a touch of the occult will find the courtroom scenes sharp and the mystery well sustained.
33048-jap-herron-a-novel-written-from-th:
Jap Herron, a novel written from the ouija board and published in New York in 1917, comes with an introduction, The Coming of Jap Herron, by Emily Grant Hutchings. Hutchings tells how, on a Thursday afternoon in March 1916, she attended a small psychical research society where a lecture on cosmic relations was expected. When the lecturer was detained, the hostess asked Mrs. Lola V. Hays to entertain the company, and the sittings that followed, recorded over years of meetings, produced the novel.

The book presents itself as received through the board, and its interest lies less in proving that claim than in the story and the period belief it records. Readers of the 1910s took psychical research seriously, and Hutchings's introduction gives that world in detail. As a curiosity of American spiritualism and popular fiction, Jap Herron remains a strange, fascinating document of its time.
33076-applied-psychology-driving-power-o:
Warren Hilton's Applied Psychology: Driving Power of Thought was issued under the auspices of the Literary Digest for the Society of Applied Psychology, founded by Hilton, in 1920. It is the third of twelve volumes on applying psychology to personal and business efficiency. Its chapters move from judicial mental operations and the vitalizing influence of certain ideas through the work of Prince, Gerrish, Sidis, Janet, and Binet. They go on to the two types of thought, causal judgments, and classifying judgments.

Hilton argues that thought drives action, and that learning how ideas form, distort, and impress themselves can make a worker or manager more effective. The volume belongs to the popular psychology movement of the early twentieth century, when business readers sought mental methods for success. It remains a window on that movement's language and hopes, blending science, self-help, and the promise of efficiency.
33125-wild-birds-in-city-parks-being-hin:
Herbert Eugene Walter and Alice Hall Walter's Wild Birds in City Parks appeared in a revised and enlarged edition in 1906. It gives hints on identifying 145 birds prepared primarily for the spring migration in Lincoln Park, Chicago. The new edition added forty-five birds, with a simple field key and check-list numbers. The text was carefully rewritten and reordered.

The booklet was made for beginners in outdoor bird study, people who wanted to name the birds they saw in a city park without carrying a heavy manual. Its hints, chart, and key let a walker in Lincoln Park match a bird in spring migration to its name. For urban naturalists and historians of birding, it remains a delightful early field guide, showing how city parks first became classrooms for bird study.
34058-the-crime-of-the-boulevard:
Jules Claretie, a member of the French Academy, wrote this Paris mystery, translated by Mrs. Carlton A. Kingsbury and published in New York in 1897. The story opens with a man seeking Bernardet's house in a passage off the boulevard, a cul-de-sac of black buildings and old storehouses. The man is a short, fat, bald workman, hurrying in warm October rain.

He labors in a concierge's lodge, mending garments for neighbors, while his wife looks after the house and complains of her lot. Claretie builds a crime tale from that humble life. The novel offers a vivid, period Paris mystery.
34992-encyclopaedia-britannica-11th-edit:
Volume eight, slice ten of the Encyclopaedia Britannica, eleventh edition, runs from Echinoderma to Edward. The slice forms one part of a vast work of arts, sciences, and letters. Two columns of heads show the spread at a glance. Starfish kin open the set, and kings named Edward close it.

Long pieces treat economics and schooling in full. Ecuador and Edinburgh get place studies with maps in mind. Thomas Alva Edison earns a life sketch in the list. Maria Edgeworth and her kin take their place in print. Saints and kings named Edmund crowd the last pages. Readers can dip from sea beasts to coin terms in a few leaves. The slice shows the scale of the great eleventh edition.
35188-the-fire-bird:
The Fire Bird is a novel by Gene Stratton-Porter, printed at Garden City, New York, in 1922. Gordon Grant drew the illustrations and Lee Thayer the decorations. The book is dedicated to Edward Sheriff Curtis, called a blood brother to the Indians by ceremonial. The frontispiece shows Princess Yiada before the medicine man.

She begs him for a new and sure medicine to ease her scorched heart of the fire of a flaming red bird. The tale is told in three parts: The Love Dance of Princess Yiada, Couy-Ouy and Mountain Lion, and Yiada's Flight to the Mandanas. Verses in the book chant of white toluache lilies and sacred turtle drums. They call to drive back the flaming ghost of the fire bird to the far Shadow Land. Stratton-Porter, famed for her Limberlost nature books, here writes a tale of Native American romance and legend.
3528-beethoven-the-man-and-the-artist-as:
This volume presents Ludwig van Beethoven through his own words, edited by Friedrich Kerst and Henry Edward Krehbiel and first translated into English in 1905. A brief life sketch opens the book, followed by Beethoven's remarks on art, music, and the composer's calling, drawn from his letters and conversation books. The editors arrange his sayings by theme.

Readers hear Beethoven on genius, work, deafness, and the moral power of music, in his own blunt and passionate voice. The book does not retell his life in full; it lets his sentences speak for his character. It suits music lovers who want to meet Beethoven as a thinker and a worker, not only as the composer of famous symphonies.
36029-a-speckled-bird:
Augusta Evans Wilson, author of St Elmo and Vashti, wrote this novel, published in 1902 and dedicated to the loyal readers who had asked her to write again. Its title comes from Jeremiah: as a speckled bird, the birds round about are against her.

The heroine is Eglah, a sharp-tongued small girl arguing with her grandmother over breakfast about her ugly name. She insists the Queen of Sheba was David's wife, misnamed Bath Sheba because he saw her going to her bath-house. Her grandmother sighs over a silver coffee urn that has been in the family one hundred fifty years. Readers get a Southern domestic novel with a precocious child at its center.
36161-a-letter-to-thomas-f-bayard:
Lysander Spooner, the American writer on law and liberty, printed a sharp open letter at Boston in 1882. He aimed it at Senator Thomas Bayard of Delaware, but its charge runs at the whole Congress. Spooner denies that Bayard, or any senator or member, has any right to make laws that bind the people of the United States. The letter grew out of a claim by Bayard that a man could serve as a lawmaker and still be honest.

Spooner argues that laws of men's own making stand apart from the law of nature and from plain justice. To hold that such laws truly bind, he says, is to claim a right of sheer rule over others, which no grant can give. The pamphlet is a late, plain statement of his lifelong case against forced rule.
36804-the-league-of-the-leopard:
The League of the Leopard is an adventure novel by Harold Bindloss. Frederick Stokes published it in New York in June 1914. Bindloss had earlier written Prescott of Saskatchewan. A colour frontispiece by Carlton Glidden faces the title page. The chapter list promises treachery, pestilence, and a dangerous señorita.

The story opens at a small West African trading factory. The trader Niven lies dying there. Two traders, Redmond and Gilby, lounge on the veranda. The heat is heavy and the air still. The men are gaunt from the climate. They toil long hours when trade is good. They defy the French authorities at times. The first chapter is called A Dangerous Bequest.
36828-pastor-pastorum-or-the-schooling-o:
It was printed at Cambridge by Deighton Bell and Company in 1899. The contents run to thirteen chapters with a preface and an opening chapter. A chronological appendix and indexes of texts close the book.

The chapters lay out the book's plan. After the opening come Human Freedom and Of Revelation. Then Latham treats Our Lord's use of signs and the laws of the working of signs. The schooling of the apostles comes next, with their mission to the cities. Later chapters treat the road from the Mount to Jerusalem, the later lessons, and the lessons of the Resurrection. The book reads the Gospels as the record of a teacher's slow training of his men. It is a scholar's study of how the apostles were taught, step by step, by their master.
36877-emerson-radio-model-39-warranty-ca:
The Emerson Radio Model 39 warranty card is a printed post card from the Emerson Radio and Phonograph Corporation of New York. Its office is given as on Eighth Avenue in that city. One side carries a place for a one cent stamp. A picture frame names the Model 39 set and lists world cities the firm reached.

Text on the card urges the buyer to explore short wave thrills and reach out across the world by radio. As a warranty card it was meant to be filled in and mailed back by the set's owner. The small card is a piece of early home radio marketing, when short wave listening was sold as adventure.
36895-william-the-third:
William the Third, by H D Traill, stands in the Twelve English Statesmen set from Macmillan. It was first printed in May 1888 and reprinted through 1906. Traill traces the life of William of Orange, who came to rule England.

The first chapter runs from 1650 to 1672, on William birth, kin, and boyhood in a split Dutch state. It treats his temper, his aims, and the hate of De Witt and his party. Later chapters cover the war of 1672 and the road to the English crown. Heads name the flight of James, the advance to Exeter, and the defection of Churchill. Readers get a clear, brisk life of a cold, great king who reshaped two lands.
37464-bluebeard:
Bluebeard is a book of tales for children by Clifton Johnson, printed in New York by the Macaulay Company in 1920. It is one of the Bedtime Wonder Tales, a set of books of favourite stories from the folk lore of all lands. The tales are meant for children from four to twelve years old. The pictures are by Harry Smith. The title tale, Bluebeard, comes from France and opens the book.

The tales that follow come from many sources: Grimm, England, Hindustan, Italy, Germany, Scotland, Japan and Ireland. One comes from American Negro folk lore. They include A Goblin in a Bottle, Yallery Brown, The Little Jackal, The Blind Ogre, Blockhead Hans and Time and His Mother. The note adds that nothing has been lost of the ease, fun and sweetness that give the tales their lasting charm.
38180-an-american-at-oxford:
John Corbin's An American at Oxford was published by Houghton, Mifflin in Boston and New York in nineteen three, after his Schoolboy Life in England. An opening plate shows tea on the lawn at the Oxford Union. The contents divide the report into plain parts. First comes the university and the college: what a university of colleges means, the freshman, a day in a college, dinner in hall, and an evening.

Club life and social life follow, then Oxford out of doors. Corbin slacks on the Isis and the Cherwell, rows in an Oxford tub, plays a scrimmage of English rugby, and reports track and field sports. Later parts treat reading for examinations, the examination itself, Oxford's qualities and defects, reform, and the university's tie to the people.
38296-wild-adventures-round-the-pole-or-:
Wild Adventures round the Pole, in an edition of 1883, is Gordon Stables's tale of the Snowbird crew in the Arrandoon. The book opens in Scotland where the Clyde and the Tweed rise near each other. Stables gives the two rivers a parting talk: the Tweed turns south for ease, while the bold Clyde heads north and west. The scene sets the theme of daring over comfort.

A great ship is built for the polar cruise, and public voices argue over the plan. Highland homes, old friends with new faces and hard northern seas fill the voyage. The story sells the far north as the true test of a crew's nerve and skill.
38357-by-right-of-sword:
Arthur Marchmont's novel of eighteen ninety seven, published in New York and London, throws an English narrator into the Russia of the nihilists. The contents map a tale of duels, plots, and rescues. Chapters cover a legacy of love, a lesson in nihilism, Olga's abduction, and an attack on the Czar.

The story opens with a despairing letter from Moscow. The writer has done with England after a rupture at home and means to volunteer for war. He hopes a Turkish bullet finds him, yet his years in Russia pull him toward Saint Petersburg. Marchmont builds the book as a first person confession of a man drawn step by step into conspiracy. Swordplay and secret societies mix with a love plot. It is a brisk late Victorian adventure novel of conspiracy and romance.
38872-a-little-wizard:
A Little Wizard is a tale by Stanley J Weyman, copyright in 1895. Weyman was known for A Gentleman of France and Under the Red Robe. The tale opens after the battle of Naseby, when lands near Ripon fall to General Skippon as his reward.

An agent rides to take the house at Pattenhall and finds a boy of about twelve on a heap of stones. The boy will not speak, then points him on past the church. Nine chapters follow, with names like The Meal Chest and Treasure Trove. A strange trial and a high judgment close the tale. Readers get a short, tense tale of war spoils, a lone boy, and hidden wealth.
39066-the-white-blackbird:
Hudson Douglas wrote The White Blackbird, a novel issued in Boston in 1912 with color art by Herman Pfeifer. Douglas gave the book to his wife Isobel and their daughter of the same name. A front plate shows a fake doctor whose patient bids him feel her pulse before he goes.

Thirty one parts open with a tropical talk, move through Dutch courage and a place called El Farish, and reach the white blackbird of the title at part seven. Unmasking, bets on the future, the goddess of chance, and the price of freedom drive the middle. A masterstroke, a law and profits part, and a Jura succession tangle the end. Luck, fraud, and rank all play their part.
394-cranford:
Elizabeth Gaskell sketches the small Cheshire town of Cranford in this gentle novel, told by a young visitor named Mary Smith. The town runs on old ladies, strict manners, and small economies, where a silk dress or a letter can stir a week of talk. Captain Brown, Miss Matty, and Signor Brunoni pass through its quiet streets.

A bank failure, a lost brother, and a panic over burglars test the town's kind heart. Gaskell writes with humor and tact, never mocking her folk. The book endures as a warm portrait of English village life, where gossip hides real care and old friends rally in need.
39922-juggernaut-a-veiled-record:
George Cary Eggleston and Dolores Marbourg wrote a novel in 1891, calling it a veiled record. Edgar Braine was never so blithe, the first line says, as on the morning of his suicide. Years later, amid an extraordinary career, that June morning would rush back on him. He would recall each detail with more than photographic vividness.

Braine is shown young, poor, strong, and full of ambition in a little western city. He had already mastered the tools of his work, the hardest task, the narrator argues. Life opened its best portals to him. The title hints at a crushing force driving the tale. The veiled form suggests real people behind the fiction.
39929-a-dialogue-upon-the-gardens-of-the:
William Gilpin wrote A Dialogue upon the Gardens of Lord Viscount Cobham at Stow in Buckinghamshire in seventeen forty eight. The Augustan Reprint Society issued a fresh form in nineteen seventy six from the William Andrews Clark Memorial Library in Los Angeles. John Dixon Hunt wrote the intro. Before seventeen fifty three, the intro notes, no guide to any English garden but Stowe yet stood in print.

Gilpin walks the great grounds at Stowe in talk with a friend. Stowe was famed for temples, lakes, and walks laid out to stir thought as much as sight. The talk weighs taste, nature, and art in garden design of that age. Notes at the end aid the modern reader. Garden lovers get an early, keen voice on a landmark of English design. The piece helps show how the landscape garden was first praised.
40136-the-mercy-of-the-lord:
The Mercy of the Lord is a book of short tales of India by Flora Annie Steel, author of On the Face of the Waters. George Doran published it at New York in 1914, printed in England. The title tale opens with Craddock, an engine man, polishing the brass of his safety valve and singing a hymn badly. His fit of goodness springs from love for a good little Eurasian girl fresh from her convent.

Twenty-five tales stand in the contents. Their titles sketch the world Steel knew: Salt Duty, The Wisdom of Our Lord Ganesh, The Value of a Vote, and An Appreciated Rupee. Others, like The Finding of Private Flanigan and Slave of the Court, mix soldiers, clerks, and courts of British India.
40181-to-leeward:
To Leeward is a novel of Rome by Marion Crawford, first copyrighted in 1883 and issued here in his complete works by Collier of New York. Crawford dedicates it to his uncle Samuel Ward of New York. The frontispiece shows the last rays of the sun shining across a terrace. The opening chapter states the book's ground at once: there are two Romes.

One Rome belongs to the intelligent foreigner, of excavations, monuments, tramways, hotels, and wax candles. The other is the Rome within, a city of antique customs, aristocratic prejudices, intrigue, and religion. Old-fashioned honour and new-fashioned scandal live side by side there. A passage preserved in the copy looks further ahead. People say, Crawford writes, that this state of things cannot last. There must come an amalgamation, a deluge, a unity of fraternity and equality.
40319-the-life-of-mrs-humphry-ward:
Janet Penrose Trevelyan wrote The Life of Mrs Humphry Ward, a life of her own mother. Dodd, Mead and Company issued the book in New York in nineteen hundred twenty three. Trevelyan had written a short history of the Italian people. Friends sent her stacks of Ward’s letters for the work.

Mary Arnold was born to a famed line of scholars. Her youth in Tasmania and her school years open the tale. Oxford life from eighteen hundred sixty seven fills the next part. She wed T Humphry Ward and helped found Somerville Hall. London years brought her great fame as a novel writer. Robert Elsmere made her name known round the world. Letters trace each stage in her own words.
40690-roger-kyffin-s-ward:
W H G Kingston wrote this tale of London in a panic. Early in 1797, crowds of all ranks hurried through lanes and alleys toward the Bank of England. Rich merchants, shopkeepers, lawyers, squires, dandies, widows, and duchesses all pressed the same way. Carriages with coronets on their panels rolled up from Cheapside.

Fear sat on most faces in the throng. Part of the crowd turned into the Bank and pushed toward the counters, coin in mind. Part flowed into the Royal Exchange, and more carriages ran on along Cornhill. Kingston sets his ward's story against the great money scare of that year, when trust in paper shook and all London ran for gold.
40872-the-history-of-the-hen-fever-a-hum:
George Burnham wrote this humorous record of the hen fever, published at Boston in 1855. A daguerreotype of Queen Victoria, from a portrait in Burnham's possession, fronts the book. Her Majesty presented that portrait to him in 1853, the plate explains with a letter reference.

Burnham dedicates the history to amateurs, fanciers and breeders of poultry everywhere. Successful and unfortunate dealers alike get a nod in that dedication at the front. When rare Cochin and Shanghai fowls fetched wild prices across America, Burnham, a Boston breeder, kept the jokes and the prices, and his record reads the craze like a comic bubble.
41139-the-drunkard:
The Drunkard is a novel on drink and heredity by Guy Thorne, published in New York in nineteen twelve. Sturgis and Walton issued it, and Thorne had written When It Was Dark before. A long dedication letter to Louis Tracy tells how the tale was planned. Talks in the Isle of Wight and the Italian Alps shaped the story early.

A foreword warns that one chapter rests on a real man's private notes. Those notes came to Thorne from a man of letters shortly before his death. Students of the drunkard's mind may trust the document as genuine, he says. Thorne thanks a doctor's study of drink and blood for backing his theme. The tale aims to show drink as a curse passed down through families. Its hero's fall is traced with that science in plain view throughout.
41216-sonnets-of-a-budding-bard:
Sonnets of a Budding Bard is a book of comic dialect verse by Nixon Waterman, with drawings by John Williams, published by Forbes of Chicago in 1907. Waterman's books listed here include A Book of Verses, In Merry Mood, and Boy Wanted. The sonnets are spoken by a schoolboy poet. Their contents titles keep his spelling: Lines Wrote in School Whilst I Shouldst Have Been Studyin' My Lesson.

Thoughts Thought whilst Thinkin' about Mary and Her Pet Lamb follows. Other sonnets treat how Pa acts when dressing up, kindness to dumb brutes, our parents in the Garden of Eden, and punishment received for lying. Peary is thought of on a hot summer day, and a Thanksgiving turkey gets its thoughts. The opening sonnet, preserved in the copy, declares the ambition.
41418-contraband-or-a-losing-hazard:
Whyte-Melville, author of 'Digby Grand' and 'Cerise,' wrote this novel, shown here in a London edition of 1871. Its first chapter, 'Rain-Clouds,' opens after a hunt, as Mrs. Lascelles rides home with Sir Henry Hallaton. She is a widow near thirty, fond of her horse, and just finding she may love something better than the horse itself.

The contents hint at the turns ahead: an alliance, Amazons, a kidnapping, a day in London and a drawn battle. Hunting, riding and country society give the book its ground, while love and risk supply the plot that his readers expected.
41820-the-champagne-standard:
Mrs John Lane wrote these observations on two great nations, England, America. John Lane printed The Champagne Standard in London in 1905. Her preface tells of a lead pencil bout with blank paper. A brisk fire, rain on Georgian windows, and sea roll frame it.

She was ordered to explain the liberty of her printed remarks. No ghost of an idea how to begin came to her there. An aged pair sang glory hallelujah in the narrow street below. Idle thought of tides struck motionless turned her mind at last. Kitwyk and Brown Retreat stand among her past books on the title page here.
42118-fragonard:
Fragonard is a small art book by Haldane Macfall in the Masterpieces in Colour series. Leman Hare edited the series, as its list page states for the volumes. The series assigns each painter a short life with colour plates of his works. Velazquez, Reynolds, Turner, and Romney stand at the head of its list.

Greuze, Botticelli, Rossetti, Bellini, Fra Angelico, and Rembrandt fill the list shown in this volume. Leighton, Raphael, Holman Hunt, and Titian stand there among the other masters of the set. Fragonard, the painter of The Swing and of the gardens of the French court, takes his turn in the series here. Macfall writes of the last great decorator of the old regime in France for general readers. The cheap colour volumes were the picture gallery of the Edwardian home, and this one hangs its Frenchman among Spaniards, Dutchmen, and Italians on the same small wall.
42247-nuts-to-crack-or-quips-quirks-anec:
Nuts to Crack; or, Quips, Quirks, Anecdote and Facete of Oxford and Cambridge Scholars was published at Philadelphia by Carey and Hart in 1835. The title page gives no name, only the author of Facetiae Cantabrigienses. The book is a jest-book of the two universities, and its preface is itself a performance.

The author promises a preface of a single page, in the much-in-little school, then doubts he has anything to say at all. He pictures the book's triumph: the sons of Oxford flying to the booksellers crying for the Book. Cambridge streets crowd at Deighton's and Stevenson's, and orders come thick as autumn leaves from Eton, Harrow, and Westminster. A togated son of Alma Mater thrusts it in his face, laughing, and stamps and laughs the while. The fantasy is the joke: a preface that sells the book by pretending all the world wants it.
42289-abbotsford:
Abbotsford, in the Beautiful Britain series, came out in London in 1912 from Adam and Charles Black. The slim book is a guide to the home of Sir Walter Scott in the Border Country. A gateway view serves as the frontispiece, and a dozen plates show the house and its setting.

Five chapters trace the place from the farm of Cartleyhole to the great house Scott built. One treats the creation of Abbotsford, one Scott at home there, and one his farewell. The text says crowds from all parts of the world visit each year, and the flow shows no sign of slackening. Scott came to the Border as a sickly child and spent most of his life there. His desk, chair, and sundial are among the sights.
42587-the-grey-friars-in-oxford:
Andrew G Little wrote The Grey Friars in Oxford, printed for the Oxford Historical Society at the Clarendon Press in eighteen ninety two. Little was a fellow of Balliol College, Oxford. Part one gives a history of the convent. Part two gives biographical notices of the friars, with appendices of original documents. A preface states the limits plainly. The work treats the outward life of the Franciscans.

That might include the whole activity of the friars save their scholastic philosophy, Little says, which forms a subject by itself. Even so, the account does not pretend to be complete, he grants. Documents do not cover the whole active life of the friars, he notes. For the thirteenth century and the Dissolution records are fairly numerous, but the intervening period is scanty. Scholars get a careful record based history of the Oxford Franciscans.
42960-rowlandson-s-oxford:
Rowlandson's Oxford, by Hamilton Gibbs of Saint John's College, is a book of Oxford life old and new. Kegan Paul printed it in London in 1911. A front view of Christ Church serves as frontispiece.

The first chapter sets the undergraduate then against the undergraduate now. Blissful ignorance and lonely freshers mark the opening scene. Two chapters then put the eighteenth-century fresher through his arrival. Footpads, a farewell to parents, and the advice of Terrae Filius greet him. Matriculation, the swearing-broker's fee, and the first night in garret rooms follow. The smart, the toast, and the servitor each get a chapter. The smart writes letters, drinks at coffee-houses, and runs on tick. The servitor runs errands and copies lines, as Whitefield and Wesley did.
43039-little-henry-and-his-bird:
A children's moral tale entered for copyright in 1851 at New London by John R Bolles follows little Henry into a garden. Henry took his book one day and sat where an arbor cast pleasant shade. He could smell the fragrance of flowers he himself had planted. At times he forgot his book, listening to the birds or gazing at peonies and tulips.

He was to recite in an hour, and had wisely chosen a comfortable place. He resolved bravely to conquer his lesson as soon as possible. A yellow cat watches as the tale proceeds. Such tracts taught diligence through small domestic scenes. The bird of the title draws Henry's wandering attention.
43079-the-boy-patrol-on-guard:
Edward S Ellis wrote this boys' tale, printed by the John C Winston Company of Philadelphia with a 1913 copyright. Edwin J Prittie drew the plates. Ellis had written the Flying Boys, Launch Boys, and Deerfoot series. He gives the book, without asking leave, to George Albert Hall, scout master of the Blazing Arrow Patrol, and to his nine named scouts.

Chapters train a tenderfoot: lost in the woods, a hermit, and how not to do several things. Two millionaires do a good turn. Gosling Lake hosts the camp, with a lesson in trailing and a bit of detective work. The story of Johnny Appleseed gets a chapter. Mike Murphy, a lad from the Launch Boys tales, walks into the story at its start.
43341-the-bird:
Jules Michelet wrote a warm study of birds, first issued in French in 1856 as L'Oiseau. The English form came out in London in 1868 with 210 pictures by Giacomelli. Michelet gave the book to his wife and called it one of three fireside books. The others treat insects and the sea.

The text defends birds and shows what they mean to human life. It blends close notes on habits with free, fond praise of flight and song. A note from the hand that turned it into English asks pardon for any loss of grace. Readers who like nature writing with heart will find much to hold them here.
43457-the-popular-story-of-blue-beard:
Blue Beard comes to young readers in a small book with neat engraved pictures. H and E Phinney printed and sold the tale at Cooperstown in 1828. The alphabet in full, in three styles, stands at the front for child readers. Fatima kneels to Blue Beard in the front plate as he lifts his blade.

Blue Beard is a rich man whose blue beard makes all the district fear him. He seeks a wife from two fair sisters who live far from his castle. Rich rooms, gold plate, and fine horses hide his cruel past. Children of the time got a famed tale of dread, nerve, and rescue.
44288-the-story-of-blue-beard:
The Story of Blue Beard retells Perrault's tale in a decorated gift book. Joseph E Southall supplied the pictures and ornaments. Lawrence and Bullen published it in London in 1895, with Stone and Kimball in Chicago. The tale opens with a rich man of fine houses and gilt coaches. His blue beard makes him so ugly that every woman runs from him.

A neighbour's two beautiful daughters refuse him at first. A week of hunting, balls, and collations at his country seat softens the younger one. His beard, she decides, is not so very blue. The marriage follows within the month. Blue Beard then leaves on a journey of six weeks. He gives his wife the keys to every store-room, chest, and casket. One little key he forbids her to use, on pain of his anger. The old tale's dread turns on that closet door.
44774-mamie-s-watchword:
Joanna Mathews's Mamie's Watchword, motto Thou God Seest Me, is volume five of the Little Sunbeams, published by Robert Carter and Brothers of New York in 1882. The series list prices each of the six volumes at a dollar, the set in a box at six dollars. Mathews also wrote the Bessie Books and the Flowerets, stories on the commandments.

Eleven chapters follow Mamie: the doll, the breakwater, forbidden pleasures, the duckling, and poor little Wagtail. The first step, disobedience, adrift, rescue, and repentance plot the small moral voyage. The opening chapter is a shop scene, Mamie pleading for the doll: can she have it, will Mamma buy it, not maybe, not see about it. The watchword of the title is the child's rule of life, that God sees her even when no one else does.
44783-the-seventh-regiment-a-record:
The Seventh Regiment is a regimental history by Major George Wood. James Miller issued it in New York in 1865. Its subject is the Seventh Ohio Volunteer Infantry. Wood's preface states his purpose plainly. He means to make a lasting record of the regiment. Its doings and sufferings deserve a separate history, he holds. Facts were hard to gather, since many men still served.

The book rests chiefly on the author's memory. A second preface vouches for his honesty and judgment. It asks if one regiment among thousands needs its own book. The volume itself is the answer offered. Such histories poured from the press as the war ended. Each regiment wanted its name kept green. Wood writes for the men and their home folk. Warren, Ohio, is the place of his preface.
45290-oxford:
Robert Peel and Minchin wrote the text of this picture book of Oxford, and Macmillan printed it at New York in 1906. A hundred plates in colour show the university and city. The writers state at the start that this is no formal guide.

Their aim is to show forth the chief charms of Oxford as painters have seen them. Short notes run with the plates, telling what counts in each scene. Facts rest on Chalmers, Lang, and Wells, the standard hands on Oxford. Most plates come from living artists, chief of them Matthison, with six from Ackermann's old Oxford. Walton, Tyrwhitt, Bayzant, and Cheesewright share the rest of the brush work.
46068-abbotsford:
Abbotsford is a picture book on the house of Sir Walter Scott, painted by William Smith and described by Crockett, minister of Tweedsmuir. It was published in London by Black in 1905. Twenty full-page illustrations in colour fill the book. The text is dedicated to Scott's successors at Abbotsford, his great-granddaughter and her son. The first chapter gives the scale of the shrine. In 1904 no fewer than seven thousand persons came there from all parts of the world, it says.

The plates walk the reader through the place and its country. The gateway, the garden, and Sir Walter's dial come in turn. His desk and elbow chair in the study are shown as he left them. Darnick Tower, Melrose Abbey, Dryburgh, and Kelso stand in the Border run. The Rhymer's Glen and the Eildon Hills close the tour. It is a pilgrim's book for Scott's land.
46186-germany-in-war-time-what-an-americ:
Mary Ethel McAuley spent two years in Germany during the Great War and wrote this account, published in Chicago in 1917. She dedicates the book to her mother, who shared those two years with her. A prefatory note says her first interest was art, and that she tried to write without fear or favor.

A plate at the front shows a child called Germany's youngest reserve. McAuley reports what an American girl saw and heard in homes, streets and public life under war rule. Food, schooling, talk and mood come through the eyes of a young outsider living inside the country.
4697-peter-bell-the-third:
Peter Bell the Third, by Miching Mallecho, is a satirical poem that takes its cue from Wordsworth's Peter Bell. Its epigraph asks whether a party in a parlour, crammed as on earth, sipping punch or tea, silent and all damned, describes the dead. Hamlet's line supplies the pen name's meaning: Miching Mallecho means mischief. A dedication to Thomas Brown, the younger, asks him to introduce Mr. Peter Bell to the respectable family of the Fudges.

The poem runs in seven parts, named Death, the Devil, Hell, Sin, Grace, Damnation, and Double Damnation. Its Peter Bell, the author says, may fall short of the Rat and the Apostate in active properties, yet surpasses them in intolerable dulness. Readers get a biting Shelleyan satire, for the poem is Shelley's own work under a mask, aimed at Wordsworth, Hunt, and the politics of poetry in its day.
47357-the-prairie-bird:
