Charles Augustus Murray wrote this frontier novel, published at London by Routledge with illustrations by J Zwecker. Its preface takes the odd form of a dialogue between author and reader, who begins by exclaiming that he hates a preface.

Murray answers that a good book needs none and a dull one cannot be mended by it, but the road ahead is long and the reader deserves warning. His chief aim, he says, is correct information about the North American Indians and those bordering on their territory, with incidents founded on actual occurrences. The reader recognizes him as the traveller who resided with the Pawnees and published his Travels in North America. One plate shows Monsieur Perrot scalped. Readers get a semi-factual prairie tale.
47788-motor-matt-s-triumph-or-three-spee:
Stanley Matthews wrote a weekly motor tale of Matt and his dire foes. Number eight came out on April 17, 1909, at five cents. Street and Smith of New York put the Motor Stories out. A plate shows Chub as he grabs a kill hand in time. That hand was raised to strike Motor Matt down in the tale.

White-caps and Matt's foes lead the list of parts. Shady acts and a vile plot build the knot in Dodge City. Matt hunts strife, and Higgins tells what he knows at last. Brisk work and a talk with Trueman fill the mid parts. Such weeklies gave boys a full thrill for a nickel. Fast wheels rule it.
47924-bob-the-story-of-our-mocking-bird:
Bob is the true tale of a pet mocking bird by the poet Sidney Lanier. First print came in eighteen eighty three, with a Scribner print of nineteen ten. Sixteen plates in hue show the bird through its short life. A front note tells how one of the poet boys took the bird in. The boy feared his find would not pass as fair cause to keep it.

Lanier loved long walks, bow sport, and horse rides through field and wood. That face to face life with wild things makes the sketch ring true. His flute would trill wild runs while the caged bird heard in hush awe. Each sign of mind, love, or pluck in Bob drew boy joy from the poet. Photos by Dugmore, hand toned, give the plates their rare base.
47930-brought-forward:
R B Cunninghame Graham published a volume of sketches first issued in 1916 and reprinted in 1917, dedicated to his brother, a naval commander. His earlier books are listed: Faith, Hope, Charity, Success, Progress, and Thirteen Stories. A journey in Morocco is announced in a new edition. The title sketch opens the contents. Los Pingos follows, then Fidelity.

Uno dei Mille, with the north east wind, and Elysium continue the list. Graham wrote of Scotland, Spain, and South America from long residence and travel. His sketches mix memoir, politics, and landscape. Duckworth published the volume at Henrietta Street. Graham's socialism and horsemanship both mark his prose.
47998-choffard:
Choffard is a monograph on the French book illustrator Pierre-Philippe Choffard, by Vera Salomons. Bumpus published it in London in 1912, in a series on eighteenth-century French book-illustrators. The volume carries twenty nine photogravures from negatives by the author.

Salomons opens with a challenge to the reader. You may never have heard of Choffard and never have seen his work, she writes. But if any production from his hand is set before your eyes, however small, and you fail to admire it, you confess that no artistic corner exists in your soul. Of all the vignettists, she declares, Choffard is the freshest, the most ingenious and the most charming. Little is known of the man himself, she admits: even his birth year is uncertain, 1730 against another authority's 1729. His tail-pieces for La Fontaine's tales of 1762 show his hand.
48260-geoffrey-the-lollard:
Geoffrey the Lollard is a historical tale by Frances Eastwood, author of Marcella of Rome, in a new edition from Shaw in London. Eastwood's preface names her chief authority: Fox, among whose horrors lie curious accounts of the doctrines of the so called Lollards. Their purity of life and love of the Bible, she argues, make their awakening the dawn of the Reformation.

Chapter one, The Church Underground, opens after sunset in a wild region of thick woods and rocky dells. Two lads lean against an ancient oak where three paths cross, waiting past the appointed hour for a man expected from Thomas Flynman's at noon. The elder fears discovery. Twenty three chapters follow, through a trial, hide and seek in Forest Tower, plots and counterplots, and a midnight supper.
48423-tales-of-english-minsters-hereford:
Tales of English Minsters: Hereford tells the story of Hereford Cathedral for young readers. Elizabeth Grierson wrote the volume, and Adam and Charles Black published it in London in 1911. Three illustrations in colour and four in black and white support the text. A view of the cathedral from the river stands first. Grierson had written The Children's Book of Edinburgh and tales from Scottish ballads.

The book belongs to a series, Tales of English Minsters. Sister volumes treat Durham and York. Lincoln, Ely, and St Albans stand in the publisher's list beside it. Each volume carries two full-page colour plates and four in black and white. The series aimed to give children the romance of the great churches. Legends, builders, and famous tombs supply the tales. Hereford's volume follows the pattern: the cathedral's long past retold as stories, with the building itself pictured from the Wye.
49740-orchard-and-vineyard:
Sackville-West published Orchard and Vineyard with John Lane in 1921. The Bodley Head issued the book in London, and Lane's firm in New York. Her earlier Poems of West and East is named on the title page. Some poems here first appeared in magazines and papers.

The contents fall into headed groups. Humanities opens with Mariana in the North, a lament for a woman outworn. Her hounds are dead and her lovers passed in the verses. A Home group gathers poems of place. Beechwoods at Knole and Leopards at Knole stand among them. Songs of Fancy and a Sailing group follow. War leaves its mark in A Fallen Soldier and Fallen Youth. The verse moves between moor, garden, and sea.
50148-looking-forward:
Looking Forward is a political dream by Arthur Bird, a former American vice consul general at Port-au-Prince. Its subtitle calls it a dream of the United States of the Americas in 1999. A preface submits the author's firm and immovable conviction. The United States will govern the entire western hemisphere, he holds. The Stars and Stripes will gather every nation under its folds. Every island in this hemisphere is included in that claim. Americans owe the southern republics their government, he argues.

The rule of the people under the great Constitution is his gift in mind. America holds an inviolable Monroe Doctrine today, he writes. Any European attempt on it would be promptly resented. The flag already protects every republic in the Americas, he claims. The book asks how many years will convince them to come under it. Bird's dream is annexation preached as destiny.
50418-the-romance-of-dollard:
Mary Hartwell Catherwood wrote The Romance of Dollard, in a seventh, revised edition from the Century Company. Francis Parkman wrote the preface. Rights pages date the tale to eighteen eighty-eight and eighteen eighty-nine.

Parkman calls Dollard's exploit one of the most notable feats of arms in American annals. Adam Dollard and the Huron Annahotaha were real men, he states. The heroine and Dollard's love affairs are the romance writer's own work. Chapters bring a ship from France, a Huron chief, and the heroes of the Long Saut. Jouaneaux, servant to hospital nuns, was also a real man. Sisters of the hospital appear under their true names.
50508-the-memoirs-of-admiral-lord-beresf:
The Memoirs of Admiral Lord Beresford record the life of Charles Beresford, a British naval officer. Methuen published the book at London, first in two volumes in 1914. A fourth edition in one volume followed in 1916, with twenty three pictures. Beresford dedicates the work to his brother officers of the Royal Navy.

The contents begin with a boy's first sight of the fleet. Early chapters cover his first ships, one of happiest and one of unhappy memory. A long cruise to the far side of the world fills several chapters, with Tahiti and old Japan. Politics enters with an Irish election and a seat for Waterford. The Egyptian war and the bombardment of Alexandria mark his middle career. The Sudan war of 1884 and 1885, with its desert marches and river boats, fills the later record.
50716-the-german-terror-in-belgium-an-hi:
The German Terror in Belgium, an historical record by Arnold Toynbee, was published at New York in 1917. Toynbee was a late fellow of Balliol College, Oxford. A map of the invaded country fronts the book. Chapter one follows the track of the armies across Belgium in 1914.

From the frontier the record moves road by road toward Liege. It names the Vise, Barchon, Fleron, Verviers, and Malmedy roads in turn. Then it crosses the Meuse and enters the city of Liege itself. From Liege to Malines come Aerschot and Louvain, names bound up with burned towns and shot civilians. Toynbee built his record from depositions and official papers. The book served as evidence and as argument, showing neutral readers what the invasion cost Belgian towns. It remains a stark document of the war's first months.
50988-bodyguard:
Bodyguard is a science fiction story by Christopher Grimm, with pictures, printed in a galaxy magazine in February 1956. Its head note sets the puzzle in plain terms. When danger hangs over a man at all times, of course he is entitled to a bodyguard. The annoyance was that he had to do the job himself, and his body would not cooperate.

The tale opens in a bar that serves all comers, human and not. A big young man there is fine looking to a fault, and well aware of it. A light haired girl at his side shares the glow, yet even she fades beside Gabriel Lockard. A plain man in a gray suit watches them from a corner booth. The folk of other worlds in the room are merely amused.
51170-the-fire-and-the-sword:
Frank Robinson wrote a tale of a fair world that drove a man to his death. The tale ran in Galaxy Science Fiction in August 1951. Emsh drew its pictures. Templin, the hero, straps in for a space flight at the start. Red glow fills the cab as the ship nears take-off time.

Sleep gas will let him sleep the dull star road away. Yet his mind turns to why men take their own lives. Ill health, debt, lost love, and shame all pass in his thoughts. The fair world at the tale's heart hides a worse cause. Its calm face makes the dark end seem to make sense. Mind tale fans get a grim, neat twist.
51318-the-prisoner-of-the-mill-or-captai:
Lieutenant-Colonel Hazeltine, the author of The Border Spy, wrote this Civil War tale, entered for copyright in 1864 by Sinclair Tousey of New York. The American News Company acted as publishers' agent. Chapter one, named for a brother and sister, forebodings, and Nettleton, opens with a cry against war itself. War, the page says, sums up misery: blood, broken hearts, and wasted homes.

The Army of the Mississippi, as it was called, had marched without success. It had pushed from Springfield, Missouri, down the Wilson Creek road to the field where General Lyon died. Finding no foe, it camped on Grand Prairie, west of that bloody ground, on tiptoe with expectation. Captain Hayward and his body guard carry the tale.
51344-voyage-to-far-n-jurd:
Kris Neville wrote this voyage tale for Galaxy Magazine's April 1963 issue, with art by Mack. Its blurb is grim: the crew would never live to see the trip's end. So they made a few changes in their way of life, and many in their way of death.

A gathering opens the tale, with rough talk and sharp manners. A crewman grumbles that they need not be here; the man they wait on is not liable to say a word. His wife hushes him while folk look on. I do not care a smidgen, he says. He aims to talk, and when he aims to do a thing he does it. Then the priest comes at last, and whispers fly: another delay, most like.
51363-double-standard:
Alfred Coppel wrote a tale of a man who buys a new face to reach space. The tale ran in Galaxy Science Fiction in February 1952. Kane comes past one in the night to a flat with care. The host checks the hall screen ere he lets Kane in. A rogue face man has made the host a new man in full.

He lacked the marks to fly, so he had them made, the blurb says. Kane's eyes go wide at the sight of the fresh face. Will it work, the host asks as he stands for a long look. Kane lights a smoke and grants it may, just may. A proud ship waits in the host's near thoughts. Crime and stars mix here.
52180-the-apple-of-discord:
Earle Walcott wrote this novel, drawn by Alice Stephens for Bobbs-Merrill. Grosset and Dunlap later sold the 1907 tale in New York. Chapter one presents the narrator with an overcoat at lunch. Colonel Kendrick, red whiskered, sits stunned for words across the table.

Kendrick command of speech had failed him, a rare thing indeed. The narrator suspects a hid purpose behind the kind invitation. Contents promise a house of blazes, a council of war, and deep market trouble. Big Sam diplomacy, a lottery ticket, and a call to arms follow.
5341-kilmeny-of-the-orchard:
L. M. Montgomery's Kilmeny of the Orchard tells of a girl found in an orchard, whose story unfolds among Prince Edward Island lanes and blossoms. Dedicated to the author's cousin Beatrice A. McIntyre, the book follows a young teacher who discovers Kilmeny, a girl who cannot speak, and learns the secret of her silence.

Montgomery, author of Anne of Green Gables and Rainbow Valley, writes a romantic idyll of music, orchards, and first love. Readers will find a gentle, lyrical novel, shorter and dreamier than Anne's story, in which a silent girl's voice becomes the book's central mystery.
53868-helen-ford:
Helen Ford, a novel by Horatio Alger, was entered for copyright in 1866 and issued at Philadelphia. Alger was the famed author of Ragged Dick and Luck and Pluck. His name promised readers a tale of striving in the city. The first chapter is called In Search of Lodgings, and it sets the scene at once.

Near Broadway, on a cross street in New York, stands a large lodging and boarding house. The house is far from fashionable and not inviting in its look. Into that world the young heroine must make her way. Alger builds his tales on pluck, work, and the help of true friends. A poor but honest youth rises by grit in his world. Helen Ford gives that pattern a girl at its centre, in the hard city of his day.
54452-the-bab-ballads-with-which-are-inc:
Gilbert's Bab Ballads, gathered here with his Songs of a Savoyard, come with 350 illustrations by the author in the Macmillan edition. The author's note tells the publishing tangle behind the volume: the ballads first appeared in the magazine Fun, then in two Routledge collections and a Fifty Bab Ballads selection. Readers kept missing favourites the editor had discarded, so the two early collections were reissued in one volume. The Savoy songs, drawn from the light operas, seemed kin enough to weld into the same book.

Gilbert also redrew some two hundred illustrations, judging the first ones too extravagant. The ballads are comic verse of the famous partnership's other half: nonsense situations handled with strict logic and a straight face. Songs of a Savoyard collects the opera lyrics separately within the same covers. The edition history runs from the 1904 transfer to Macmillan through reprints into 1960.
55535-mightier-than-the-sword:
Alphonse Courlander writes a press tale in Mightier Than the Sword, printed in London in 1913. Fisher Unwin made the book, first out in May 1912. Courlander had writ The Sacrifice and Eve's Apple. Four parts carry the tale: Easterham, Lilian, Elizabeth, and Paris.

The tale opens on a cold night in January. A little, stout man runs down the steps of a great building where The Day is jewelled in electric lights across the dark sky. He lands on the pavement as if to leap the roadway, then thinks better of it. A big lighted clock, its hands formed of the letters of the paper's name in red and green lights, shows nearly half past twelve. He starts off in terrible hurry towards Chancery Lane, as though pursued by some awful thing, and dodges a newspaper van at Fetter Lane.
55918-oxford:
Edward Thomas wrote the text for Oxford, published in London in November 1903 by the Black firm. John Fulleylove painted the pictures, which were engraved and printed in colour. Thomas says in his prefatory note that the chapters record his own impressions of the city. He drew on the histories of Parker, Maxwell Lyte, and Boase, and above all on Anthony Wood.

The chapters enter Oxford, study its stones, and look at dons ancient and modern. They compare undergraduates of the present and the past. The opening picture shows the Clarendon Building, raised from the sale of Lord Clarendon's History of the Rebellion. The book pairs a writer's memories with a painter's views, giving readers both the look of Oxford's streets and colleges and a sense of the life lived among them.
5671-the-visions-of-the-sleeping-bard:
Ellis Wynne's Visions of the Sleeping Bard is a seventeenth-century Welsh vision tale. Robert Gwyneddon Davies translated it from the Welsh Gweledigaetheu y Bardd Cwsc. It runs in three parts: the Vision of the World, the Vision of Death, and the Vision of Hell. A sleeper dreams his way through scenes of human life, then faces death and judgment, with notes and an introduction tracing Wynne's life and the book's history. The 1897 edition carries a frontispiece and family tables.

The visions work as both satire and sermon, since the dreamer watches pride, greed, and folly at work in ordinary life before seeing their end. Readers get a vivid picture of Welsh religious imagination, written in strong images rather than dry doctrine. It appeals to readers of Bunyan and Dante, and to anyone curious about how an older Welsh writer pictured the world, death, and what follows.
57539-cranford:
Mrs Gaskell wrote Cranford, her famed tale of a quiet English town. This drawn form came out in London in 1891 with Macmillan. Anne Ritchie adds a preface, and Hugh Thomson drew the plates. Ritchie recalls her father reading the tale in Household Words.

She names the tale of Captain Brown as one that moved them both. The book follows Miss Matty and her circle of town ladies. Small calls, gifts, losses, and gossip shape their gentle world. Gaskell writes with warmth and wit about pride, grief, and kindness in small town life.
57643-doctor-izard:
Anna Katharine Green writes a detective novel in Doctor Izard, from the author of The Leavenworth Case. Front pages list her works in a long run, with their prices in paper and cloth. The list is a mark of her fame in the trade by this time.

A Strange Disappearance and The Sword of Damocles stand in the run. Hand and Ring, The Mill Mystery, and Behind Closed Doors keep her name for crime. Shorter tales, X Y Z and 7 to 12, are billed as detective stories in so many words. Doctor Izard thus comes from a practiced hand at the puzzle tale. Readers who love the Leavenworth mode get a fresh case in her vein.
57718-index-of-the-project-gutenberg-wor:
Index of the Project Gutenberg Works of Frank Packard, compiled by David Widger, gathers the tables of contents of eleven of the Canadian crime novelist's books held by Project Gutenberg.

The volumes indexed are The Adventures of Jimmie Dale, The White Moll, Further Adventures of Jimmie Dale, The Miracle Man, The Night Operator, and The Belovéd Traitor. The rest are Doors of the Night, From Now On, Pawned, The Sin That Was His, and The Wire Devils. Chapter titles map each plot's movement, from the White Moll's underworld nights and alias Gypsy Nan to Jimmie Dale's diamond pendant and bond robbery. Compilations of this kind let readers survey a prolific popular novelist's output in one place and find the volume they want.
58163-index-of-the-project-gutenberg-wor:
Index of the Project Gutenberg Works of Henry Rider Haggard was compiled by David Widger. The volume gathers the tables of contents of Haggard books held by Project Gutenberg. It serves as a map to the adventure writer whole shelf.

The list opens with Allan Quatermain, Nada the Lily, When the World Shook, and Marie. Child of Storm, Finished, Montezuma Daughter, and King Solomon Mines follow. Queen Sheba Ring, Maiwa Revenge, Eric Brighteyes, and Morning Star stand in the mid list. Cleopatra, The Ivory Child, Elissa, Moon of Israel, and The Yellow God come in turn. Ayesha, She and Allan, Lysbeth, Doctor Therne, and Jess fill the later lines. Full chapter lists for each book follow the index. Haggard fans get a finding list for dozens of romances in one place.
59006-pogonologia-or-a-philosophical-and:
Pogonologia, or a Philosophical and Historical Essay on Beards, is a curious treatise translated from the French. Thorn printed it at Exeter in 1786, and Cadell sold it in London. Its motto comes from Montaigne: custom hides from us the true face of things. A letter to a friend stands in place of a dedication, praising plain homage over pompous titles.

The essay asks why we prefer the private life of a hero to the history of his great actions. The one gives a secret satisfaction in which self love finds its account, the writer says. The other produces only astonishment, for the hero stands too far from us. It is the man we seek, his heart, even his weaknesses. From such thoughts the book turns to beards themselves: their history, their meanings, and the customs of shaving and wearing.
60333-selections-from-the-writings-of-ki:
Selections from the Writings of Kierkegaard is a University of Texas bulletin of 1923, in its Comparative Literature series. The selections were translated by Hollander, a professor of Germanic languages at the university. The introduction calls Søren Kierkegaard the one Scandinavian thinker of the first magnitude. Yet he stayed virtually unknown to English readers, his works shut away by language and form.

The book aims to remedy that defect with pieces from his most representative works. It prints the Diapsalmata, the Banquet from In Vino Veritas, and Fear and Trembling. It also gives Preparation for a Christian Life and The Present Moment. The introduction notes his energizing influence on Scandinavian thought. It instances Ibsen's great ethical poem Brand, which owes its fundamental idea to Kierkegaard despite Ibsen's claim to have read little of him and understood less.
61349-frank-merriwell-jr-in-arizona-or-c:
Burt L Standish wrote Frank Merriwell Junior in Arizona, or clearing a rival record, a dime novel of the Merriwell line with copyright about nineteen twelve. Forty eight chapters fill the tale. Chapter one is A Slave of the Needle. Making a Raise and A Drugged Conscience follow. Blunt Takes the Warpath brings the rival camp in. A Surprise at the Gulch and The Revolver Shot raise the stakes.

A Blind Chase, Blunt Warning, and Accident or Treachery fill the early chapters. Desperate Work, The Saving Grace, and Blunt Surprise follow. The Race for Single Paddles brings sport into the mining tale. An Enemy Appeal, Taking a Chance, and The Yellow Streak deepen Lenning disgrace. Missing Bullion and The Finger of Suspicion set the mystery. Frank Merriwell Junior clears his rival name while winning the big game. Boys get mining, baseball, and morphine peril in one swift tale.
61911-the-oxbow-wizard:
The Oxbow Wizard, by Theodore Goodridge Roberts, was published at Garden City, New York, in 1924. Young Dan Evans lives on the Oxbow with his family. His Uncle Bill Tangler, his mother's brother, drifts in and out of the house. Dan's schooling came in scraps between his ninth and sixteenth years. Weather, roads, and home needs broke his terms. Chapter one is called The Stranger's Book. A sportsman from a far city spends one night at the farm.

Dan finds cigar butts and ash by the spare room lamp. Smoking in bed horrifies the household. Chapter heads promise a thief with claws, a fight in the snow, and fear of the law. Back country life, guiding, and boy adventure drive the tale.
6223-the-march-of-the-white-guard:
Field, chief factor at Fort Providence on Great Slave Lake, reads a letter by a frosty window and sends for Mr. Hume. The Hudson's Bay post stands at the edge of a white waste stretching toward the Arctic. The orders in that letter will send a small party out into snow and ice. Jaspar Hume keeps a diary of the march, writing with numbed fingers as the cold bites deeper.

Parker's short tale follows the White Guard as they dig a grave of snow for shelter and build fires at each end of it. Nights of silence by pine fires alternate with hard days of travel, hunger, and strain. It is a stark northern story, told through a diary's plain notes, about men holding together when the land itself seems set against them.
62320-the-life-and-surprising-exploits-o:
Jack Sheppard was a famed thief whose life is told in a cheap chapbook form. S and J Keys printed the short life at Devonport, with bold wood cuts. Sheppard was born in Stepney near London in the year 1702. His father, a carpenter, died while the boy was still too young to recall him.

Bound to Mr Wood to learn the trade, Jack at first won praise as a deft, sober lad. Love for Elizabeth Lyon, called Edgworth Bess, turned him to drink, theft, and flight. He beat his master, freed Bess from lockup, and stole cloth and goods. The tale warns how fast a bright youth can fall to ruin.
62652-tom-akerley-his-adventures-in-the-:
Tom Akerley is a boys' adventure novel by Theodore Roberts. Page of Boston issued it, with copyright in 1922. Its scenes are the tall timber and a river clearing. Gaspard's place on the Indian River is the hub. Ernest Fuhr drew the pictures. A frontispiece jokes about bear's grease and its smell. The contents open with The Flight. A girl and a man come in chapter two.

Catherine's plan drives the early plot. The heaviest hitter and Mick Otter follow. Black forests and grey swamps set the road scenes. Mick Otter turns match-maker near the middle. Roberts had written The Fighting Starkleys before. He knew the New Brunswick woods at first hand. Lumber camps and river drives fill his pages.
63176-buffalo-bill-s-girl-pard:
Buffalo Bill's Girl Pard is a dime novel by Colonel Prentiss Ingraham, published in New York by Street and Smith with a copyright of 1908. Its second title is Dauntless Dell's Daring. Ingraham wrote the celebrated Buffalo Bill stories of the Border Stories line. An appreciation of William Cody, the real Buffalo Bill, opens the book.

The contents promise the full dime-novel menu. A dastardly plot and foul play open the tale. A queer case, a saloon called the El Rio, and Little Cayuse on the warpath follow. An old shaft, an attack, and the worsting of red thieves raise the action. Dell of the Double D rides at the centre: treachery disclosed, a note and an arrow, and the scout's letter fill her chapters. Little Cayuse is caught and rescued. Dell, the girl partner of the great scout, was the heroine young readers followed through the yellow-backed weeklies.
64173-the-fatal-third:
Fatal Third is a science fiction story by Theodore L Thomas. It first reached print in a magazine called Planet Stories in November nineteen fifty three, the hosted note says. Its headnote sets a twenty first century where peace has had its fling. Now was the time for violence, it says. A rugged third officer and a race called the Uranians stand at its centre.

Hanford Webster, third officer of the space ship Polaris, is said to carry a first class jinx. The fleet nears its destination, Uranus, as the tale opens. In one instant nine of the ten Earth ships break up in space before his eyes. Twisted metal and frozen crewmen form a hideous cloud, the text says. His own ship, flying lookout behind, barely escapes.
64347-frank-merriwell-s-prosperity-or-to:
Frank Merriwell's Prosperity, or Toil Has Its Reward, is a tale by Burt L. Standish. It is one of the Merriwell stories and came out in New York in 1899 from Street and Smith. The scene of the first chapter is the stage of the Star Theater in Atchison, Kansas. Frank's company is at rehearsal for his new play, True Blue.

The play has been a success from its first night in the tale as told. The crowds of Puleob, Colorado, who saw its first form fail, took the new form with warmth. Roscoe Havener, the stage manager, has called the play a winner. Frank has now set his course back toward the East with his company, as the chapter When Rage Rules begins.
64747-the-enormous-word:
The Enormous Word, by William Oberfield, ran in Planet Stories in the summer of 1950. The headnote says blue men from space had ravaged Earth and cut one man down to the size of an insect. That man, Winston Eberly, now runs for his life.

Eberly dashes from tree to tree, crouching and scanning the sky for a glint of the foe. He is cut, thirsty, and half mad, but the box in his pocket keeps him going. The box holds U-235, the stuff he trusts to pull mankind out of its mess. The blue men had struck from far off with a ray that knocked out the world and killed many. That ray had hunted down refined uranium and blown it up wherever it lay.
65039-sir-isumbras-at-the-ford:
Sir Isumbras at the Ford is a tale of old days by Broster, put out at London in nineteen eighteen. Her past works, made with a next hand, are named at the front. The book is sworn to a maid and her son. A piece of the old rhyme tale of the knight of the name stands at its head. In that piece the knight lifts two young past a flood for grace.

The list of parts falls in two books. The first book bears the name of the road to France. A young man gets out of bed, and is put back once more, in its first parts. The buy of a gold fish, and more grave counts, come next.
65240-a-madman-on-board:
Robert Silverberg placed a short science fiction tale in the February 1958 issue of a magazine called Imagination. Dave Conroy wakes to find himself chained with a gang of rough men on board Earth Satellite V2-ZF. Through the dome he can see the green Earth far below. A bored voice orders the next batch inside.

Major Hawes tells the men their fate in plain words. They will feed active stuff to the power plant that keeps the wheel warm. The work will rot their bodies and kill them in a year or so. Conroy swears he is no criminal and that he never chose this duty. His mind is hazy, and even his past will not come clear. The tale turns on that fog in his head and on a doom he cannot recall earning.
65690-lair-of-the-dragonbird:
Lair of the Dragonbird is a science fiction story by Robert Silverberg, from Imagination magazine of December nineteen fifty six. Nobody on Venus knows if the dragonbird is flesh or a robot, the headnote says. Some men would kill to learn the truth of the creature. Dan Elliot has just bought his own spaceship after five years of payments.

The last payment leaves Elliot nearly broke in a cheap Venus City bar. A brawl breaks out when a scarred stranger picks a fight with him there. A flying table knocks him out cold in the middle of the melee. He wakes in a fine office, facing a fat man behind a gleaming desk. The man knows Elliot once saw the Dragonbird near the Temple of Light. He wants to know if the thing is a machine or alive.
65895-the-advanced-guard:
Sydney Grier wrote this novel, issued by Blackwood in a shilling edition of 1912. Grier had earlier written 'His Excellency's English Governess' and 'The Warden of the Marches' in the same vein. The book is third in the Modern East series, as its title page notes.

Lady Haigh's kind intentions open the contents, and an autocrat follows in chapter two. Colin serves as ambassador, an eye-witness speaks, and a prosecution arraigns a man in the middle chapters. The die is cast, and the party enters a terrible land of darkness in the list, before prisoners, fire and sword lead toward the right prevailing.
66312-earthmen-die-hard:
Earthmen Die Hard, a science fiction tale by Richard O Lewis, ran in the June 1954 issue of Imagination, a magazine of such tales. It opens with a young pair on a hill at night, watching a slim metal needle point at the sky, with only a few hours left to wait. Far above, a huge ship from beyond the Galaxy draws up beside the third planet of the sun and hangs by its lone moon.

Inspector Ryt looks through his lens and sees rows of lights on the night side, and worse lights that flare among them. He cries that the world is foul with germ life and at war with itself. His kind holds that such a world must be cleansed. The head note sums up the clash in one line: the aliens found that Earthmen die hard.
66833-stepping-westward:
Stepping Westward is a set of tales of Dorset folk by Francis, who wrote as the wife of a named man of that shire. A long list at its front names her past books of the north shire and the soil. It was first set in print in the first years of the last age.

Its gift word makes it out to a dear friend, a lady known and loved by Dorset folk of all ranks and all ages. A line from a famed ode of a bard is set as its plea: write me as one who loves his fellow men. Its tales then take a carters wife, a lone girl, and a girl on strike. A mans wee wife, burdens borne for each other, and a lads trek to a new land fill the run.
66928-the-ranger-boys-and-their-reward:
The Ranger Boys and Their Reward, a boys' adventure by Claude Labelle, was published at New York in 1922. It is one of the Ranger Boys series, written for boys of twelve to sixteen. Earlier books took the boys to rescues, hermits, border smugglers, and timber thieves. This one opens in the crude office of a lumber camp.

Garfield Boone tells his chums that all goes well at camp, so they may say goodbye and return to the West Branch. There they will resume their duties on the forest fire patrol. Dick Wallace, a heavy, good natured chap, sits quiet and resting while the others talk. Labelle's boys work in the Maine woods, guarding timber and fighting crooks as well as fires. The series mixed outdoor craft with mystery and chase. This volume carries the patrol through one more job and to the reward of its title.
6717-through-space-to-mars-or-the-longes:
Roy Rockwood, in his Great Marvel Series, sends two chums, Jack Darrow and Mark Sampson, from a laboratory table toward Mars. Jack asks for a test tube, large, to put plenty of chemical in for a good try, while Mark warns him of the last burst tube. Jack laughs at Mark's duck under the table; Mark notes Jack hid behind a chair.

From that comic lab start grows a voyage through space, the longest journey on record, with marvels and perils at each step. Rockwood writes for boys who love invention and daring. Through Space to Mars is a fun, early science tale, full of pluck, friendship, and starry wonder.
67611-the-old-card:
The Old Card is a tale by Roland Pertwee, out at New York in nineteen nineteen. The book is given to his son and to that sons godfather, a famed stage man. It stands in two parts, first a few parts and then a rough mix. Part names run past duels, a cure, sand traps of old ways, and a last drop of the stage cloth.

The tale opens as a great stage man steps from a first class car to a town stage. His dresser, who rode past the stop in the still car, holds his coach door with care. This star bears in his head the words and griefs of scores of great roles. Porters touch their caps, and the gate man waves him past with no check of his pass. Fame is his coin in the first scene.
67815-hilaria-the-festive-board:
Hilaria, or The Festive Board, is a book of mirth printed in London in 1798 for its author. Lines from Milton and Horace front it, one bidding mirth admit the writer to its crew, the other telling men to drive cares off with wine. Men differ in their notions of pleasure, the preface owns, but felicity is the aim of all.

Love and wine, happily blended, are named the summit of human enjoyment. The writer says so with triumph, from the experience of a laughing life. Songs, toasts, and tales for the table fill the book. It shows the drinking club culture of its day, when a festive board was a school of wit, song, and good fellowship.
68063-the-red-vineyard:
The Red Vineyard is a war memoir by Murdoch, who served as a chaplain with the Canadian forces in the Great War. It was published at Cedar Rapids, Iowa, by the Torch Press in 1923. The book is dedicated to the men with whom he walked the ways of the vineyard.

Some of those men, the dedication says, now rest in little green bivouacs in the shadow of small white crosses. The chapters are short and many. They take the reader from a training camp to a portable altar and mass said out of doors. Orders for France, base depots, hospitals, and trains follow. A transfusion, two brothers, and the ministering angels of the wards all appear. The vineyard of the title is the field of war, red with its cost.
68503-the-end-of-the-house-of-alard:
Sheila Kaye-Smith ends a line in The End of the House of Alard, printed in New York with copyright in 1923. Dutton made the novel. Kaye-Smith had writ Joanna Godden, Tamarisk Town, and Green Apple Harvest. A line of Chesterton fronts the book: we only know that the last sad squires ride slowly towards the sea, and a new people takes the land.

Four parts divide the tale: Conster Manor, Leasan Parsonage, Fourhouses, and Starvecrow. Part one opens on the family tombs. There are Alards buried in Winchelsea church. They lie in the south aisle on their altar tombs, with lions at their feet. At least one of them went to the Crusades and lies there cross legged. He was the first Gervase Alard, a man of mighty stature. Those were the days just after the great storm, when the sea swallowed the first parish church.
687-a-personal-record:
Joseph Conrad looks back on his own life in this memoir, from his youth in Poland to his years at sea and his turn to writing in English. He tells how a boy who read tales of travel grew into a sailor, and how that sailor later found his voice as a novelist. Friends, ships, ports, and first drafts all play a part.

Conrad does not write a straight life story. He dwells on moments that shaped him: a first voyage, a meeting, a book begun in doubt. His prose is rich and reflective, yet the facts stay close to home. The book gives readers the writer's own account of how a seaman from abroad became one of the great English novelists.
69698-the-war-against-japan-pictorial-re:
The Center of Military History issued this second edition in 2006 of the army's pictorial record of the war against Japan. The first printing of 1952 was among the first volumes of the United States Army in World War Two series. The text was written and the photographs compiled by Hunter and Tackley. More than five hundred pictures make the book.

The images freeze the soldiers, the weapons, the operations, the geography, and the tenor of the moment. The edition keeps every photograph, caption, and section introduction, but prints from new negatives for clarity. Outdated references were removed, and an appendix gives information on sources and photograph numbers for researchers seeking prints. The chief of military history commends the volume as proof of the determination, courage, and sacrifices of the American soldier. The official history here is a camera's history, chosen and captioned by the army itself.
70120-the-blackguard:
The Blackguard is a tale of a huge man of the Mounted Police. Roger Pocock wrote it, and it opens with a bugle song at dusk. The man sits on the bench land in the calm of the set sun. His build is that of a Greek god, with a hint of the faun.

His arms are as thick as the thighs of most men who sin. A grey slouch hat and a dry towel lie by his side in the scene. The smell of the horse lines hangs on him as he sits at rest. The whole force of five score men stands half in awe of him. One man alone does not fear him in the ranks of the force. No town man dared speak ill of him and keep his head whole. The nick name is worn as a badge of love, not of shame.
70156-the-house-of-the-wizard:
The House of the Wizard, by Taylor, was published in 1899. McClurg issued the romance at Chicago that year. Taylor had written On the Red Staircase before. A plate of Queen Anne Boleyn, after Holbein, fronts the book. Thirty one chapters make the tale. The Carews of Devon open it. A messenger from my lord privy seal comes early. The queen at Kimbolton and the wizard's visit follow. Mistress Betty goes to court at chapter ten. A precontract, Greenwich jousts, and a strange house by the Thames fill the middle. Love at the Traitor's Gate and a prince's baptism come late. The wizard in the Tower and the wizard's fate close the list. Chapter one sets the Carews' great house in Devon.

Mohun's Ottery stood at Luppit, built like a fortress.
70400-the-cheerful-blackguard:
Roger Pocock wrote this tale, printed in 1915. A jest at its front states the aim of the book in the voice of a clown. Good folk, it says, God alone can make you wise and kind. The part of the jester is just to make you laugh. The list of parts runs from the charm of youth through the age of knights, the swing of deeds, and the heats of war. A ship with no helm, a rite by pain, and the soul of La Mancha mark its turns.

The man who tells it names his self at the start of the first part. He is José de la Mancha y O'Brien, born on the ninth day of November 1865 in Spain. His mother was of Ireland and his sire of Spain. Ten years on, both his kin went to the serve of God.
70470-the-bodleian-library-at-oxford:
Falconer Madan wrote a brief account of the Bodleian Library at Oxford, first published in nineteen nineteen. Madan had served as Bodley's Librarian and was a fellow of Brasenose College. A notice to readers says the library was founded in sixteen two and ranks first among university libraries for size and worth joined. Readers are asked to use it for study and research, not for light ends.

Six parts trace the library from its kinds and roots to its modern ways. Sir Thomas Bodley and his foundation, from fifteen ninety-eight to sixteen thirteen, get a part of their own. Later parts treat the years to eighteen sixty, the modern library, and its manuscript treasures. A last part tells how students now work with its books and papers.
70579-the-philosophy-of-elbert-hubbard:
Elbert Hubbard's creed fills The Philosophy of Elbert Hubbard, printed by the Roycrofters with copyright in 1916. The edition runs to copies on hand made paper from Fabriano, Italy, stamped with the Roycroft mark. A front creed is headed An American Religion.

Work, play, breathe, bathe, study, laugh, live, love, the creed chants. No one can harm us but ourselves, it holds. Sin is misdirected energy, there is no devil but fear, and the universe is planned for good. Heads in the book treat freedom and responsibility, marriage and divorce, and the taxation of church property. Free motherhood, vaccination, and equal suffrage stand in the run. Why I Am a Philistine and a set of epigrams close the text.
71061-a-wilful-ward:
Ruth Lamb wrote A Wilful Ward, a tale put out in London by a tract group. Lamb had written tales of wives, choice, and girls in past years. A plate at the front shows a man who says he will not choose again, to Kathleen. The tale opens on the fourth of November, in rain.

Kathleen frets that rain will spoil her ride to the first hunt meet of the year. Her aunt tells her the rain is right for the time of year. The meet at Hollingsby is set to be the best in the county for years. The young earl has just come of age, and all wish to mark the day. Later parts bring Captain Jack, a steep price, and life under watch and ward. Faults, a first clash, and light at dusk shape the close.
71263-richard-richard:
Richard Richard is a novel by Hughes Mearns, published in London by Constable and Company in 1921. Mearns dedicates it to Lelia Cora of Petersburg, Virginia. The first chapter is headed Stony Broke, and the hero begins with exactly that much money.

Passengers pour off a steamer at Naples to do Vesuvius and Pompeii before the evening sailing. One angular man lounges on the starboard rail and watches them go. A lone woman passenger, clean-cut and tailor-made, whom he noticed boarding at Genoa, drifts up beside him. He does not know her name. He knows, instinctively, that he will borrow money from her. Shipboard etiquette ignores introductions, and by eight in the morning they are chatting like old companions over the Bay of Naples. The contents promise the comedy to come: an assistant widow, a lady detective, and love limericks of a left-tenant.
71923-the-will-to-live-les-roquevillard:
Henry Bordeaux wrote The Will to Live, or Les Roquevillard. Pitts Duffield translated the French novel. Duffield and Company issued it at New York in 1915. Bordeaux had written The Parting of the Ways. The Fear of Living and The House stand his. Three parts divide this family tale.

The Vintage opens Part One in the country. The Conflict and Lemenc's Calvary follow there. Mr Frasne's vengeance closes that first part. The Maker of Ruins opens Part Two in ruin. The Anniversary and The Return follow it. Part Three holds a family council. Margaret's Betrothal and The Defender build late. Jeanne Sassenay and the voice of the dead come. The Will to Live itself names the last chapter. Bordeaux wrote to Ferdinand Brunetiere of tradition. Tradition lives in the present from the past, he quotes. A Savoy family's fall and rise argues that roots, not revolt, save a house.
72028-mary-russell-mitford:
Roberts wrote Mary Russell Mitford: The Tragedy of a Blue Stocking, published in London by Andrew Melrose in 1913. The biography follows the author of Our Village from childhood onward. Photographs by the author and pictures of her day illustrate it. A frontispiece shows her cottage at Three Mile Cross.

Early chapters cover her days in Alresford and at Lyme Regis. School at Chelsea and the pull of Rowden's teaching follow. The family settles at Bertram House, then loses its fortune by slow degrees. Writing turns from pastime into serious, purposeful work. Her first book and a year of anxiety come in turn. Critics surprise her with an unmatched compliment. Literary friends crowd the later chapters. The book closes at the cottage shown in Our Village.
72274-a-song-bird:
A Song-Bird, by Eleanora Stooke, was published in London. The Religious Tract Society issued the tale there. Pearse drew the illustrations. Stooke had written Angel's Brother and Little Maid Marigold before. Eleven chapters make the story. Mavis and her mother open it. Miss Dawson, the Mill House, and a departure follow. Petty jealousy and Rose in trouble fill the middle. A great gift and Christmas time come next. Sickness at the Mill House darkens the late chapters. Happy days close the list. Chapter one sits in a dingy London lodging house. A September evening draws in by six o'clock. Mrs Grey finishes a grave letter at the table. Her daughter Mavis, ten years old, waits on a stool at her feet.

Mavis has hazel eyes and soft brown curls that will not stay tidy. Her mother is a widowed nurse.
72355-watch-and-ward:
Watch and Ward is an early novel by Henry James, published by Houghton at Boston in 1878. It first appeared in the Atlantic Monthly in 1871. James notes that he has now revised it minutely, with many changes of words. Roger Lawrence, its hero, had come to town for the express purpose of doing a certain act.

As the hour for action approached, Roger felt his ardour rapidly ebbing. Of the ardour that comes from hope he had felt little from the first. In default of hope he was sustained, James says, almost by despair: he should fail, he was sure, but he must fail again before he could rest. In the evening he dressed with a painful sense that he made a poor figure as a suitor.
72581-lady-molly-of-scotland-yard:
Baroness Orczy, the author of The Scarlet Pimpernel, wrote twelve tales of a woman detective at Scotland Yard. Cassell published the fifth edition in 1910, with sixteen full page pictures by Cyrus Cuneo. The teller is a member of the Female Department. She keeps the secret of her chief's past, though some say Lady Molly is a duke's daughter and others that she was born in the gutter.

The cases bear brisk names. They run from The Ninescore Mystery and The Frewin Miniatures to The Irish-Tweed Coat and The Fordwych Castle Mystery. A castle in Brittany, a Christmas tragedy, and a bag of sand fill later tales. The last treats the will of Sir Jeremiah and is called The End. The teller holds that women have ten times the insight of men, and that half the dark cases would clear if put to their test.
72689-border-guard:
Border Guard is a history of the United States Customs Service by Don Whitehead, published in nineteen sixty three. Whitehead was also the author of The FBI Story and Journey into Crime, as the title page notes. Contents open with a slight case of conscience and move to a time of crisis. Pirates of New Orleans and dark years follow in order.

Booze and bribes mark the Prohibition chapters in that list. The customs service guards ports, borders, duties, and smuggling, and its story runs from the young republic to the jet age. Whitehead writes popular official history, with cases and characters in the foreground. Smugglers and honest officers share the stage throughout.
72729-a-history-of-the-university-of-oxf:
Brodrick wrote this history of the University of Oxford in brief form. Longmans printed the fourth impression in London in 1900. Brodrick was Warden of Merton College when he wrote it. The book stands in an Epochs of Church History series run.

Creighton, Bishop of London, edited that series of small volumes. Sister volumes treat Cambridge, the Reformation, and the early church fathers. The preface calls Oxford among the oldest institutions in Europe. Its origin is uncertain, the preface owns at the start. Each series volume sold at two shillings six pence in cloth of the day.
73330-good-men-and-true-and-hit-the-line:
Eugene Manlove Rhodes wrote the western tales bound here as Good Men and True and Hit the Line Hard. Henry Holt held the copyright in nineteen hundred ten. Grosset and Dunlap later sold the pair in one cloth volume. H T Dunn drew the pictures.

Good Men and True opens on Jeff Bransford in a town office block. Thirty six years of sun and wind have tanned his face brown. He asks for a lawyer named Simon Hibler. Hibler has gone to Arizona near San Simon for rest. Bransford jokes that the man will bring back change. Rhodes fills his tales with dry humor and open range men. Readers who like short western tales with talk as sharp as action will settle in fast.
73547-the-case-of-charles-dexter-ward:
The Case of Charles Dexter Ward, a weird novel by Lovecraft, ran in Weird Tales in 1941. The May and July issues of that magazine carried the long tale. An editor note calls it the last, and many think the best, of his fantasies. Derleth and Wandrei pieced the scattered manuscript together after his death, it states.

Pages came from attics, forgotten strong boxes, and old bureaus over years of search. Readers would meet Cthulhu and the fearful Necronomicon again in these pages, the note promises. Charles Ward puts careful patience into terrifying researches of his own in the tale. Old Salem lore, grave robbing, and a changed young man drive the horror. Providence antiquarian dread stands at the centre of this longest of his tales.
74713-the-opinions-of-je-ro-me-coignard:
The Opinions of Jérôme Coignard brings Anatole France into English dress. Mrs Wilfrid Jackson made the translation for John Lane in 1913. Frederic Chapman shaped the set of France's works in English form. The book first sketches the life of the abbé Coignard himself. His pupil Jacques Tournebroche, the cook's son, tells that life tale.

Coignard taught speech craft, kept a bishop's books, and died in care of a great library. Then the Opinions give his talk on the world in short parts. Ministers of state, the army, schools, and justice all draw his fire. The Mississippi affair and Easter eggs take their turns in the talk. Sedition men and the writing of history close the long table. Dry wit, not rage, is the weapon of the old abbé.
75518-the-just-steward:
The Just Steward is a novel by Richard Dehan, author of other books named on the title page, issued at New York in 1922. Its contents divide the tale into four books with pointed names. They are The Seeking, The Sending, The Finding, and The Passing. A dedication looks to a day when all faiths shall merge in one faith.

A prefatory note by the author makes one fact plain. The work is fiction and its people are imaginary, with one exception. A camp commandant near Smyrna in 1917, whose activities are called sinister, is drawn from life. Care was taken to avoid surnames and titles of real persons, the note adds. The story opens in its first book with a city fair even behind trench and wall.
76223-when-oriole-traveled-westward:
Amy Bell Marlowe wrote this girls' novel, published by Grosset and Dunlap in 1921, a sequel to When Oriole Came to Harbor Light. Oriole Putnam, raised near Bahia in Brazil, is spending her first winter in Littleport, New England, and the harbor has frozen solid.

She frets for Uncle Nat's rheumatism and a friend's sore finger across the ice at Harbor Light, and takes to skates for the first time. The contents send her west: partings, a range camp, a spring round-up, a bear on the line, and twins in trouble. Marlowe wrote many series for girls. Readers get a plucky heroine traded from lighthouse ice to cattle country.
76477-skinny-mccord:
Percy Keese Fitzhugh writes a scout tale in Skinny McCord, printed in New York with copyright in 1928. Grosset and Dunlap made the book, with plates by Howard Hastings. Fitzhugh had writ the Tom Slade, Roy Blakeley, and Pee Wee Harris books.

Thirty four chapters fill a camp summer. Skinny loses something at the start, and shadows, dark plans, and stealth build the puzzle. Scout Law Number Two and The Pioneer Scout keep the scout frame. The Accused and The Masquerader raise the stakes for the camp. The tale opens at a camp fire in great excitement. Skinny has lost his compass, and all the boys make a show of help in the hunt.
76677-the-girl-from-scotland-yard:
The Girl from Scotland Yard is a detective novel by Edgar Wallace, printed at Garden City, New York, in 1928. It opens at tea, with Lady Raytham drawing aside long velvet curtains to look down into Berkeley Square. It is half past four on a cheerless February evening. Rain and sleet fall, and a thin yellow mist deepens the gloom.

Cars and taxicabs stream toward Berkeley Street, their black roofs shining under the new-lit lamps. Lady Raytham stares at the bare trees of the gardens as if she expects some fog wraith to take a menacing shape. The chapter titles map the mystery: the girl detective, a dead man, a doctor's confession, and a document. Later come an arrest, a trap, the telltale perfume, and a silk shawl. Leslie, the girl from Scotland Yard, works the case through them. Wallace was a master of the fast English thriller.
77032-the-garden-yard:
Bolton Hall wrote a handbook of close farming for McKay of Philadelphia, copyrighted in 1909. Hall had written Three Acres and Liberty before it. Nelson wrote the opening essay, and two farm men revised the text. A contents index at the front sorts the whole book by theme, so a reader can find any point at once.

The first chapter weighs how much land a man needs and what ownership is worth. Chapters on soil follow, its making, its texture, and how to get and hold moisture in it. Hall then treats what soil fertility is and how the national farm office can help. Seeds, plant breeding, and the needs of plants come in order. Light, lime, and plant foods are set out in plain terms. Brain work, not mere toil, is what makes a small farm pay.
77450-upward-and-onward:
Lucy Ellen Guernsey's Upward and Onward; or, the History of Rob Merritt was published in New York in 1856 by Anson Randolph of Broadway, entered the year before. Guernsey had written Irish Amy and Alice and Bessie. Twelve chapters, named by number alone, make the book, and a plate shows its hero answering, I have no work to go to.

Chapter one walks a village with its new minister. Mr Ellison has arrived in Grandville only the day before, and Mr Vanderburgh, a prominent member of his church, is pointing out the families house by house, with shrewd and amusing remarks. The aim under the kindness, the narrator notes, is to exalt Vanderburgh himself in the minister's eyes. The minister's eye stops at a poor-looking house his guide has passed over in silence.
77584-the-lass-of-the-silver-sword:
Mary Constance Du Bois wrote The Lass of the Silver Sword, held in 1908 and issued at New York in September 1909 by the Century Company. Du Bois had writ Elinor Arden, Royalist. Charles M Relyea drew the pictures. The book is given to Grace Winifred and Cecily Jean. Twenty seven chapters carry the girls camp tale.

A girl with ideals leads the plot at the Orioles Nest. A tornado, Castle Afterglow, and the Queen of the Silver Sword follow. Camp Huairarwee holds the summer scenes. The queen saves a halcyon's life in one chapter. Douglas Gordon, Jasper Brook, and a trail to the North Pole build the middle. A camp baby, a battle maid, and forest fire press the late plot. A coronation closes the tale of a girls order and its rites.
7853-quentin-durward:
Sir Walter Scott's Quentin Durward sets its romance in the fifteenth century, when feudal defense and chivalry began to fade before grosser men who chased private aims. Scott's introduction praises chivalry's generous, self-denying spirit, without which virtue itself seems hard to picture.

Chief among those who mocked such ideals stands Louis XI of France, purely selfish and guiltless of scruple, in Scott's harsh phrase. Young Quentin, a Scots archer trained in knightly honor, must navigate a king's cunning court. The novel remains a classic tale of loyalty tested by realpolitik.
79094-kitty-maynard:
Kitty Maynard was issued by the American Sunday-School Union. The Philadelphia house entered it in 1857. Its subtitle is a text: To Obey Is Better Than Sacrifice. Guernsey wrote it, the title page hints by her other works. Irish Amy and Ready Work stand among them. Seven chapters make the tale. Kitty, about thirteen, is being fitted with a white tunic. Huldah, tall and prim at fifty, does the fitting. She scolds as she works: Kitty goes to the country all summer. Aunt Sarah will keep her there, running wild in fields and woods. Boarding school would be far more sensible, Huldah holds.

Kitty answers that other things are learned besides book lessons. She is the only daughter of a merchant in a smaller New York city. Her mother, lovely and kind, has been an invalid for years.
8158-barlasch-of-the-guard:
Henry Seton Merriman's novel Barlasch of the Guard follows the Napoleonic wars through the retreat from Russia. Its chapters run from a summer's day and a campaigner, through the clouded moon, the shoemaker of Königsberg. And the way of love, to Borodino, Moscow, the ebb of the invasion, a forlorn hope, Kovno, Vilna, and the fulfilment. Barlasch himself, an old soldier of the Guard, stands at the story's centre, with Desiree and Mathilde choosing their paths through war.

Merriman writes historical romance with pace and feeling, letting great events press on private lives. The retreat, with its cold, hunger, and loyalty, gives the novel its sombre power. For readers of Napoleonic fiction, it is one of Merriman's best, and a stirring tale of soldiers and civilians in a collapsing empire.
8191-our-master-thoughts-for-salvationis:
General Bramwell Booth, head of the Salvation Army, wrote Our Master as thoughts for Salvationists about their Lord, dedicating the book to his wife. Its motto holds that as man he suffered, as God he taught. Chapters include The Man for the Century, The Birth of Jesus, Contrasts at Bethlehem, Christ Come Again. And The Secret of His Rule, each anchored in Scripture, from Luke's nativity to Paul on Christ formed in believers.

Booth writes for soldiers of his Army, plainly and devotionally, urging them to follow a suffering and teaching Lord. The book's directness suits its audience: short chapters for reading and preaching. For historians of the Salvation Army, it captures Bramwell Booth's theology and leadership, and the movement's Christ-centred piety.
9103-miracles-of-our-lord:
George MacDonald wrote these papers on the miracles of Jesus in 1870, at the request of friends. He treats each miracle as a mode in which Christ's unseen life found expression. Chapters cover healings sought and unsought, devils cast out, the dead raised, and nature ruled. The resurrection and transfiguration close the set.

MacDonald argues that through these deeds we may know God, since Christ is the Word of God. His tone is reverent and searching, not dogmatic. The book remains a thoughtful Victorian meditation on wonder, faith, and the life behind the stories.
934-songs-of-a-savoyard:
W. S. Gilbert gathered songs from his Savoy operas in this volume, under the name Songs of a Savoyard. The Darned Mounseer, The Englishman, The Disagreeable Man, and The Coming By-and-By head the set, with The Highly Respectable Gondolier and other favourites following in order.

Gilbert's lyrics, read without Sullivan's music, still sparkle with wit, rhyme, and topsy-turvy logic. The songs show his range, from patriotic choruses to sly character pieces. The book delights Savoy fans who want the words at hand, and readers who enjoy Gilbert's verse as comic poetry in its own right.
9409-five-thousand-dollars-reward:
Frank Pinkerton wrote this detective tale in 1886, opening at a country cottage near a village edge. A ragged, bearded tramp begs a drink from a pretty girl at the door. She fetches a pitcher, fills it at the pump, and notes his keen, unpleasant eyes as he asks after her household. She says she is alone, but a man named Ransom will come.

The tale builds to an arrest for the murder of Victoria Vane, as the title's reward implies. Pinkerton, of the detective family, writes briskly. The novel is a brisk dime-novel mystery, full of village suspense and sudden turns.
951-tom-swift-and-his-sky-racer-or-the-q:
A great prize for the quickest flight sets Tom Swift to work in this tale by Victor Appleton. Mr. Swift falls ill, the plans disappear, and anxious days follow, while Andy Foger vows to contest the race. Tom builds his Sky Racer in haste, through a trial flight and a midnight intruder.

The race itself tests speed, nerve, and fair play, as rivals try every trick to win. Appleton keeps the pace fast and the invention plausible, with Tom's skill at the fore. The book is a lively early aviation adventure, from the years when flight records were fresh news and every boy dreamed of wings.
9928-a-chair-on-the-boulevard:
Leonard Merrick's 1921 collection gathers short stories set in Paris, with an introduction by A. Neil Lyons. The title piece watches life from a boulevard chair, and the other tales visit cafés, theatres, and lodgings where small hopes meet hard luck.

Among them are the tragedy of a comic song, Tricotrin entertaining, a fatal flower, a café of the broken heart, and a conspiracy for Claudine. Merrick writes with sympathy for actors, dreamers, and the poor. Readers get Paris in miniature: witty, sad, and human, story by story, each one complete in a few pages.
a-chair-on-the-boulevard: Leonard Merrick gathers Paris stories around a chair on the boulevard. Its tales include a comic song turned tragic, a fatal flower, a cafe of the broken heart, and suicides in a dark street. Other pieces treat twins, a fairy poodle, a miracle in Montmartre, and the judgment of Paris. Merrick mixes humor, pathos, and irony in short stories of Paris life.
a-king-s-comrade-a-story-of-old-hereford: Charles Watts Whistler tells of a king's comrade in old Hereford. Wilfrid meets Ecgbert the atheling, an old acquaintance in Norwich, and the flint folk. He speaks with Ethelbert the king, whose journey begins with portents. Queen Quendritha weaves plots while Ethelbert travels to Sutton palace. The old tale moves at a brisk pace from court to marsh and town.
a-personal-record:
Joseph Conrad called this book of memoirs A Personal Record. It opens with A Familiar Preface. That preface weighs words, persuasion, and the hunt for the right word with the right accent. Conrad warns the reader not to expect a straight life story. The book grew from a friend's urging, and some friendly pressure. He writes about himself sideways.

In seven chapters he recalls his Polish boyhood under Russian rule. He recalls the uncle who guarded him. He tells of his choice to go to sea. His years in the French and British merchant services follow. Last comes the slow turn toward writing in English, his third language. Events surface out of order, as memory gives them. The record shows, in his own guarded way, how a sailor named Korzeniowski became the novelist Joseph Conrad.
a-splendid-hazard: Harold MacGrath opens this romance in Paris under a blurring rain, following chapters through a butterfly man, a plaster statuette, pirates and secretaries, and a woman who knew. M. Ferraud introduces himself, Cathewe advises, an admiral discloses and then doubts, and a captain meets a duke. Through sailing, cross-purposes, an old scandal, and the pines of Aitone, a splendid hazard plays itself out to the end of a dream.
across-the-zodiac-the-story-of-a-wrecked: Percy Greg tells the story of a wrecked record across the zodiac, deciphered, translated, and edited for the first volume, under a Courthope epigraph on a new world. The contents run from a shipwreck and the outward bound through an untravelled deep to a new world. Its language, laws, and life follow, with an official visit and escort duty. Faith and a founder, manners and customs, woman and wedlock, a country drive, and a river carry the record toward the children of light.
aristotle-complete-works-oxford:
Aristotle, Plato's pupil and teacher of Alexander the Great, wrote the body of works gathered here around 350 BC. The Oxford translation, edited under W. D. Ross, is the standard English Aristotle. The set holds 26 works drawn from the Internet Classics Archive at MIT, each by its noted translator.

The range is unmatched: logic, physics, metaphysics, ethics, politics, rhetoric, poetics, and a vast biology. His History of Animals alone fills a full study of creatures from direct observation. Aristotle built the first full system of Western thought, sorting every field into its own science. For two thousand years, students simply called him 'the Philosopher.'
barlasch-of-the-guard:
Henry Seton Merriman set this novel of Napoleon's Russian campaign in Dantzig, where old soldier Barlasch lodges with a shoemaker's family. Contents trace the arc of 1812 exactly: the clouded moon, the golden guess, Borodino, Moscow, then Kowno, the Warsaw road, and Vilna on the retreat. Desiree and Mathilde, the shoemaker's daughters, must each choose amid the wreck of the Grande Armée.

Barlasch, a campaigner of the Guard, carries the tale's warmth. Fumbling in his haversack with unsteady hands, he draws out a little square ikon wrapped in a Cashmere scarf. It travelled from Moscow with horseflesh and muddy roots. He offers it awkwardly to Desiree. Merriman writes the retreat through small loyalties: a despatches ride, a bargain, and its fulfilment on a bridge.
beethoven-the-man-and-the-artist-as-reve:
Ludwig van Beethoven speaks for himself in Beethoven, the Man and the Artist, a gathering of his sayings edited by Friedrich Kerst and Henry Edward Krehbiel. The edition was translated and published in New York in 1905. A brief sketch first outlines Beethoven's life, from Bonn to Vienna and deafness. His nine symphonies and thirty-two piano sonatas frame the man. Then the editors step back.

Quotations are sorted by subject rather than date. Beethoven discourses on art, nature, composing, and performing music. He judges his own works and other artists, sometimes sharply. Sections on education, character, and suffering show his pride and pain. Closing pages gather his worldly wisdom and his thoughts on God. An appendix weighs doubtful letters attributed to him. Readers hear a great composer's voice directly, irritable, funny, and unshakably sure of his art.
betty-at-fort-blizzard:
Molly Elliot Seawell published this army-post novel with Lippincott in 1916, after serial life as Colonel Fortescue's Betty. Betty is the colonel's daughter at a snowbound western fort, where her friend Anita comes down the stairs in the frontispiece to face Broussard and Mrs. Lawrence. Seawell, who wrote Papa Bouchard and Little Jarvis, knew service society and writes it from the veranda.

Gossip is the fort's nervous system. Sergeant McGillicuddy keeps the colonel informed of everything; his wife, a woman of great qualifications who would have made a good scout, keeps Mrs. Fortescue supplied from Major Harlow down to the smallest drummer boy. Mrs. Fortescue and Mrs. McGillicuddy are sisters under their skins. Balls, scandals, and courtships at the After-Clap's bedtime hour fill a tale of rank observed from both sides of the parade ground.
britannica-1911-abbotsford:
Abbotsford receives a house entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The house on the Tweed's south bank near Melrose was Sir Walter Scott's home and creation. Scott bought the small farm of Cartleyhole, nicknamed Clarty Hole, in 1811 when his Ashestiel lease lapsed.

Land bought piece by piece grew the estate, and the Scottish Baronial house rose from 1817 to 1824. Relics from old buildings, like the Tolbooth doorway, went into its walls. Fortune's fall in 1825 bound the estate in debt, cleared at last in 1847 by publisher Robert Cadell for a share of Scott's copyrights. Lockhart and Hope Scott held it after. The Abbotsford Club, founded 1834, printed history in Scott's honor till 1864.
britannica-1911-accord:
Accord, in law, is an agreement between two parties where one holds a right of action against the other. The 1911 Britannica entry defines it briefly: the parties agree to give and accept something else, some good legal consideration, in substitution for that right. The word comes from a French verb meaning to agree.

Execution completes the device. Once such an agreement is carried out, it discharges the original cause of action, so the old claim can no longer be pursued. In that completed form the arrangement bears the double name Accord and Satisfaction. Readers are given the core of a doctrine lawyers use to settle claims without a court fight.
britannica-1911-agobard:
Agobard (about 779-840) was a Carolingian prelate and reformer. He became coadjutor to Archbishop Leidrad of Lyons in 813. Leidrad's death in 816 made him archbishop. Nothing is known of his early life or descent. He continued his predecessor's vigorous church reform. Charlemagne had made Leidrad his active agent in it. Agobard opposed the empress Judith's schemes strongly. She sought redivision of the empire for Charles. He blamed those schemes for later evils.

Rebellion cost him his see briefly. Agobard supported Lothair and Pippin against Emperor Louis. The council of Thionville deposed him in 835. Peace with the emperor reinstated him in 837. His writings attack popular superstitions uniquely. He denounced trial by ordeal and witchcraft beliefs. Tempests ascribed to magic drew his scorn. Saint adoration also faced his logic.
britannica-1911-alcock-sir-rutherford:
Sir Rutherford Alcock (1809–1897) began as a doctor and ended as an envoy in the far east. A doctor's son from Ealing, he followed medicine himself. In 1836 he went as surgeon with the marine brigade that fought in Spain's Carlist war. Good service raised him to deputy inspector-general of hospitals before he quit in 1837.

Seven years on he was named consul at Fuchow in China, a port opened by the treaty of 1842. The post was brand new, and among the Chinese officers Alcock had to act, in his own words, as all things from a lord chancellor to a sheriff's man. A step up sent him to Shanghai in 1846, where he laid out the British settlement. In Japan, years later, his interpreter was slain at the legation gate in 1860, and ronin burst into the legation itself before he and his staff fought them off.
britannica-1911-alleine-richard:
Richard Alleine, an English Puritan divine who lived from 1611 to 1681, has a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Ditcheat in Somerset, where his father was rector, he was a younger brother of William Alleine of Blandford. He was schooled at Oxford, at Saint Alban Hall and then at New Inn. On ordination he became assistant to his father at Ditcheat.

His burning eloquence stirred the whole county from the start of his ministry. In March 1641 he became rector of Batcomb in Somerset in succession to Richard Bernard. He signed the Solemn League and Covenant and helped the envoys of parliament eject unfit ministers. He held Batcomb for twenty years in all. In 1662 he was one of the two thousand ministers ejected from their posts. The Five Mile Act then drove him to Frome Selwood, where he preached on in that district.
britannica-1911-allestree-richard:
Restoration honours came fast for Richard Allestree, the English clergyman. He became canon of Christ Church and Oxford's regius professor of divinity. Eton College took him as provost in 1665, and there he put its finances back in order. He died on 28 January 1681 and lies in the Eton chapel. His sermons and tracts are listed, with the disputed claim that he wrote The Whole Duty of Man.

War work had made his name before that. Through the Civil War years he ran despatches between the exiled king and royalists at home. In May 1659 he carried a command from Charles at Brussels telling surviving bishops to consecrate clergymen, lest the Church of England's succession die out. On one trip home he was seized at Dover and held at Lambeth Palace before release.
britannica-1911-arber-edward:
Edward Arber (1836– ) is an English man of letters. He was born in London in December 1836. An Admiralty clerkship occupied him until 1878. He then lectured on English at University College. Professor H. Morley was his chief there. In 1881 he became professor at Mason College. Birmingham held him until 1894. He then lived in London as emeritus professor. Oxford gave him an honorary doctorate in 1905.

His fame rests on scholarly editing. The English Reprints series is his monument. It ran from 1868 to 1880. Thirty volumes placed rare texts within public reach. Gosson's School of Abuse appeared there. Ascham's Toxophilus appeared there too. The English Scholar's Library followed it. Captain John Smith's Works featured in that series. His Stationers' Company transcript was a huge labour. It covered the registers from 1553 to 1640.
britannica-1911-arkwright-sir-richard:
Sir Richard Arkwright, an English inventor who lived from 1732 to 1792, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born at Preston in Lancashire, the youngest of thirteen children of poor parents. His schooling was poor. He learned the barber's trade, set up at Bolton about 1750, and made a little money by trade in human hair and a dye of his own.

About 1767 he gave up that trade to build a spinning frame. The spinning jenny of James Hargreaves could spin many threads at once, but its thread was too soft for warp. Arkwright's frame spun thread of any fineness and strength. In 1767 he hired John Kay, a watchmaker, to help make the parts. He took out his patent in 1769 and set the first model up at Preston.
britannica-1911-ashford:
Ashford is a place article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a market town in Kent. Ashford stands fifty-six miles south east of London, on a gentle rise near the meeting of the upper branches of the river Stour. Its population in 1901 was 12,808. It notes its Perpendicular church of St Mary and a grammar school founded under Charles the First.

The article mixes present business with old rights. The town has farm tool works, breweries, and the railway's locomotive and carriage works. The history traces the town from Domesday through grants of markets and fairs by three kings. Rich pasture in Romney Marsh built up the cattle trade, and a stock market opened in 1784. The article notes, as a point of pride or oddity, that the town was never incorporated.
britannica-1911-atkinson-edward:
Edward Atkinson, an American economist who lived from 1827 to 1905, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Brookline in Massachusetts, he spent many years running business ventures. In 1877 he became president of a Boston fire insurance company for mill owners. He held that post until his death.

Atkinson was a strong debater and a busy writer on money topics. He wrote on banking, railways, cotton making, tariffs, and the money question. In 1887 the state sent him to report on the use of two metals for coin in Europe. He also studied mill building and fire safety with care. His device, the Aladdin oven, improved home cooking. He backed the anti imperial cause with vigour. His books cover fire safety in mills, the spread of goods, and food science.
britannica-1911-aungervyle-richard:
Richard Aungervyle, known as Richard de Bury, an English book lover, writer, and bishop who lived from 1287 to 1345, has a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born near Bury Saint Edmunds in Suffolk, the son of Sir Richard Aungervyle. His line came from a soldier of William the Conqueror. His uncle saw to his schooling, and he went on to Oxford.

At Oxford Aungervyle is said to have shone in philosophy and theology. He was made tutor to Prince Edward of Windsor, the next Edward the Third. He is said to have passed his own love of books on to the prince. He was drawn into the plots that came before the fall of Edward the Second. In 1325 he sent funds from Guienne, where he was treasurer, to Queen Isabella and Mortimer in Paris, and then had to hide in Paris from arrest.
britannica-1911-award: Award, from an Old French word also linked to reward, means the decision of an arbitrator. An arbitrator is a person chosen to settle a dispute outside a court judgment. The very short entry gives that definition and its word origin. It then sends readers to the Arbitration article. That article gives the fuller account of how such decisions are reached and used.
britannica-1911-aylesford:
Aylesford is a town in Kent, England, standing at a hill's base on the right bank of the Medway, north-west of Maidstone, with 2,678 people in 1901. Its old church of St Peter mixes Norman and later work and holds brasses of the 15th and 16th centuries.

West of the town stand remains of a Carmelite friary founded in 1240. It is claimed, though not surely, as the first Carmelite house in England. The order held its first general chapter there in 1245. Nearby antiquities include Kit's Coty House, a stone tomb linked by tradition to Catigern, slain in a Briton and Saxon battle here in 455. The Countless Stones nearby owe their name to the belief that they cannot be counted.
britannica-1911-ayrton-william-edward:
Ayrton, William Edward (1847-1908), was an English physicist born in London and educated at University College there. In 1868 he went to Bengal with the Indian Government Telegraph department.
