Five years later he became professor of physics and telegraphy at the Imperial College of Engineering in Tokyo.

Back in London, Ayrton taught applied physics at Finsbury, then electrical engineering at the Central Technical College, South Kensington, from 1884. His many papers dealt chiefly with electrical subjects. With Professor John Perry he invented a long series of electrical measuring instruments, the work his name clung to. His wife Hertha, married in 1885, assisted his research and won fame herself for work on the electric arc.
britannica-1911-bache-francis-edward:
Bache, Francis Edward, was an English composer born in Birmingham. The entry's heading gives his years as 1833 to 1888. Alfred Mellon taught him violin. Sterndale Bennett taught him composition. From 1853 he studied at Leipzig with Hauptmann and Plaidy. He died young, of consumption, at Birmingham.

For so short a life his works are fairly many. They include two operettas, a piano concerto, piano pieces, and songs. The entry holds that these mostly show promise rather than fulfil it. His trio for piano and strings stands higher, still held in high esteem. The account then turns to his younger brother Walter, a fine pianist who studied with Liszt in Rome and worked for years to win English audiences for Liszt's music.
britannica-1911-bacon-leonard:
Bacon, Leonard (1802-1881), was an American Congregational preacher and writer born in Detroit, son of David Bacon, a missionary among Michigan's Indians. Educated at Yale and Andover, he became pastor of the First Church in New Haven in 1825. He held that famous pulpit until his death. He gave up active work only in 1866.

Called in jest the Congregational Pope of New England, Bacon swayed his denomination as editor as much as preacher. He ran the Christian Spectator. He helped found the New Englander and the Independent. The Independent was started to fight slavery's spread. In heated doctrinal fights, above all over Horace Bushnell's views, he worked for harmony, chairing great church councils with skill. At Yale he taught theology and American church history in his later years.
britannica-1911-baines-edward:
Baines, Edward (1774-1848), was an English newspaper owner and politician. He was born at Walton-le-Dale near Preston. Preston and Hawkshead grammar schools taught him. At sixteen he was apprenticed to a printer. He finished his training at Leeds and started business there.

In 1801 party friends helped Baines buy the Leeds Mercury. Provincial papers then carried little weight. Editors wrote no leading articles. Reporting was poor and defective. Baines changed both things at once. His strong political writing made the Mercury Leeds's Liberal voice. He backed parliamentary reform with ardour. His influence helped Macaulay win Leeds in 1832. Baines himself took the seat in 1834. He held it until 1841. He also wrote county histories and gazetteers.
britannica-1911-baker-sir-richard:
Baker, Sir Richard (1568-1644/5), was an English author. He was probably born at Sissinghurst in Kent. He entered Hart Hall, Oxford, in 1584. He left without a degree. Law studies in London followed. He then travelled in Europe.

Parliament took Baker in 1593 for Arundel. East Grinstead returned him in 1597. James I knighted him in 1603. He served as high sheriff of Oxfordshire in 1620. Marriage brought him into Mainwaring family debts. He stood surety for those debts. Ruin followed from that step. Creditors seized his Oxfordshire property in 1625. The Fleet prison received him in 1635. He died still confined in 1645. Prison gave him time for writing. His Chronicle of the Kings of England appeared in 1643. It stayed popular for many years. Its many errors give it slight value now.
britannica-1911-bancroft-richard:
Richard Bancroft (1544–1610) was archbishop of Canterbury, born at Farnworth in Lancashire in 1544. He studied at Christ's College and Jesus College, Cambridge, taking degrees in 1567 and 1570. Chaplain to the bishop of Ely and rector of Teversham, he rose fast on his ability and his zeal as a champion of the church.

Posts at St Paul's and on the church commission followed. The 1911 Britannica entry lingers on his sermon at Paul's Cross in February 1589, a fierce attack on the Puritans. He mocked their motives, denied the right of private judgment, and stated the divine right of bishops so strongly that a royal councillor heard in it a threat to the crown itself.
britannica-1911-bard:
Bard is a word of Celtic origin, in Gaelic baird, in Welsh bardh, naming the ancient Celtic poets. The title and the special privileges of that class of poets are found, so far as can be told, only among Celtic peoples. The name is sometimes used loosely for any poet, but the entry keeps the stricter sense.

Caesar never uses the word in his account of Gaul and Britain, though he seems to give the bards' functions to a branch of the Druids, a class close to them. Later Latin writers name the Bardi outright as the national poets of Gaul and Britain. In Gaul the order soon vanished under Latin and Teutonic conquest. The 1911 Britannica entry traces its survival in Wales, Ireland, Brittany, and the Scottish north, above all in Wales and Ireland.
britannica-1911-bargeboard:
Bargeboard is the name for the boards fastened to the projecting gables of a roof. Their job is twofold: to strengthen the gable edge, and to mask or hide the horizontal roof timbers to which they are fixed. The word probably comes from a medieval Latin term for a scaffold, and not from its old synonym vergeboard.

Such boards might be merely moulded, or carved, but as a rule their lower edges were cusped, cut into scallops, and their spandrels filled with tracery. The 1911 Britannica entry calls the richest example the board at Ockwells in Berkshire, moulded and carved as finely as if it were meant for indoor work.
britannica-1911-barnes-sir-edward:
Sir Edward Barnes (1776–1838) was a British soldier who entered the 47th regiment in 1792 and rose fast to field rank. He became lieutenant-colonel in 1807 and colonel in 1810, then went to the Peninsula on Wellington's staff. As a major-general he led a brigade at Vittoria and in the Pyrenees battles, earning the cross and three clasps.

As adjutant-general Barnes served in the campaign of 1815 and was wounded at Waterloo, collecting foreign orders for his service. His link with Ceylon began in 1819; he governed the island from 1824 to 1831. There he built the great military road from Colombo to Kandy, made the first census, and introduced coffee growing on the West Indian system. He died in 1838, a year after winning a seat in Parliament.
britannica-1911-barnfield-richard:
Richard Barnfield (1574–1627) was an English poet, born at Norbury in Staffordshire and baptized on 13 June 1574. His obscure but close link with Shakespeare has long drawn students to him, and new finds about his life added interest. Until lately, the entry says, nothing whatever was known of his career, and his very existence had been doubted.

Dr Grosart's research fixed him as the son of Richard Barnfield and Maria Skrymsher of Norbury. His mother died bearing a daughter in 1581, and an aunt raised the children. Barnfield entered Brasenose College, Oxford, in November 1589 and took his degree in February 1592. He seems then to have left abruptly, without the master's degree, and is thought to have come to London in 1593. The 1911 Britannica entry builds his life from such recovered facts.
britannica-1911-bartholinus-gaspard:
Gaspard Bartholinus, also given as Caspar Berthelsen (1585–1629), a physician born at Malmö in Sweden, opens a family entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. A prodigy who read at three and delivered Greek and Latin speeches at thirteen, he studied at Copenhagen, Rostock, and Wittenberg and travelled through the universities of Europe. In 1613 he became professor of medicine at Copenhagen. After a dangerous illness he kept a vow and switched to divinity, becoming professor of that subject and a canon of Roskilde.

Descendants fill the second half. His son Thomas became professor of anatomy at Copenhagen and was noted for observations on the lymphatics, the vessels that carry lymph through the body. Another son, Erasmus, discovered double refraction in Iceland spar, the splitting of light into two rays in that crystal. A grandson, Caspar Thomeson, taught anatomy too and is linked with a duct of the sublingual gland.
britannica-1911-barton-bernard:
Bernard Barton (1784–1849), an English poet born at Carlisle, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica as the Quaker poet, a name taken from his parents' faith. After some time in business he became a clerk at Alexander's bank in Woodbridge, Suffolk, in 1809 and kept that post until his death. His first verse volume, Metrical Effusions, appeared in 1812 and brought him letters from Southey and a friendship with the poet Hogg.

Friendship with Charles Lamb defines Barton's later story. It began when Barton wrote to protest how freely Lamb had handled the Quakers in the Essays of Elia. When Barton thought of leaving the bank to live by writing, Lamb talked him out of it: “Keep to your bank, and the bank will keep you.” Barton's Household Verses of 1845 won him a Civil List pension. His daughter Lucy married Edward FitzGerald, the translator of Omar Khayyám.
britannica-1911-basedow-johann-bernhard:
Johann Bernhard Basedow (1723–1790), a German educational reformer born at Hamburg, the son of a hairdresser, is the subject of a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica biography. Educated at the Johanneum in Hamburg under the rationalist Reimarus, he studied theology at Leipzig but gave himself to philosophy, which first shook and then reshaped his Christian belief. Work as a private tutor in Holstein revealed remarkable gifts for teaching the young.

Chairs, clashes, and a great plan followed. Basedow taught at Sorö in Denmark from 1753 until his religious views cost him the post, then at Altona, where the orthodox clergy blocked his teaching. In 1768, influenced by Rousseau's Émile, he proposed a general reform of German schools and a training institute for teachers. Subscriptions let him publish his Elementarwerk in four volumes in 1774, a complete system of primary education meant to develop pupils' intelligence rather than drill them.
britannica-1911-bastard:
Bastard, from an Old French word explained as “pack-saddle child,” is a legal term for a person born out of legal wedlock, treated at length in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Roman law split such children into nothi, born in concubinage, and spurii. Both had succession rights through the mother. Germanic law took a different line. Only children whose parents matched in rank counted as legitimate, a rule aimed at purity of race, not morals. Bastards lost inheritance rights through the feudal period.

English law keeps the core of the article. There a bastard could inherit nothing, being treated as the son of nobody, filius nullius. He could gain a surname by reputation, and even be made legitimate by act of parliament. Royal bastards such as William the Conqueror escaped the usual stigma. The long second half follows poor-law rules on settlement, custody, and the father's forced share in support.
britannica-1911-bauhin-gaspard:
Gaspard Bauhin (1560–1624), a Swiss botanist and anatomist, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born at Basel, the son of Jean Bauhin, a French doctor who had fled his own land on turning Protestant. Gaspard studied medicine at Padua, Montpellier, and schools in Germany. Back at Basel in 1580 he took his doctor's degree and gave private lessons in botany, plant science, and anatomy. He then held chairs in Greek, anatomy and botany, and medicine, and served as city physician, rector, and dean.

Order among plants was his great aim. His Pinax Theatri Botanici of 1596, an index to the plant writings of Theophrastus, Dioscorides, Pliny, and later botanists, is called his most valuable work. It gathered the plant names of the old writers into one ordered list.  He also listed the plants round Basel and wrote a chief work on anatomy.
britannica-1911-baxter-richard:
Richard Baxter (1615–1691), an English Puritan divine, is the subject of the longest biography in this stretch of the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Dean Stanley called him “the chief of English Protestant Schoolmen.” Born at Rowton in Shropshire, he was poorly taught as a boy, then better served at the free school at Wroxeter. He was pushed toward court life in London against his will. He soon came home, set on divinity, and read hard at Ludlow Castle.

 His best-known book, The Saints' Everlasting Rest, came in 1650, and the entry says it will always win the grateful praise of pious readers. He helped bring about the Restoration in 1660 and settled in London. Churchmen and dissenters alike came to his funeral in December 1691.
britannica-1911-beard:
Beard, the hair of honour, is traced in a custom entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. In new usage the word names hair on a man's chin and cheeks. Shave the chin and what is left is called whiskers today. Hair on the top lip takes the name moustache in our speech. Old usage was far less strict in its split of these words.

Bearded races have held the beard in high honour at all times. It marks full manhood, for the lad and the eunuch lack it. A tug at the beard is pain and shame in one act. King John gave deep offence in Ireland by such a pluck. His host's men felt the slight as a blow to their name. David's men had their beards shorn by a heathen king in scorn.
britannica-1911-beecher-henry-ward:
Henry Ward Beecher (1813-1887) was an American preacher and reformer from Connecticut. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica presents him as son of Lyman Beecher and brother of Harriet Beecher Stowe. Amherst study gave him more self reading than class success, it says. Hard drill in speaking turned him into a fluent talker without notes.

A deep faith shift in youth set his path toward the ministry. Small Indiana pulpits came first, at Lawrenceburg and then Indianapolis. Bold preaching there drew crowds unused to churchgoing in a pioneer town. In 1847 he took Plymouth Church in Brooklyn, New York. That pulpit soon became a national platform for his voice.
britannica-1911-bell-henry-glassford:
Henry Glassford Bell (1803–1874) was a Scottish lawyer and man of letters born at Glasgow. Schooled there and at Edinburgh University, he fell in with the Blackwood’s Magazine circle of Hogg, Wilson and Moir. He edited the Edinburgh Literary Journal from 1828 and joined the bar in 1832.

Bell served Lanarkshire as sheriff-substitute from 1839 and as sheriff-principal from 1867, filling the post with marked success. His poems came out as Summer and Winter Hours in 1831, the best known treating Mary, queen of Scots. He also wrote a two-volume prose Life defending that queen, and he appears as “Tallboys” in the Noctes Ambrosianae.
britannica-1911-bellamy-edward:
Edward Bellamy (1850–1898) was an American author and social reformer born at Chicopee Falls, Massachusetts. He studied at Union College and in Germany, joined the bar in 1871, then turned to newspaper work in Springfield and New York. Three novelettes of his drew little notice.

Fame came in 1888 with Looking Backward, 2000–1887, a romance picturing a co-operative, half-socialist America. Readers took the book as a real programme, and Bellamy spent his last years pushing its ideas, which he called “nationalism,” as editor, lecturer and party man. A sequel, Equality, followed in 1897, a year before his death at Chicopee Falls.
britannica-1911-bellingham-sir-edward:
Sir Edward Bellingham (died 1549) was lord deputy of Ireland, son of Edward Bellingham of Erringham in Sussex. His mother came of the Shelley family. Bellingham fought as a soldier in France and elsewhere, then sat in parliament and on the privy council, and served in Ireland in 1547.

In May 1548 he went back to Ireland as lord deputy, facing a country in deep disorder. Bellingham crushed an O’Connor rising in Leinster, cleared the Pale of rebels, built forts, and made English power felt in Münster and Connaught. Headstrong and always at odds with his council, he was recalled in 1549, yet even a foe called him the best man of war seen in Ireland.
britannica-1911-beneke-friedrich-eduard:
Friedrich Eduard Beneke (1798–1854) was a German psychologist born at Berlin, educated at Halle and Berlin. He served as a volunteer in the war of 1815, studied theology under Schleiermacher, then turned to philosophy. English writers, and German followers of Kant such as Jacobi and Fries, shaped his thought.

Beneke’s books of 1820 and 1822 set his psychology against Hegel, then all-powerful in Berlin, and against Kant’s ethics. His lectures were banned there in 1822, a blow he laid to Hegel’s influence, and he taught at Göttingen until Berlin let him return. Made professor extraordinarius in 1832, he held that in sense-based psychology, psychology drawn from experience, lies the ground of all knowledge.
britannica-1911-benlowes-edward:
Edward Benlowes (about 1603–1676) was an English poet, son of Andrew Benlowes of Brent Hall in Essex. He entered St John’s College, Cambridge, in 1620 and afterwards made a long tour of Europe. A Roman Catholic in middle life, he turned Protestant in his later years.

Open-handed giving to friends and kin, and perhaps Civil War service, ate up Benlowes’s fortune, and he died poor at Oxford in December 1676. His chief work is Theophila, or Love’s Sacrifice of 1652, a divine poem in an odd three-line stanza, telling how the soul climbs by humility, zeal and contemplation. Butler mocked him, yet later editors reprinted Theophila and granted his piety its due.
britannica-1911-berkshire-thomas-howard:
Thomas Howard, 1st Earl of Berkshire (1587–1669), was an English nobleman, the second son of the 1st Earl of Suffolk. The 1911 Britannica entry traces his rise through court posts: master of the horse to Prince Charles, Lord Howard of Charlton and Viscount Andover in 1622, and Earl of Berkshire in 1626.

During the Civil War he joined the king at York, was captured at Watlington while raising forces in Oxfordshire, and was briefly held in the Tower. Sent to govern the Prince of Wales, he proved, in the entry's judgment, poorly suited to the post. Restored at the Restoration as a privy councillor, he died in 1669 and lies in Westminster Abbey.
britannica-1911-bickersteth-edward:
Edward Bickersteth (1786–1850) was an English evangelical divine, born at Kirkby Lonsdale. He worked as a solicitor at Norwich from 1812 to 1815. In 1816 he took holy orders. He became a secretary of the Church Missionary Society that year. In 1830 he accepted the living of Watton in Hertfordshire and resigned the secretaryship. He still lectured and preached for mission causes after that.

His books include A Scripture Help of 1816, translated into many European languages. His Christian Psalmody of 1833 gathered over 700 hymns. That book later grounded the Hymnal Companion of 1870, compiled by his son. The 1911 Britannica entry credits him with backing the Evangelical Alliance of 1845. He opposed the Tractarian movement strongly. He also helped found the Irish Church Missions and the Parker Society.
britannica-1911-biddeford:
Biddeford is a city in York County, Maine, on the Saco River opposite the town of Saco. It stands on the Atlantic coast, 15 miles south-west of Portland. The 1911 Britannica entry gives 16,145 people in 1900 and 17,079 in 1910. Many residents were foreign-born, mostly French Canadians. The Boston and Maine railway serves the city. Electric lines link it to Portland and Old Orchard Beach.

The city is chiefly a manufacturing centre, third in Maine in 1905. Water power from the river drives its mills. Cotton goods rank first among its products, well ahead of foundry work and lumber. Factory output rose 27 percent between 1900 and 1905. Granite quarries of fine quality also work nearby. Settlement began about 1630 under Richard Vines, first under the name Saco.
britannica-1911-bideford:
Bideford is a seaport and market town in Devonshire, England, in the Barnstaple parliamentary division. It stands on the river Torridge, three miles above its junction with the Taw estuary. Houses climb two hills rising from the river banks. A bridge of 24 arches, first built in the 14th century, joins the two parts of the town. The population in 1901 was 8,754.

Its trades include earthenware, leather goods, sails, ropes, and linen, plus ironfounding. The small harbour holds about 17 feet of water at high tide and dries at low tide. Anthracite and potter's clay are dug nearby. In the 16th century Sir Richard Grenville boosted its trade with America and Spain. Tobacco imports from Maryland and Virginia were then a noted line. Coasting trade later replaced that commerce.
britannica-1911-bignon-louis-pierre-edou:
Louis Pierre Édouard Bignon (1771–1841) was a French diplomat and historian. He was born on 3 January 1771, son of a dyer at Rouen. He had a good education, yet served the early revolutionary wars as a private soldier. In 1797 Talleyrand noticed his rare abilities and took him into diplomacy. Posts in Switzerland, Italy, and Berlin followed in quick order. By 1802 he was chargé d'affaires at Berlin.

He helped shape the Confederation of the Rhine from his Cassel post. After Jena he ran Prussian domains and finances for France. He held a like role in Austria after Wagram, then ruled French affairs at Warsaw. The 1911 Britannica entry ends with his great history of France under Napoleon. Its fourteen volumes, finished after his death, stay a prime source for the reign.
britannica-1911-bilfinger-georg-bernhard:
Georg Bernhard Bilfinger (1693–1750) was a German philosopher, mathematician, and statesman. He was born at Kanstatt in Württemberg, son of a Lutheran minister. He first studied theology, then turned to mathematics and philosophy. The writings of Wolff and Leibnitz shaped that turn. His 1725 treatise tried to join theology with Wolff's philosophy in clear form. It held nothing original, the 1911 Britannica entry admits, but it presented Wolff well.

Success brought him chairs at Halle and Tübingen in turn. In 1725 Peter the Great invited him to lecture at St Petersburg, on Wolff's advice. He was well received in Russia. Later posts took him back to German courts and pulpits. His other works treat the harmony of soul and body and the origin of evil. The second gives an account of Leibnitz's theodicy, the defence of God's goodness despite evil.
britannica-1911-bishop-stortford:
Bishop Stortford is a market town in Hertfordshire, England, on the Cambridge line of the Great Eastern railway. It lies on the river Stort, close to the Essex county boundary. Water links run to London through the Lea and Stort Navigation. Its urban district held 7,143 people in 1901. St Michael's church stands high above the valley. It is a fine embattled Perpendicular building with a western tower and spire.

The high school, founded under Elizabeth, educated the historian Sir Henry Chauncy. Cecil Rhodes was born in the town in 1853, the 1911 Britannica entry notes. Brewing, malting, coach-building, lime-burning, and founding fill its trade list. Horse and cattle markets there are called important. Before the Conquest the manor is said to have passed to the bishop of London, giving the town its name. Its supposed borough charter of 1206 from King John cannot now be found.
britannica-1911-blackmore-sir-richard:
Sir Richard Blackmore (about 1650–1729) was an English doctor and writer famed in his day for long epic poems. Born at Corsham in Wiltshire, he studied at Westminster and Oxford, taught school for a time, and took his medical degree at Padua. He then practised as a physician in London.

Because he backed the Revolution he was knighted in 1697 and served as physician in ordinary to William III and to Anne. His Prince Arthur appeared in 1695 and six more long poems followed. Creation (1712), meant to answer atheist writers and set out Locke's thought, won high praise from Johnson and Dennis. The entry judges all his verse dull, though Creation kept a place in collections of British poets.
britannica-1911-blake-edward:
Edward Blake (born 1833) was an Irish-Canadian lawyer and Liberal leader in Ontario and Dominion politics. The son of a Galway man who became chancellor of Ontario, he studied at Upper Canada College and Toronto, and was called to the bar in 1856. He became queen's counsel in 1864.

Elected to both the Dominion and Ontario parliaments in 1867, he led the Ontario Liberals and briefly served as the province's premier in 1871. He helped bring down Sir John Macdonald's ministry in 1873 and joined the Mackenzie cabinet. As minister of justice from 1875 he took the chief part in framing the act that set up the supreme court of Canada.
britannica-1911-bluebeard:
Bluebeard is the fiend of a tale by Charles Perrault, and the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica sets out the tale and its kin. He slew his wives and hid their corpse forms in a shut room. The tale was first put in print in a book of tales of past times in sixteen ninety seven. The core of the tale is a ban and a breach of that ban.

The wife is told not to open a set door in the time her lord is past the house. She breaks the ban and finds the grim truth in that room. A save at the last breath rounds out the tale. The same core is found in tale lore of more than one land, but no kin tale has won the fame of this one.
britannica-1911-board:
Board, an old English word for a plank of wood, is explained in a 1911 Britannica article. The word enters many joined terms for flat things made for set tasks. Such terms list drawing board, chess board, and cardboard. In book work, the stiff covers of a book are called boards.

Board was used early for a table, which gave phrases like bed and board. From table use came names such as Board of Trade for state groups. A third sense is edge or side, most of all the side of a ship. That sense gave seaboard, aboard, and overboard. Starboard, the piece notes, means the steering side of the ship.
britannica-1911-bolsward:
Bolsward is a town in Friesland, Holland, 6½ miles west-north-west of Sneek, with 6517 people in 1900. A steam tramway linked it to Sneek, Makkum, Harlingen, and Franeker. It first appears in records in 725, when it stood on the Middle Sea.

When that sea shrank back, a canal was cut to the Zuider Zee, and in 1422 Bolsward became a Hansa town. Its Great Church of St Martin, built 1446–1466, holds fine carving, a noted organ, and tombs of Frisian nobles. The Small Church, from about 1280, is the remains of a Franciscan house. A handsome Renaissance town hall of 1614–1618 is also praised. Trade in farm goods, spinning mills, and tile and pottery works close the account.
britannica-1911-bolzano-bernhard:
Bernhard Bolzano (1781–1848) was an Austrian priest and thinker who taught the philosophy of religion at Prague. Born in Prague, he shone early, was ordained in 1805, and took the university chair the same year. His lectures, arguing that Catholic teaching and reason agree fully, drew eager crowds of young thinkers.

Opposition grew anyway, and only the archbishop's shelter kept him in post. In 1820 he was accused of links to student revolutionary clubs and forced to resign. Rome condemned several doctrines drawn from his works, and he was suspended from priestly duties. He spent the rest of his life writing. His chief book, the Wissenschaftslehre (1837), set out a scientific method for the study of logic in four volumes.
britannica-1911-boppard:
Boppard is a town in the Prussian Rhine province, on the left bank of the Rhine, 12 miles south of Coblenz. It had 5806 people in 1900. It stands in the Rhine gorge, less hemmed in by hills than many gorge towns. That has made it a place to live as well as to visit. Old medieval walls still ring part of it.

Sights named include a parish church of the 1100s and 1200s and a Carmelite church of 1318. The old castle is now used as offices. The Marienberg monastery, founded in 1123, became a water-cure house in 1839, on a hill above the river. Founded by the Romans as Baudobriga, the town was a royal seat under the Merovingians and a free imperial city under the Hohenstaufen.
britannica-1911-borden-robert-laird:
Robert Laird Borden (born 1854) was a Canadian lawyer who led the Conservative opposition at Ottawa. Born at Grand Pré, Nova Scotia, on 26 June 1854, he was called to the bar in 1878 and became a leading lawyer in his home province. His rise in politics came late and fast.

In 1896 he entered the Canadian parliament for Halifax. He later lost that seat and was elected for Carlton instead. In February 1901, when Sir Charles Tupper resigned, Borden took over as Conservative leader in opposition. At the general election of 1908 he was returned once more for Halifax. The entry is short and stops at that point, giving schooling, the bar, and the steps of his political climb, and nothing of policy.
britannica-1911-bridgett-thomas-edward:
Thomas Edward Bridgett (1829–1899) was a Roman Catholic priest and writer on history, born at Derby on 20 January 1829. Raised a Baptist, he joined the Church of England at sixteen and entered St John's College, Cambridge, in 1847 meaning to take orders. Unable to sign the Thirty-Nine Articles, he left without a degree and became a Catholic in 1850, soon joining the Redemptorists.

After training at St Trond in Belgium and five years of theology at Wittem in Holland, he was ordained and returned to England in 1856. More than forty years of mission work in England and Ireland followed, with preaching in over 80 missions and 140 retreats, and a lay brotherhood of 5000 members founded at Limerick. His books treat the English Reformation, with lives of Blessed John Fisher (1888) and Sir Thomas More (1890) and a two-volume history of the Eucharist in Great Britain (1881).
britannica-1911-brocklesby-richard:
Richard Brocklesby (1722–1797) was an English physician born at Minehead, Somersetshire, on 11 August 1722. He was schooled at Ballitore in Ireland, where Edmund Burke was a schoolfellow, studied medicine at Edinburgh and graduated at Leiden in 1745. Made physician to the army in 1758, he served in Germany during part of the Seven Years' War, then settled to practise in London.

In 1764 he published Economical and Medical Observations, holding suggestions for better hygiene in army hospitals, the work his medical name rests on. Later years went wholly to private life, but his friendships light up the entry. He was warmly attached to Dr Johnson, offered him an annuity of 100 pounds for life about 1784 and attended his deathbed. In 1788 he gave Burke, an intimate friend, 1000 pounds and offered to repeat the gift yearly until merit was rewarded at court.
britannica-1911-brome-richard:
Richard Brome (died 1652) was an English dramatist who began as servant to Ben Jonson and owed much to his master. Jonson's mark shows in his plot building, his strongly drawn characters and the store of curious information packed into his plays. Service ripened into friendship, and Jonson's lines printed before The Northern Lasse in 1632, the play that made Brome's name, give most of what is known of his character.

Comedy was his whole gift, and fifteen pieces survive. Two sets of Five New Playes, one edited by Alexander Brome, hold ten of them, among them The Novella, Court Begger and City Witt. The Antipodes, The Sparagus Garden and A Joviall Crew, later revised as an opera in 1731, appeared apart. He also worked with Thomas Heywood on at least one play, a partnership the entry begins to record.
britannica-1911-brown-sequard-charles-ed:
Charles Edward Brown-Sequard (1817–1894) was a British physiologist and neurologist born at Port Louis, Mauritius, on 8 April 1817. His father was American and his mother French, yet he always wished to be looked on as a British subject, though his restless life showed his mother's nation's enthusiasm. He graduated in medicine at Paris in 1846 and returned to Mauritius meaning to practise there.

Practice there did not hold him. He went to America in 1852, back to Paris, then in 1859 to London as physician to the national hospital for the paralysed and epileptic. Five years of lectures on the nervous system drew wide attention. Harvard made him professor of physiology and neuro-pathology in 1864. He left in 1867, taught at the Ecole de Medecine in Paris from 1869, crossed again to practise in New York in 1873. Finally returned to Paris in 1878 to succeed Claude Bernard in experimental medicine.
britannica-1911-brown-thomas-edward:
Thomas Edward Brown (1830–1897) was a British poet, scholar and divine born on 5 May 1830 at Douglas in the Isle of Man. His father, the Rev. Robert Brown, held St Matthew's, a homely church in a poor district, and his mother was of Scottish parentage though island-born. Thomas, sixth of ten children, was two when the family moved to Kirk Braddan vicarage.

His scholarly father shared the boy's tutoring with the parish schoolmaster until, at fifteen, he entered King William's College, where his abilities soon declared themselves. At Christ Church, Oxford, his place as a servitor cost him humiliation he remembered all his life. Yet he won a double first and was elected fellow of Oriel in April 1854. After Dean Gaisford had refused him a senior studentship at his own college on the ground that no servitor had ever held that honour, a slight the entry weighs carefully.
britannica-1911-brunel-sir-marc-isambard:
Sir Marc Isambard Brunel (1769–1849) was a British inventor and engineer born at Hacqueville in Normandy on 25 April 1769. His father, a small landowner and farmer, meant him for the church. A taste for mathematics and mechanics turned him elsewhere, and he obtained a place in the navy, serving six years. Paid off in 1792, he found revolutionary France dangerous for a pronounced royalist and had to flee.

Reaching New York in September 1793, he practised as architect and civil engineer: land surveying and canal work first, a rejected ornamental design for the National Capitol, the Bowery theatre. Ingenious machinery for an arsenal and cannon factory he built there. Early in 1799 he sailed for England to lay plans before the British government, the crossing that opens his English career and the great works. The Thames Tunnel among them in his son's generation, that the entry goes on to tell.
britannica-1911-bulstrode-sir-richard:
Sir Richard Bulstrode is the subject of a life entry in the 1911 Britannica. He was an English writer and soldier from 1610 to 1711. He was the son of Edward Bulstrode, who died in 1659. He studied at Cambridge and then read law in London. He joined the army of King Charles the First in 1642. That was the year the Civil War broke out. In 1673 he became an agent at Brussels.

He was knighted in 1675 for his service there. He followed King James the Second into exile abroad. He died at Saint Germain in October 1711. He is best known for a book of memoirs. That book covers the reigns of both Charles kings. It came out in print after his death in 1721. He also wrote a life of James and a set of letters. Those letters report chief events in the Netherlands in 1674.
britannica-1911-burford:
Burford, a market town in Oxfordshire, England, is drawn in a 1911 Britannica place entry. It sits in the vale of the Windrush River, west north west of Oxford. Its broad main street slopes up from the stream to a ridge road. Its folk count for nineteen oh one was one thousand one hundred forty six. The church of Saint John the Baptist stands by the stream.

That church mixes old Norman bulk with fine late Gothic craft. A spire of light build caps its stout tower in sharp contrast. Homes on the High Street near all show great age. An old town hall and a crypt of early English work get note. Past tales span a church meet in seven oh five and a win by Cromwell in sixteen forty nine.
britannica-1911-burujird:
Burujird, both a province and its capital town in Persia, is covered in a place entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The province is ringed by Luristan, Nehavend, Irak, and Isfahan. It holds perhaps a quarter of a million people in all. The land is rich and grows much wheat, barley, rice, and opium.

The entry says grain output could triple if roads let growers ship it out. Four parts make up the province, from the town and its villages to nomad Bakhtiari land. The town itself sits in the fertile Silakhor plain at a high level. About twenty five thousand people lived there. Its shops made cotton cloth, carpet covers, and felt hats and caps. Post and telegraph offices served the town as well.
britannica-1911-bustard:
The bustard, the largest British land fowl, is treated in a 1911 Britannica article. It once ranged over open country from East Lothian to Dorsetshire. By the time of writing, the native race had been wiped out in Britain. The piece traces that loss county by county, with dates and sources.

In Suffolk the race ended in 1832, and on the Yorkshire wolds near 1826. The last known native birds were two killed in 1838 near Swaffham in Norfolk. A few hen birds had held on there for years with no cock bird near. On Salisbury Plain none had been seen since near 1810. Other counties lost the bird with no record kept.
britannica-1911-buzot-francois-nicolas-l:
François Nicolas Léonard Buzot, a French revolutionist who lived from 1760 to 1794, is profiled in this 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. Born at Evreux in March 1760, he studied law and was an advocate in his native town. In 1789 he was elected deputy to the states-general. There he became known for advanced opinions. He demanded that church property be nationalized and that all citizens may carry arms.

After the Constituent Assembly dissolved, Buzot returned to Evreux as president of the criminal tribunal. In 1792 he was elected to the Convention and sat with the Girondists. He proposed a national guard from the departments to guard the Convention against the Paris crowd. In the king's trial he voted for death, with an appeal to the people. Proscribed in June 1793, he escaped to Normandy and helped raise a federalist revolt.
britannica-1911-cameron-richard:
Richard Cameron (1648?-1680) was the founder of a Scottish religious sect, the Cameronians. That sect formed the core of the regiment of the same name in the British army. He was born at Falkland in Fife and schooled at the village school. His success there was so great that he was made schoolmaster while still a youth. In that post he fell in with the more fervent field preachers.

At their urging Cameron gave up his post and joined the household of Sir Walter Scott of Harden as chaplain and tutor. He refused to accept the Indulgence and joined the nonconforming clergy. He stirred the folk of the south counties to open protest against the new edict. The state then made armed meetings for worship acts against the law. Cameron took refuge in Holland for a time, then came back in the autumn of 1679.
britannica-1911-cardwell-edward:
Edward Cardwell (1787–1861) was an English theologian. This 1911 Britannica entry gives his scholarly career. He was born at Blackburn, in Lancashire, in 1787. He was educated at Brasenose College, Oxford. He took degrees there across more than twenty years. In 1814 he became one of the university's examiners. In 1825 he was chosen Camden professor of ancient history.

During his five years in that chair Cardwell published steadily. He edited Aristotle's Ethics for his students. He lectured on the coinage of the Greeks and Romans. In 1831 he became principal of St Alban Hall. He published a student's Greek Testament in 1837. He also edited Josephus' History of the Jewish War. His greatest work lay in English church history, though. He planned a full synodical history of the English church. Only parts of that great design were ever finished. His Documentary Annals of the Reformed Church appeared in 1839.
britannica-1911-carew-richard:
Richard Carew (1555–1620) was an English poet and antiquary. This 1911 Britannica entry gives his life and chief work. He was born on 17 July 1555 at Antony House, Cornwall. At eleven he entered Christ Church, Oxford. At fourteen he debated in public with Sir Philip Sidney. The earls of Leicester and Warwick watched that debate. From Oxford he went to the Middle Temple for three years.

Carew then travelled abroad before settling in Cornwall. His marriage in 1577 added the Coswarth estate to his lands. He served as high-sheriff of Cornwall in 1586. He sat in parliament from 1584, and served under Raleigh. In 1589 he joined the Society of Antiquaries. He was a friend of Camden and of Spelman. His great work is the Survey of Cornwall, of 1602. It still holds interest beyond its antiquarian value. It pictures the life of an Elizabethan country gentleman. He also translated five cantos of Tasso's epic.
britannica-1911-carlile-richard:
Richard Carlile (1790–1843) was an English freethinker and radical publisher. This 1911 Britannica entry tells of his prosecutions. He was born at Ashburton, Devonshire, on 8 December 1790. His father was a shoemaker of that town. Carlile was apprenticed to a harsh tinman as a boy. He then worked in London as a journeyman tinman. Reading Paine's Rights of Man made him an uncompromising radical.

In 1817 Carlile sold the Black Dwarf weekly all over London. He walked 30 miles a day to spread its doctrines. He printed 25,000 copies of Southey's Wat Tyler that year. His own Political Litany cost him eighteen weeks in prison. In 1818 he published Paine's works in full. For that and like publications he was fined £1500. He was sentenced to three years in Dorchester gaol. From prison he published his periodical the Republican. His wife continued it and was jailed in 1821.
britannica-1911-carlingford:
Carlingford is a small market town and port of Ireland. It stands in county Louth, on Carlingford Lough. Its population in 1901 was only 606. This 1911 Britannica entry describes its setting and remains. The town sits on the western shore of the lough. Carlingford Mountain rises 1935 feet behind it. The Mourne Mountains face it across the water in county Down. A railway links it to Greenore and Newry.

Carlingford was once a place of great importance. Numerous remains in the town attest that past. King John's Castle, of 1210, commands the lough from a rock. Castellated houses from the old wars also survive. A Dominican monastery was founded there in 1305. The town held charters from Edward II to James II. It sat in the Irish parliament until the Union. It even possessed a mint from the year 1467.
britannica-1911-carnot-sadi-nicolas-leon:
Sadi Nicolas Léonhard Carnot (1796–1832) is the subject of a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a French physicist, the elder son of Lazare Nicolas Carnot. Born in Paris, he entered the École Polytechnique in 1812 and left with an engineer's commission in 1814. His father's exile under the Restoration stalled his own career, and dull postings pushed him to resign and study on his own. He ranged across mathematics, chemistry, natural history, and even political economy.

Carnot's health broke under heavy study, and cholera killed him in Paris in August 1832. His single published work, the Réflexions on the motive power of fire, appeared in 1824 and holds only part of his findings. The entry ranks him among the most original minds in science, while noting that Lord Kelvin first showed the work's full worth in 1848 and 1849. Preserved manuscripts, printed by his brother in 1878, reveal how far his grasp of heat had run.
britannica-1911-castle-guard: Castle-guard is a short feudal law entry from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It names a duty laid on certain baronies under the feudal system. Those baronies had to supply knights to guard the royal castles, and the duty was split among their knights' fees. Great barons laid the same duty on their own knights. In both cases the service was swapped very early for a fixed cash payment, called castle-guard rent, which lasted into modern times.
britannica-1911-chandler-richard:
Richard Chandler, a British antiquary who lived from 1738 to 1810, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born at Elson in Hampshire in 1738. Winchester and two Oxford colleges educated him in turn. His first work gathered fragments of the minor Greek poets, with notes.

In 1763 Chandler published a fine edition of the Arundel marbles. It carried a Latin translation and many guesses at the missing text. The Dilettanti Society then sent him to explore the antiquities of Greece. An architect and a painter travelled with him on that mission. Their three years of work yielded two grand folios of Ionian antiquities in 1769. Chandler later held church posts and died a Berkshire rector in 1810. His travel books on Asia Minor and Greece won lasting use. He also wrote a history of Troy defending Homer's geography as accurate.
britannica-1911-chard:
Chard, a market town in Somersetshire, England, is described in a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. It stands on high ground near the Devonshire border, about one hundred forty miles west of London by rail. Its population in 1901 was 4,437. The town is ruled by a mayor, four aldermen, and twelve councillors.

The entry notes the cross shaped parish church of Saint Mary, of the fifteenth century, with a fine east window. Local trades include linen, lace, woollens, brass goods, and iron goods. Chard grew as a trade centre near a Roman road, and two Roman villas lie in the parish. The bishop of Bath held the town in 1086. A charter of 1234 made it a free borough, with each holding paying a small rent.
britannica-1911-charles-edward:
Charles Edward is a life story from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about the Stuart prince called the Young Pretender. Charles Edward Louis Philip Casimir Stuart was born at Rome on the thirty-first of December 1720 and died in 1788. He was the grandson of King James the Second of England. His father, the Old Pretender, named him prince of Wales at his birth.

The boy was raised at his father's small court in Rome. His governor was James Murray, the Jacobite earl of Dunbar, and his tutors were learned men. He soon spoke English, French, and Italian with ease. Yet the article notes that his English letters are oddly ill-spelt. In 1734 his cousin, the duke of Liria, passed through Rome on his way to war in Naples. He offered to take the young prince with him.
britannica-1911-chaumette-pierre-gaspard:
Pierre Gaspard Chaumette (1763–1794) is the subject of a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a French revolutionist born at Nevers. Until the Revolution he lived a wandering life, with a strong interest in botany. He was studying medicine at Paris in 1790. He became an orator of the Cordeliers club and wrote for the Révolutions de Paris without signing his work.

As a member of the insurrectionary Commune of 10 August 1792, Chaumette was sent to visit the prisons. He held full power to arrest suspects. He was later accused of a part in the September massacres. He proved that he had been away in Normandy at the time, overseeing a requisition of 60,000 men. The portion hosted here breaks off at his return, but it fixes his place among the loudest voices of the Paris Commune.
britannica-1911-chelmsford:
Chelmsford is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a market town in Essex, England, the county town. It stands in the valley of the Chelmer, 30 miles east north east of London by rail. Its population in 1901 was 12,580. The river links it with Maldon and the Blackwater estuary. The parish church of St Mary is a graceful Perpendicular building, largely rebuilt.

The town is the seat of the county assizes and quarter sessions, with a handsome shire hall. Its corn and cattle markets are among the largest in the county. A bronze statue of Lord Chief Justice Tindal, a native of the parish, stands by the corn exchange. Industries include farm implement works, iron foundries, engineering works, breweries, and corn mills. A race course lies two miles south. The entry traces the town's rise to its place on the London to Colchester road.
britannica-1911-chingford: Chingford is an urban district in Essex, England, in the Epping division. The short 1911 Britannica note sets it about ten miles north of London by the Great Eastern railway. Its count in 1901 was 4,373 people. The district lies between the river Lea and the west edge of Epping Forest. Its church of All Saints keeps work from early English and late Gothic days, and a famed half timbered hunting lodge of Queen Elizabeth stands preserved near a great oak.
britannica-1911-churchyard:
Churchyard is a piece of consecrated ground attached to a parochial church and used as a burial place. A cemetery, by contrast, is separate from any parochial church and belongs to a company or a local authority. Burial in churches or churchyards is linked in the entry to the custom of praying for the dead. In England, about the year 750, spaces by the churches were enclosed for those entitled to attend service there.

Every man has a common law right to burial in his own churchyard, or in the parish where he dies. Yet the ground is the parson's freehold, and he can deal with it in many respects as a private estate. Fees, rights of way and strangers' burials all raise disputes the entry works through. Scotland differs, since there the heritors must provide and maintain the churchyard.
britannica-1911-claparede-jean-louis-ren:
Claparède, Jean Louis René Antoine Édouard (1832–1870) was a Swiss naturalist, born at Geneva on 24 April 1832 to a French refugee family. From 1852 he studied medicine and natural science at Berlin under J Müller and C G Ehrenberg. With J Lachmann he studied the Infusoria and Rhizopods there, and in 1855 he accompanied Müller to Norway for reef observations. He took his doctor's degree in 1857 and became professor of comparative anatomy at Geneva in 1862.

Voyages to the Hebrides with W B Carpenter in 1859 and months in the Bay of Biscay in 1863 widened his field work. On Darwin's Origin of Species he adopted its theories and published valued articles on them in the Revue Germanique in 1861. Ill health sent him wintering to Naples, where two elaborate volumes on the Annelidae of the gulf attested his energy. He died at Siena on 31 May 1870, on his way home.
britannica-1911-clifford-of-chudleigh-th:
Clifford of Chudleigh, Thomas Clifford, 1st Baron (1630–1673) was an English lord treasurer, born on 1 August 1630 to an ancient family descended from Walter de Clifford. Educated at Exeter College, Oxford, and entered at the Middle Temple, he represented Totnes in the Convention Parliament and in the parliament of 1661. He joined the young men who sought power by attacking Clarendon, then offered his services to Arlington. Naval service in the Dutch war brought knighthood and a prize ship at Lowestoft in 1665.

Pepys called him a very fine gentleman, much set by at court for his activity and stoutness at sea. Offices followed fast, controller of the household, privy councillor, treasury commissioner and treasurer of the household by 1668. Clifford was an ardent Roman Catholic, a supporter of royal prerogative and of the French alliance. He favoured seeking French help to force Romanism and absolute government, the account breaks off in saying.
britannica-1911-cobden-richard:
Cobden, Richard (1804–1865) was an English manufacturer and Radical politician, born at a farmhouse called Dunford near Midhurst in Sussex on 3 June 1804. His family had lived in that neighbourhood for many generations, partly in trade and partly in agriculture, with a small hosiery manufacture once in Midhurst town. His grandfather was a maltster and chief magistrate there, energetic and prosperous. His father, forsaking that trade, took to farming at an unpropitious time and did not succeed.

His father died while Richard was a child, and the care of the family fell on his mother, a woman of strong sense and great energy. She left Dunford and returned to Midhurst after her husband's death. Educational advantages for the boy were not very ample, since the grammar school at Midhurst had fallen into decay. From his earliest years he was indefatigable in self-cultivation, the entry stresses.
britannica-1911-cock-edward:
Edward Cock (1805–1892) was a British surgeon and a nephew of Sir Astley Cooper. Through that link he joined the staff of the Borough hospital in London while still young. He worked thirteen years in the dissecting room there. In 1838 he became assistant surgeon at Guy's.

At Guy's he rose step by step. He served as surgeon from 1849 to 1871, then as consulting surgeon until 1892. He became president of the College of Surgeons in 1869. The entry praises his skill in anatomy and bold work in the operating room. It also notes his clear writing. He edited Guy's Hospital Reports from 1843 to 1849. His name rests most on an operation that opened the urethra through the perineum.
britannica-1911-cocker-edward:
Edward Cocker (1631–1675) was an English engraver who taught writing and arithmetic. His name lives in the phrase according to Cocker, drawn from a famed book of sums. He is credited with some fourteen sets of copy slips for learners. One set, from 1664, survives in the British Museum. Pepys spoke well of his skill in his Diary.

Doubt hangs over the famed book itself. Cocker's Arithmetick first appeared in 1678, after his death. It ran through about 112 editions in all. Augustus de Morgan argued in 1847 that the book was a forgery. He blamed the editor and publisher, John Hawkins. The entry agrees that proof looks strong. A weak book under a strong name, it says, pushed out better ones.
britannica-1911-codrington-sir-edward:
Sir Edward Codrington (1770–1851) was a British admiral from a family long settled at Dodington in Gloucestershire. Orphaned young, he was raised by an uncle. After a short time at Harrow he entered the navy in July 1783. He served on the American station, in the Mediterranean and at home. Lord Howe chose him as signal lieutenant on the Channel fleet flagship.

In that post he served in the Queen Charlotte at the battle of 1 June 1794. His notes on that fight hold great value for its history. Rank rose fast after that. He was post-captain by April 1795. Later he served off North America in the war years. He took the Mediterranean command in December 1826 and held it until his recall in June 1828. Two sons followed him into service.
britannica-1911-coke-sir-edward:
Sir Edward Coke (1552–1634) was an English lawyer born at Mileham in Norfolk on 1 February 1552. He went from Norwich grammar school to Trinity College, Cambridge. In 1572 he entered Lincoln's Inn and was called to the bar in 1578. His deep and exact learning soon won him a practice said to be without match.

High office followed in quick steps. He became recorder of Norwich in 1586 and recorder of London in 1592. That same year he was made solicitor-general. In 1593 he sat for his home county and served as speaker of the Commons. In 1594 he rose to attorney-general, ahead of Bacon. The later part of the entry turns to his clash with King James. The king sought to hold back a judgment in a church grant case. Coke resisted that royal pressure on the courts.
britannica-1911-colomb-philip-howard:
Philip Howard Colomb (1831–1899) was a British vice-admiral, historian, critic and inventor, son of a general. He was born in Scotland on 29 May 1831 and entered the navy in 1846. First sea service took him off Portugal in 1847. The Mediterranean followed in 1848. From 1848 to 1851 he served against piracy in Chinese waters.

War service filled the next years. He was in the Burmese War of 1852 and 1853. He joined the Arctic expedition of 1854. In the Russian War he served in the Baltic and at the attack on Sveaborg. Gunnery, signalling and steam tactics then took his skill. From 1868 to 1870 he commanded the Dryad against the slave trade. The later entry stresses his thought as much as his service. Study of how fleets are ordered and led marks his name.
britannica-1911-colston-edward:
Edward Colston (1636–1721) was an English philanthropist born at Bristol on 2 November 1636. His father was a Bristol merchant of good standing. Colston is thought to have spent some years in Spain as a factor. His family had long trade links there. Wine and oil trade from that link built much of his vast fortune.

On his return he settled in London and bent his mind to making money. In 1681 his father died, and Colston shows as a governor of Christ's Hospital. He gave to that school often and largely. That same year he took an active part in Bristol life. A sugar refinery drew his funds there. Later gifts to the city grew huge in scale. In 1708 he built and endowed a great school foundation at a cost of 41,200 pounds. School books for it, he ruled, must hold no trace of Whig views.
britannica-1911-congreve-richard:
Richard Congreve (1818–1899) was an English Positivist born at Leamington on 4 September 1818. He was schooled at Rugby under Dr Arnold. Arnold is said to have rated him above any other pupil. Congreve took first-class honours at Oxford and a fellowship at Wadham College. He taught for a time at Rugby, then came back to Oxford as a tutor.

A Paris trip after the revolution of 1848 changed his course. There he met Barthélemy Saint Hilaire and Auguste Comte in person. The Positive philosophy drew him in full. He gave up his fellowship in 1855 and gave his life to spreading that system. Work in Chapel Street, Lamb's Conduit Street, bears his lead. In 1878 he broke with Laffitte, Comte's named heir. English Positivism split on that break. He also rendered works of Comte into English.
britannica-1911-copleston-edward:
Edward Copleston (1776–1849) was an English bishop born at Offwell in Devonshire and schooled at Oxford. In 1797 Oriel College chose him as a tutor. In 1800 he became vicar of Saint Mary's, Oxford. As professor of poetry from 1802 to 1812 he won wide note. Clever literary judgment and sound Latin built that fame.

He served as dean of Oriel for some years, then as provost from 1814. Under his sway the college rose to rare prosperity in the first quarter of the century. In 1826 he became dean of Chester. A year later he was consecrated bishop of Llandaff. There he backed the new drive to restore the church in Wales. More than twenty new churches rose in his diocese in his time. Politics drew his pen as well. Two able letters to Sir Robert Peel close the list of his works.
britannica-1911-cord:
Cord is a length of twisted or woven strands, as the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica explains. In thickness it comes between a rope and a string, a smaller kind of rope. The word comes through French from the Latin chorda, the string of a musical instrument. From the use of a cord for measuring, the word is applied to a quantity of cut wood. 

The variant spelling chord, which reverts to the Latin form, is used in special senses. In physiology it names cord like structures such as the vocal chords in the throat. In mathematics a chord is a straight line that joins two points on the same curve. In music the word names several notes sounded at once in harmony, though in that sense it is in truth a short form of accord, for agreement.
britannica-1911-crashaw-richard:
Crashaw, Richard, is the subject of a 1911 Britannica life of an English poet. Born in London about 1613, he was called the divine by his fans. His father was a churchman famed for harsh anti-Catholic writing. Yet the son was drawn to Catholic prayer forms in his work.

He went to Charterhouse school, then to Pembroke College at Cambridge in 1631. He took his first degree there in the year 1634. Herbert's Temple, out in 1633, set his bent toward holy verse. The next year his first book of Latin verses came out in print. In 1637 he was made a fellow of Peterhouse at Cambridge. He grew close to the poet Cowley in that same time.
britannica-1911-creasy-sir-edward-shephe:
Sir Edward Shepherd Creasy (1812–1878) was an English historian born at Bexley in Kent. He was educated at Eton and at King's College, Cambridge, and became a fellow there in 1834. Called to the bar at Lincoln's Inn three years later, he worked as an assistant judge at the Westminster sessions court. In 1840 he became professor of history at the university of London. In 1860 he went to Ceylon as chief justice and was knighted.

Ill health forced Creasy home in 1870, and he died in London on 27 January 1878 after one more short stay in Ceylon. His best known book is Fifteen Decisive Battles of the World, first published in 1851 and often reprinted. He also wrote a history of the Ottoman Turks and a history of England. Other works cover the English constitution, invasions of England, and a novel called Old Love and the New.
britannica-1911-cromwell-richard:
Richard Cromwell (1626–1712), lord protector of England, was the eldest surviving son of Oliver Cromwell and Elizabeth Bourchier. He was born on 4 October 1626. He served in the parliamentary army and entered Lincoln's Inn in 1647. In 1649 he married Dorothy, daughter of Richard Mayor of Hursley in Hampshire. He sat for Hampshire in 1654 and for Cambridge University in 1656, yet lived quietly in the country.

Oliver had not prepared his son for rule, but the second protectorate recognized his right to name a successor. Richard became chancellor of Oxford in July 1658 and joined the council of state that December. Proclaimed protector on 3 September 1658, he was at first welcomed at home and abroad. Quarrels soon split the military faction from the civilians, and the officers resented a protector who was not general of the army. The hosted narrative follows that clash into the parliament of January 1659 and the army council's defiance that spring.
britannica-1911-crosby-howard:
Howard Crosby (1826–1891) was an American preacher and teacher born in New York City on 27 February 1826. He graduated from the University of the City of New York in 1844. He became professor of Greek there in 1851 and at Rutgers College in 1859. Ordained a Presbyterian pastor in 1861, he later served as chancellor of his university from 1870 to 1881. He was an American reviser of the New Testament and, in 1873, moderator of the Presbyterian general assembly.

Crosby spoke out on questions, urging excise reform, and backed better Indian policy and international copyright. He founded the New York Society for the Prevention of Crime and led it as president. His books include The Lands of the Moslem, a Bible Companion, and commentaries on Joshua, Nehemiah, and the New Testament. The entry closes with his son Ernest Howard Crosby, a social reformer shaped by Tolstoy and Henry George. Ernest led settlement work and fought child labour.
britannica-1911-cupboard:
Cupboard is a term entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It traces a piece of home furniture from an open shelf stand for cups. The first such stands showed off plate and cups for all to see. In time the word came to mean a closed store place with shelves.

The entry follows the shift from a loose piece to a fixed nook in a wall. In the age before last, homes prized stores of china and preserves in such nooks. Church store pieces for robes form a rare grand class of the type. The court type, a low sideboard with small doors, is named the oldest form. A plainer type for food stores is also picked out.
britannica-1911-elgar-sir-edward:
Edward Elgar is the subject of a life entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was an English composer born in Worcester in eighteen fifty seven. His father played the organ in a church there and helped run local music groups. The boy learned to play more than one instrument as he grew up.

The entry follows his slow rise through local posts as a band leader and organist. His big church work of nineteen hundred made his name at home and abroad at once. Later church works and songs kept that fame strong. He was made a knight in nineteen hundred and four. The entry ends with his first large work for full band of players.
britannica-1911-empson-sir-richard:
Empson, Sir Richard (died 1510), was a minister of Henry VII of England and a son of Peter Empson, a man of weight at Towcester. Trained as a lawyer, he soon did well in his profession. In 1491 he was a member of parliament for Northamptonshire and speaker of the House of Commons. Early in Henry's reign he joined Edmund Dudley in working the king's harsh tax system, and so became widely hated.

Empson kept the king's favour all the same. He was knighted in 1504 and was soon high steward of Cambridge university and chancellor of the duchy of Lancaster. His career ended with Henry's death in April 1509. The new king, Henry VIII, had him thrown into prison on a charge of constructive treason, and he was convicted at Northampton in October 1509. After attainder by parliament he was beheaded on 17 or 18 August 1510. His estates were restored to his elder son Thomas about 1513.
britannica-1911-estcourt-richard:
Richard Estcourt was an English actor of the late sixteen hundreds who began in comic parts in Dublin. His first London bow came in a play by a famed poet of the age, and he went on to take key parts at a great London house. He was the first to play famed comic roles in new hits of the day.

The 1911 Britannica entry calls him a first rate mimic and a great favorite in company off stage. He wrote plays of his own as well. One was a comedy of manners on a modish town man. The other was a short musical piece set between the acts of a main play. Short as the entry is, it gives his stage path, his best first roles, and his own works in one sweep.
britannica-1911-euler-leonhard:
Leonhard Euler, a Swiss mathematician, is the subject of a life story in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Basel in seventeen hundred seven, he was the son of a Calvinist pastor. His father had strong skill in maths himself and gave his son his first lessons. The boy was then sent to the university of Basel.

Geometry soon became his favourite study there, the entry says. His genius won him a high place in the esteem of Jean Bernoulli. Bernoulli was then one of the first mathematicians in Europe. His sons Daniel and Nicolas also held Euler in regard. He took his master's degree in seventeen twenty three.
britannica-1911-falck-anton-reinhard:
Anton Reinhard Falck, a Dutch statesman who lived from 1777 to 1843, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Utrecht, he studied at Leiden and entered the Dutch diplomatic service at Madrid. Under King Louis Napoleon he served as a senior foreign affairs officer. He gave up that post when France annexed the Batavian republic.

Falck took a lead part in the revolt of 1813 against French rule. He helped shape the new kingdom of the Netherlands that followed. As minister of education he rebuilt the universities of Ghent, Louvain, and Liege. He also ran the trade and colonies offices at the same time. In Holland he was called the kings good genius, until the king tired of his advice. As envoy in London in 1830, he saw that Belgium must split from Holland and resigned.
britannica-1911-fanshawe-sir-richard:
Sir Richard Fanshawe was an English poet and envoy who lived from sixteen eight to sixteen sixty-six. He was born in June of that first year and schooled in London. He read at Cambridge and at a law house, but law irked him. Trips to France and Spain made him a skilled tongue man.

He served at the court in Madrid, then joined the king in the Civil War. He wed in that time and went with the prince on his roams. Seized at a great fight, he spent his free years on verse. His turns of famed works from Spain and the south won high praise.
britannica-1911-fitz-neal-richard:
Richard Fitz Neal, treasurer of Henry the Second and Richard the First of England, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was also bishop of London in his career. He died in 1198 after a long life of service. His house was a great family of rule, tied in fate to three kings in a row.

Roger, bishop of Salisbury, founded the family rise as chief minister of Henry the First. Care of the treasury passed from Roger to his nephew Nigel, bishop of Ely. Stephen cast the whole family down in disgrace in 1139 for a time. Nigel backed the empress and won reward when her son Henry the Second took the throne. Nigel son Richard took the treasurer post in 1158 in his turn. He held it without break for forty years of service.
britannica-1911-fjord:
A fjord is a long thin arm of the sea that runs far inland, with steep cliffs on each side. The word is the Norwegian term in English dress. Such sea lochs, as they are called in Scotland, show traits that set them apart from all shore forms.

The 1911 Britannica entry parts a fjord from a river mouth in one sharp trait. A rock sill in shallow water bounds a fjord at its mouth. Past that sill the floor deepens for a long way before it rises once more. A fjord is thus a true rock basin drowned in sea water. The piece sets Scots fresh and salt lochs side by side to prove the shared shape, and ends at a giant fjord of Norway.
britannica-1911-flecknoe-richard:
Richard Flecknoe (about 1600-1678), English dramatist and poet, is best known as the target of Dryden's satire. He was probably English by birth, though one guess made him nephew of a Jesuit priest of Oxford. Most facts of his life come from his own Relation of Ten Years' Travels, letters written to friends and patrons. The first is dated from Ghent in 1640, where he had fled to escape the troubles of the Civil War.

In Brussels Flecknoe served the wife of Charles IV of Lorraine, who sent him to Rome in 1645 to get her marriage made lawful. There Andrew Marvell met him and mocked his leanness and his rage for verse-making in a witty satire. He then travelled in the Levant and crossed in 1648 to Brazil, which he described in detail. The entry follows his wanderings, his plays and poems, and the mocking fame that outlived his own work.
britannica-1911-fleming-richard:
Richard Fleming, who died in 1431, was bishop of Lincoln and founder of Lincoln College, Oxford. Born at Crofton in Yorkshire, he came of a good family and was educated at University College, Oxford. He became prebendary of York in 1406 and junior proctor the next year. About that time he was an ardent Wycliffite, winning people of rank to the reformer's side. Archbishop Arundel censured him for it. Later he turned into a firm opponent of Wycliffe.

Fleming was made rector of Boston in Lincolnshire before 1415 and consecrated bishop of Lincoln in 1420. He attended the councils of Pavia and Siena in 1428-1429 and spoke for his country and the papacy before Pope Martin V. To him fell the task of digging up and burning Wycliffe's remains. The pope gave him the see of York, but Henry V refused to confirm it.
britannica-1911-fleming-sir-sandford:
Sir Sandford Fleming (1827- ), Canadian engineer and publicist, was born at Kirkcaldy in Scotland on 7 January 1827 and emigrated to Canada in 1845. Great powers of work and care for detail brought him to the front. From 1867 to 1880 he was chief engineer of the Dominion government. Under his control the Intercolonial railway was built, and much of the Canadian Pacific. He retired in 1880 with a wide name in his field.

After retirement Fleming studied Canadian and imperial problems. He worked for the unification of time reckoning across the world and for a state-owned telegraph system through the British empire. In 1902 he saw the first link forged: the Pacific Cable between Canada and Australia. He had urged Federation in 1864-1867 and in 1891 attacked the Liberal policy of free trade with the United States. He cared deeply for education and became chancellor of Queen's University, Kingston, in 1880.
britannica-1911-flodoard:
Flodoard, a French chronicler who lived from 894 to 966, is profiled in a 1911 Britannica article. He was born at Epernay. He was schooled at Reims, in the cathedral school set up by Archbishop Fulcon. As canon of Reims, he was a favourite of two archbishops in turn.

While still young, he held a key post at the archbishop's court. Twice he was stripped of his benefices by Heribert, count of Vermandois. The cause was his steady stand against the count's plan. The count sought the archbishopric for his infant son. When Archbishop Artold won out in 947, Flodoard became his chief adviser for a time. In 952 he withdrew to a monastery. He spent his last years in writing and devotion. The article goes on to his history of the cathedral of Reims.
britannica-1911-fontaine-pierre-francois:
Pierre Francois Leonard Fontaine (1762-1853), French architect, was born at Pontoise on 20 September 1762. He came of a family in which several members had made names as architects. Leaving college at sixteen, he went to L'Isle-Adam to help with water works under the architect Andre. Andre let him study his plans and copy his designs, a kindness that trained his eye. In October 1779 he went to Paris to study under Peyre the younger.

At Paris Fontaine met Percier, and acquaintance ripened into a lifelong friendship and partnership. After six years he won second prize at the Academy for an underground chapel and was sent to Rome on a pension in 1785, Percier going with him. The Revolution drove Fontaine to refuge in England after his return. Under the Consulate Bonaparte employed him, and the entry follows the two friends into their fame as the architects of the Empire style.
britannica-1911-ford-richard:
Richard Ford (1796-1858), English author, wrote one of the earliest and best of travellers' handbooks. He was eldest son of Sir Richard Ford, member of parliament for East Grinstead and for many years chief police magistrate of London. His mother was the daughter and heiress of Benjamin Booth, a noted connoisseur of art. Ford was called to the bar but never practised. In 1830 to 1833 he travelled in Spain, spending much time in the Alhambra and at Seville, and Spain became his subject for life.

His first work was a pamphlet of 1837 on a war in Spain. After a winter in Italy, he began, at John Murray's invitation, his Handbook for Travellers in Spain. His name is chiefly tied to that book. He died on 1 September 1858, leaving a fine private picture collection. His entry stands in a file that opens with the bibliography of John Ford's plays.
britannica-1911-forrest-nathan-bedford:
Nathan Bedford Forrest, a South horse general, is the own subject of the main part of a shared page in the 1911 Britannica. The page first ends a life of John Forrest the explorer, then turns to him. Born near Chapel Hill in Tennessee in eighteen twenty one, he was the first son of his house. His father died in eighteen thirty seven while the house sat in Mississippi. Nathan then bore the weight of the brood on his young back.

No school taught him in form, the text says in plain words. He taught himself to a fair point and showed skill with sums. Horse and cattle trade in Mississippi filled his first work years. Slave trade and horse trade at Memphis came next in his path. In eighteen fifty nine he turned to cotton plant work to close the shown text.
britannica-1911-fort-edward:
Fort Edward is a place article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a village in Washington county, New York, on the Hudson river. The village lies 56 miles by rail north of Albany, mostly at the foot of a steep hill, where rail lines and the barge canal meet the river. Its people numbered 3,521 in 1900 and 3,762 in 1910.

Long before the village, the site was the Great Carrying Place, where Indian war parties portaged from the Hudson toward Lake George or Lake Champlain. A third fort of 1755, first Fort Lyman, took the name Fort Edward in 1756. In the War for Independence it was the base of General Schuyler against Burgoyne, and the killing of Jane McCrea nearby in 1777 roused many men to join the American army.
britannica-1911-foss-edward:
Edward Foss (1787-1870), English lawyer and biographer, was born in London on 16 October 1787. He was a solicitor by profession. On retiring from practice in 1840 he gave himself to the study of legal antiquities, the history hidden in the records of his own profession. His Judges of England, in nine volumes issued from 1848 to 1864, is a standard work. The entry marks it out for its accuracy and its wide research into the lives of the men who held England's courts.

Foss's Biographia Juridica, a biographical dictionary of English judges, appeared shortly after his death. He helped found the Incorporated Law Society and served as its president in 1842 and 1843. The short entry is a plain record of a working lawyer who spent his retirement writing the history of his profession's bench. He died of apoplexy on 27 July 1870, with his dictionary still in the press.
britannica-1911-fowler-edward:
Edward Fowler (1632-1714), English divine, was born in 1632 at Westerleigh in Gloucestershire. He was educated at Corpus Christi College, Oxford, and afterwards moved to Trinity College, Cambridge. He became rector of Norhill in Bedfordshire in 1656 and of All Hallows, Bread Street, London, in 1673. In 1676 he was elected a canon of Gloucester. His friend Henry More, the Cambridge Platonist, resigned the post in his favour.

In 1681 Fowler became vicar of St Giles, Cripplegate, but after four years he was suspended for Whiggism. When the Declaration of Indulgence came out in 1687 he successfully turned the London clergy against reading it. In 1691 he was consecrated bishop of Gloucester and held the see until his death on 26 August 1714. He was suspected of Pelagian leanings, and his first book defended the practices of certain moderate divines against their critics.
britannica-1911-fox-edward:
Edward Fox (about 1496-1538), bishop of Hereford, was born about 1496 at Dursley in Gloucestershire. He is said, on very doubtful authority, to have been kin to Bishop Richard Fox. From Eton he went to King's College, Cambridge, and after graduating became secretary to Wolsey. In 1528 he was sent with Gardiner to Rome. Their errand was to get from Clement VII a decretal commission for trying the case between Henry VIII and Catherine of Aragon, the king's great matter of divorce.

On his return Fox was elected provost of King's College. In August 1529 he carried to the king Cranmer's famous advice: to ask the universities of Europe, rather than the pope, about the divorce. That introduction in time raised Cranmer, over Fox's head, to Canterbury. After a short mission to Paris, Fox befriended Latimer in January 1530. The entry follows one of the quiet agents who set England's break with Rome in motion.
britannica-1911-fox-richard:
Richard Fox (about 1448-1528) was bishop in turn of Exeter, Bath and Wells, Durham and Winchester, lord privy seal, and founder of Corpus Christi College, Oxford. He was born about 1448 at Ropesley near Grantham in Lincolnshire, of yeoman parents. His schooling is obscure: Magdalen College, Oxford is the likely guess, since he drew so many of his college's first men from there. He also seems to have studied at Cambridge. Nothing definite is known of his first thirty-five years, a rare blank in so public a life.
