In 1484 Fox was in Paris, whether for learning or because he had offended Richard III is speculation. There he met the earl of Richmond, the future Henry VII, at the start of that prince's rise. The long entry follows the bishop through forty years of Tudor service. It ends with his Oxford college, the work by which students still know his name.
britannica-1911-frere-sir-henry-bartle-e:
Sir Henry Bartle Edward Frere (1815-1884), British administrator, was born at Clydach in Brecknockshire on 29 March 1815, nephew of John Hookham Frere. He joined the Bombay civil service in 1834, worked at Poona, and in 1842 became private secretary to the governor of Bombay. As chief commissioner of Sind from 1850 he improved Karachi harbour and spread roads, canals, and schools.

When the mutiny came in 1857, Sind stayed quiet under only 178 British soldiers while he sent his regiment to Multan. He joined the viceroy council in 1859 and governed Bombay from 1862, clearing the old ramparts for fine public buildings, though the Bombay Bank failure of 1866 brought him censure. After a Zanzibar mission against the slave traffic in 1872, he went to South Africa in 1877 to push confederation. The scheme failed amid war and cabinet fights, Gladstone recalled him in 1880, and he died in 1884.
britannica-1911-frost-william-edward:
William Edward Frost (1810-1877), English painter, was born at Wandsworth near London in September 1810. Through William Etty he was sent about 1825 to a Bloomsbury drawing school. He studied also at the British Museum and entered the Royal Academy schools in 1829. He won medals in nearly every school and kept himself by portraits, painting some 300 of them.

In 1839 he took the Academy gold medal for Prometheus bound by Force and Strength. In 1843 he won a prize at the Westminster Hall cartoon show for Una alarmed by Fauns and Satyrs. His Una and the Wood-Nymphs of 1847 was bought by the queen, and that year marked his peak of popularity. Later pictures mostly repeated earlier motifs of nymphs and graces. Elected a full Academician in December 1871, he soon resigned the honour. He died in June 1877.
britannica-1911-fry-sir-edward:
Sir Edward Fry (1827- ), English judge, was born at Bristol on 4 November 1827, second son of Joseph Fry. He was educated at University College, London, called to the bar in 1854, and made a Queen Counsel in 1869. Practice in the rolls court made him a leading equity lawyer, and in 1877 he rose to the bench with a knighthood.

As a chancery judge he is remembered for careful readings of the new Judicature Acts. He became a lord justice of appeal in 1883 and resigned in 1892. After that the government used his skill in equity and arbitration on special work, often as chairman of commissions. He sat for Britain at the Paris North Sea Inquiry of 1905 and joined the Hague Permanent Arbitration Court. His treatise on the specific performance of contracts first appeared in 1858.
britannica-1911-fuchs-leonhard:
Leonhard Fuchs (1501-1566), German physician and botanist, was born at Wembdingen in Bavaria on 17 January 1501. He took his medical degree at Ingolstadt in 1524 after turning to the Reformation, practised at Munich, and in 1526 became professor of medicine at Ingolstadt. As physician to the margrave of Anspach he saved many lives in the English sweating-sickness epidemic.

In 1535 the duke of Württemberg placed him in the medical chair at Tübingen, which he held until his death on 10 May 1566. A follower of the Galenic school, he published Latin versions of Galen and Hippocrates. His great work is De historia stirpium commentarii insignes, printed at Basel in 1542. It carries more than five hundred fine outline pictures of plants, among them the common foxglove and another Digitalis, the genus he himself named.
britannica-1911-gans-eduard:
Eduard Gans, a German jurist who lived from 1797 to 1839, is profiled in a 1911 Britannica article. He was born at Berlin in March 1797, of prosperous Jewish parents. He studied law first at Berlin, then at Göttingen. He finished at Heidelberg, where he attended the lectures of Hegel.

There he was filled through and through with the Hegelian philosophy. In 1820, after taking his doctor's degree, he returned to Berlin as a lecturer on law. In 1825 he turned Christian. The next year he was made an extraordinary professor in the Berlin faculty of law. In 1828 he rose to ordinary professor. At that period, the historical school of law was coming to the front. Gans, by his Hegelian bent, treated law in a historical way. He applied that method to one special branch of law. Law readers meet a thinker caught between two schools.
britannica-1911-gibbs-josiah-willard:
Josiah Willard Gibbs is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Gibbs was an American mathematical physicist, born at New Haven in 1839. His father taught sacred literature at Yale Divinity School. Gibbs entered Yale College in 1854 and graduated in 1858.

He stayed at Yale as a tutor, teaching Latin, then natural philosophy. Study in Paris, Berlin, and Heidelberg followed in the late 1860s. In 1871 Yale made him professor of mathematical physics, and he held the chair until his death in 1903. The article turns to his first great papers of 1873. They dealt with graphical methods in the thermodynamics of fluids. Readers are introduced to a quiet scholar whose work reshaped how heat and energy are studied.
britannica-1911-gilpin-bernard:
Bernard Gilpin (1517–1583), called the Apostle of the North, came of a Westmorland family. He was born at Kentmere in 1517 and was schooled at Queen's College, Oxford. He took his degrees there in 1540, 1542, and 1549, and he was made a fellow of Queen's and ordained in 1542. Later he was chosen as a student of Christ Church. At Oxford he first held to the old side of the church and spoke against Hooper.

A public debate with Peter Martyr shook Gilpin's trust in his first views. In 1552 he preached before King Edward VI a sermon on sacrilege, which was put in print. That sermon shows the high mark he had set for the office of a churchman. About that time he was given the vicarage of Norton, in the diocese of Durham.
britannica-1911-glencorse-john-inglis-lo:
John Inglis, Lord Glencorse, a Scottish judge who lived from 1810 to 1891, is the subject of a short life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Edinburgh, the son of a minister, he went from Glasgow University to Balliol College at Oxford. He joined the Faculty of Advocates and soon made his name as a strong and fluent pleader.

In 1852 Inglis became solicitor general for Scotland in Lord Derby's first ministry, and Lord Advocate three months later. He held the same post again in 1858 and sat in the Commons for Stamford. He carried the Universities of Scotland Act that year, then rose to the bench as lord justice clerk. In 1867 he became lord justice general and lord president of the court of session, taking the title Lord Glencorse. He also did much public work for higher learning, and was chancellor of Edinburgh University from 1869.
britannica-1911-goliard:
Goliard, a name for wandering students and clerks of the middle ages, is the subject of an entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Such men roamed England, France, and Germany in the twelfth and thirteenth centuries. They were known more for rioting, gambling, and hard drinking than for learning. The source of the word is not sure.

One view links it to a Latin word for gluttony, another to a gay fellow. The goliards themselves tied it to a mythic Bishop Golias, in whose name their mocking poems were cast. Those poems were aimed almost all at the church, even at the pope. Church councils struck back, and in 1227 the council of Treves barred priests from letting goliards perform. Their fake orders and rules aped those of the church too boldly to pass unnoticed.
britannica-1911-gomm-sir-william-maynard:
William Maynard Gomm, a British soldier who lived from 1784 to 1875, is profiled in a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. He was gazetted to a foot regiment at the age of ten. That honour marked the service of his father, who was killed in an attack in 1794. The boy joined his regiment as a lieutenant in 1799 and fought in Holland.

In 1803 he became a captain and trained as a staff officer at a military college. On the general staff he served at Copenhagen, in the Peninsula, and at Corunna. He was also on staff in the disastrous Walcheren expedition of 1809. Back in the Peninsula, he fought through the battles of three years and rose step by step. Wellington valued his careful scouting and skilful leading so highly that he became one of the most trusted men on staff.
britannica-1911-gough-richard:
Richard Gough, who lived from 1735 to 1809, was an English antiquary born in London. The 1911 Britannica article says he was born on the twenty-first of October 1735. His father was a rich member of parliament and a director of the East India Company. Gough was a bright child who turned French books into English at the age of twelve. At sixteen he printed a work on geography. He entered Cambridge in 1752.

At Cambridge Gough began his great work on British topography, printed in 1768. He then toured Britain on quests for old remains. In 1789 his English edition of the Britannia of Camden came out. His grand book on the tomb monuments of Britain began in 1786. It used tombs to show the life and arts of each age. He led the Society of Antiquaries for twenty years and left his stores to Oxford.
britannica-1911-gourd:
Gourd is the name for plants of the cucumber order, above all the genus Cucurbita, as the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica explains. They are trailing herbs with tendrils, rough lobed leaves, and big yellow or orange flowers. The fertile flowers give the large juicy fruit that is the gourds' chief worth.

The kinds cross so freely that sorting them into species is hard, and no wild original may now survive. Naudin traced the garden kinds back to six first species, three or four of them the source of the kinds men eat. The greatest is Cucurbita maxima, whose round fruit can pass 240 pounds in weight. In Turkey and Asia Minor it is a staple food in season, sold in heaps like snowballs at Constantinople. Its flesh keeps well, feeds cattle too, and its seeds yield a mild oil.
britannica-1911-grafton-richard:
Richard Grafton (died 1572) was an English printer and chronicler, and his Bible work fills an entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Probably born about 1513, he gained the freedom of the Grocers' Company in 1534. He was soon in touch with the leaders of religious reform.

The entry tells how in 1537 he joined with Edward Whitchurch to produce Matthew's Bible at Antwerp, then went to Paris to print the Great Bible under a French licence. When officials seized the presses, Cromwell bought them and the work was finished in England. Grafton later held the sole right to print church service books and became king's printer under Edward VI.
britannica-1911-gray-john-edward:
John Edward Gray, who lived from 1800 to 1875, was an English naturalist born at Walsall in Staffordshire. The 1911 Britannica article says his father was a druggist and a writer on plants. Gray trained for medicine in London hospitals. From youth, though, plants drew him more. He helped his father with notes drawn from the library of Sir Joseph Banks at the British Museum. A joint work on British plants came out in 1821.

When the Linnaean Society shut him out in 1822, Gray turned to zoology. He wrote on shells, molluscs, and butterflies, still backed by museum staff. In 1824 he won a post there as an assistant. By 1839 his hard work on the animal stores had marked him as the fit man to lead them. As keeper he reworked the whole order of the stock. Catalogues poured out, and the fame of the department rose.
britannica-1911-grey-sir-edward:
Sir Edward Grey, 3rd Baronet (born 1862), was an English statesman, educated at Winchester and Balliol College, Oxford. The 1911 Britannica entry has him succeeding his grandfather at twenty and entering the Commons in 1885, as Liberal member for Berwick-on-Tweed. He was then best known as a country gentleman and amateur champion tennis-player.

A disciple of Lord Rosebery, Grey served as under-secretary for foreign affairs in 1892-1895. There he earned a name for straightforwardness and grit, and for holding British interests above party. With Asquith he ranked as the ablest of Rosebery's Imperialist followers. Through the opposition years he kept the public's trust as indispensable to a Liberal government. In December 1905 he became foreign minister under Campbell-Bannerman. He kept the office under Asquith from April 1908, and the entry leaves him in it, in post as the volume closed.
britannica-1911-hailes-david-dalrymple-l:
David Dalrymple, Lord Hailes, a Scottish lawyer and historian who lived from 1726 to 1792, has a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Edinburgh on 28 October 1726, he was the eldest of sixteen children. His father was auditor general of the exchequer of Scotland, of the house of Stair. 

Hailes was educated at Eton and studied law at Utrecht in his youth. He was intended for the Scottish bar, to which he was admitted shortly after his return to Scotland in 1748. As a pleader he attained neither high distinction nor very extensive practice at the bar. But he rapidly established a well deserved reputation for sound knowledge, unwearied application, and strict probity. In 1766 he was elevated to the bench, when he assumed the title of Lord Hailes. Ten years later he was appointed a lord of justiciary in Scotland.
britannica-1911-hakluyt-richard:
Richard Hakluyt, who lived from about 1553 to 1616, was a British geographer of a Welsh family settled in Herefordshire. The 1911 Britannica article says he was born in or near London about 1553. At Westminster School a visit to his cousin, a lawyer of the same name, fixed his course. Maps, books of travel, and the Bible on that table made the boy vow to chase that learning. He entered Christ Church, Oxford, in 1570.

Hakluyt read every voyage and discovery he could find, in print or by hand. After his degrees he began at Oxford what were held to be the first public talks on geography. His first book, on voyages touching America, came out in 1582. It brought him to the notice of Lord Howard of Effingham. By the age of thirty he knew the chief sea captains and merchants of the land.
britannica-1911-hamilton-william-gerard:
William Gerard Hamilton (1729–1796) was an English statesman. People called him Single Speech Hamilton. He was born in London on 28 January 1729. His father was a Scottish bencher of Lincoln's Inn. Winchester and Oriel College, Oxford, educated him. He inherited his father's fortune and entered Parliament for Petersfield. His maiden speech came on 13 November 1755. Walpole admired that speech greatly.

The nickname misleads, since he spoke well on other occasions. He sat in both the English and Irish parliaments. In 1761 he became chief secretary to Lord Halifax in Ireland. Ireland's chancellor of the exchequer followed in 1763. Dr Johnson thought very highly of him. Hamilton strongly opposed British taxation of America. He died in London on 16 July 1796. His Parliamentary Logick appeared after his death.
britannica-1911-harrigan-edward:
Edward Harrigan was an American actor born in New York in eighteen forty five. His life entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born of Irish parents on the twenty sixth of October that year. He first acted in San Francisco in eighteen sixty seven on stage.

Harrigan soon formed a stage pair with Tony Hart, born Anthony Cannon. As Harrigan and Hart they won fame for scenes of low New York life. Short sketches grew into full plays with songs set by David Braham. Titles like The Mulligan Guards and The O Regans show their themes. The pair lasted from eighteen seventy one to eighteen eighty four in all.
britannica-1911-hawkins-sir-richard:
Sir Richard Hawkins (c. 1562–1622) was a British seaman. He was the only son of Admiral Sir John Hawkins. Ships and the sea filled his life from childhood. In 1582 he sailed to the West Indies with his uncle William. He captained a galliot in Drake's 1585 expedition. In 1588 he commanded a queen's ship against the Armada. Portugal's coast saw him serve in 1590.

In 1593 he bought the Dainty and sailed for the South Seas. Plunder of Spanish possessions was his real project, he later denied. He claimed the voyage was pure geographical discovery. The Dainty passed Magellan's straits and plundered Valparaiso. At San Mateo bay two Spanish ships attacked her in 1594. Hawkins fought courageously while hopelessly outmatched. He surrendered, wounded, on a promise of safe-conduct. Spain broke it and imprisoned him until 1602. He died in London in 1622.
britannica-1911-hazard:
Hazard is a game of dice, called craps in America. Its name comes from the Arabic word for dice through Spanish. It was once very popular in England. Crockford's and Almack's rooms hosted play for large stakes. The caster calls a main, any number from five to nine. He then throws with two dice. Certain throws, called nicks, win at once. Aces or deuce-ace, called crabs, lose at once.

Other throws set a chance number for the caster. He keeps throwing until the chance or the main appears. The chance wins him the stake; the main loses it. The setter lays odds on the chance meanwhile. Seven is the best main to call. It can be thrown in six different ways. The rules fill the account in full tabular detail. Note: this record's hosted file is a shared page chunk; the hazard entry stands complete within it.
britannica-1911-hertford:
Hertford, the county town of Hertfordshire in England, is described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The town sits in the Lea valley, 24 miles north of London, at the end of two rail branch lines. Its count in 1901 was 9,322 souls. Key sites are the old castle, the town hall, the corn exchange, and two churches built on old sites.

Trade rests on farm goods, with malt works, beer works, iron works, and print works. Schools in or near the town are also named at length. The past is traced from a church synod in 673 through Danish wars and Norman rule. Charters, fairs, and seats in Parliament are then listed step by step to 1885.
britannica-1911-hildebrandt-eduard:
Eduard Hildebrandt (1818–1868) was a German painter, apprenticed to his father, a house-painter at Danzig. Not yet twenty, he came to Berlin and was taken in hand by Wilhelm Krause, a painter of sea pieces. Early works show a careful student of nature held down by his school's formal habits. French masterpieces shown at the Berlin Academy woke his curiosity, and about 1842 he entered Isabey's studio in Paris.

In Paris Hildebrandt quickly mastered touch and effect, and learned to paint figures. His French street scenes of about 1843 keep the Paris stamp but grasp quick changes of tone and air. Under Humboldt's influence he travelled widely, and in 1864–1865 he went round the world. As his experience grew, his concentration broke down: a fatal ease of hand cheapened his later work. He painted less in oil and more in water colour, and his fame rests on those sketches. He died in 1868.
britannica-1911-hincks-edward:
Edward Hincks was a British student of old east scripts who lived from seventeen ninety-two to eighteen sixty-six. He was born at Cork in Ireland and schooled at a Dublin school of high rank. He took church orders and served as rector of Killyleagh from eighteen twenty-five till his death. His spare hours went to hard script work.

He taught himself the picture script of Egypt and the wedge script of the east. In that wedge work he was a first path maker. On his own he worked out the vowel scheme of old Persian script, at the same time as a famed peer. His papers hold high worth.
britannica-1911-hitchcock-edward:
Edward Hitchcock was an American geologist who lived from seventeen ninety three to eighteen sixty four. His life entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born of poor parents at Deerfield in Massachusetts, he taught himself most. Weak eyesight forced him to drop plans to enter Harvard College.

Hitchcock led his home town academy from eighteen fifteen, then studied for ministry. Ordained in eighteen twenty one, he surveyed the west counties in free hours. From eighteen twenty five he taught chemistry and natural past at Amherst. He led Amherst College as president from eighteen forty five to eighteen fifty four. In eighteen thirty he became state geologist of Massachusetts by appointment.
britannica-1911-horsman-edward:
Edward Horsman, English politician who lived from 1807 to 1876, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was the son of a well to do gentleman of Stirling. Kinship through his mother linked him to the earls of Stair. Rugby and Cambridge gave him his schooling, and he was called to the Scotch bar in 1832.

Politics drew him away from the law at once. He won a seat as a Liberal for Cockermouth in 1836 and held it till 1852. Stroud returned him from 1853 to 1868, and Liskeard from 1869 till his death. A junior post at the treasury came his way in 1841 for a few months. He won note for attacks on the church policy of Lord John Russell from 1847. In 1855 he became chief secretary for Ireland, but resigned in 1857.
britannica-1911-howe-julia-ward:
Julia Ward Howe (1819–1910) was an American author and reformer, born in New York City on the 27th of May 1819. Her father, Samuel Ward, was a banker; her mother, Julia Rush Cutler, was a poet of some ability. At sixteen she was already placing poems in New York periodicals. In 1843 she married Dr Samuel Gridley Howe, and spent the next year with him in England, France, Germany and Italy.

She helped her husband edit the Commonwealth in 1851–1853. Her study of German philosophy bore fruit in essays and in lectures on doubt and belief, given in Boston in 1860–1861 and later in Washington. Her verse volumes include Passion Flowers, Later Lyrics (1866) and From Sunset Ridge (1898). Her most popular poem is The Battle Hymn of the Republic, written to the tune of John Brown's Body when she was at the front in the Civil War. Reform work fills the rest of the long life.
britannica-1911-hug-johann-leonhard:
Johann Leonhard Hug (1765-1846), a German Roman Catholic church scholar, is the subject of an article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Constance, he entered the university of Freiburg in 1783. There he trained for the priesthood in the seminary. He soon stood out in the study of the classic tongues, the tongues of the East, and the close reading of the Bible.

The article follows his long hold on Freiburg. He became head of studies at the seminary in 1787. In 1791 he took the chair for the tongues of the East and the Old Testament, with the New Testament chair added two years later. He turned down calls to three other universities and stayed more than thirty years. He gave up part of his work in 1827 but stayed in harness until a painful illness struck in 1845.
britannica-1911-hughes-sir-edward:
Sir Edward Hughes, a British admiral who lived from about 1720 to 1794, is the subject of a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He entered the Royal Navy in 1735 and was present at Porto Bello four years later. In 1740 he became a lieutenant, and in that rank he served on the Cartagena expedition and at the drawn battle of Toulon.

Hughes was with Boscawen at Louisburg and with Saunders at Quebec, and he was in steady employment through the peace. As commodore he commanded in the East Indies from 1773 to 1777. He soon returned east as a rear admiral with a strong force, and on the way out he retook Goree from the French. For two years he had only minor work, since the foe could not muster a fleet fit to meet his. In 1782 he stormed Trincomalee days before Suffren arrived.
britannica-1911-hurd-richard:
Richard Hurd (1720–1808) was an English divine and writer who became bishop of Worcester, and a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica follows his early years. He was born at Congreve in Staffordshire on the thirteenth of January 1720. His father was a farmer there. Hurd was schooled at Brewood and at Emmanuel College, Cambridge.

He took his first degree in 1739 and became a fellow of his college in 1742. He was ordained deacon that year and given charge of a parish in Norfolk. He soon came back to Cambridge and was ordained priest in 1744. In 1748 he published remarks on a work about the rejection of Christian miracles by the heathens. Editions and essays followed from his pen. The entry traces a scholar cleric on his slow rise through the church.
britannica-1911-james-george-payne-rains:
George Payne Rainsford James, English novelist born in London on 9 August 1799, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was the son of Pinkstan James, a physician of that city. A private school at Putney and schooling in France shaped his youth. He began to write at an early age in life.

By his own account he had composed tales later printed as A String of Pearls before age seventeen. Work for papers and magazines brought him to the eye of Washington Irving. Irving urged him to produce his Life of Edward the Black Prince in 1822. Richelieu was finished in 1825 and well thought of by Sir Walter Scott. It did not come out in print till 1829 in the end. He took up historical romance at a lucky hour, when Scott had made the style a favourite with readers.
britannica-1911-jeffrey-francis-jeffrey-:
Francis Jeffrey, Lord Jeffrey, who lived from 1773 to 1850, was a Scottish judge and critic of books. The 1911 Britannica article says he was born at Edinburgh on the twenty-third of October 1773. His father was a clerk in the Court of Session. Jeffrey read at Glasgow and at Queen's College, Oxford, then went back to law at Edinburgh. He joined the bar in December 1794.

His Whig views hurt his law work, since he had been raised a Tory. A trip to London in 1798 to try letters brought no luck. In 1801 he wed Catherine Wilson, and the need for a steady income grew sharp. A plan shared with Sydney Smith and Brougham bore fruit in 1802. The first number of the Edinburgh Review came out that October. Jeffrey soon became its editor at a fixed wage.
britannica-1911-jenner-edward:
Edward Jenner, an English physician who lived from 1749 to 1823, is profiled in a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. The entry names him as the discoverer of vaccination. Born at Berkeley in Gloucestershire, he was the son of a clergyman with land in that county. His father died when he was six, and an elder brother raised him.

The article traces his schooling at Wotton under Edge and Cirencester, where he showed a strong taste for natural history. He trained first under a surgeon near Bristol, then went to London at age twenty one. There he became a favoured pupil of John Hunter and lived in his house for two years. He also prepared zoological specimens brought back from Captain Cook's first voyage.
britannica-1911-kames-henry-home-lord:
Henry Home, Lord Kames (1696–1782), was a Scottish lawyer and thinker, son of George Home of Kames in Berwickshire, where he was born in 1696. His schooling from a private tutor was imperfect. In 1712 he was bound to a writer to the signet in Edinburgh. A chance meeting with Sir Hew Dalrymple, president of the court of session, turned his aim to the bar.

He read widely, above all in metaphysics and moral thought. He was called to the bar in January 1724. He used his leisure on a book of Remarkable Decisions of the court of session. The work drew notice, and his sharp reasoning won him a leading place at the bar. In 1752 he became a judge as Lord Kames, and in 1763 a lord of justiciary. He kept his seat on the bench almost to his death.
britannica-1911-kelly-edward:
Edward Kelly (1854–1880) was an Australian bushranger, born at Wallan Wallan in Victoria. His father was a transported Belfast convict, and his mother's family counted several thieves. As boys he and his brothers were in constant trouble for horse stealing, and Ned served three years in prison for that offence.

In April 1878 an attempt was made to arrest his brother Daniel on a like charge. The whole family resisted, and Ned wounded one of the constables. His mother and others were taken, but Ned and Daniel fled to the hills, where Byrne and Hart joined them. For two years the gang, under Kelly's lead, terrorized the border country of Victoria and New South Wales. They held up towns and plundered banks, though a reward of £8000 stood on their heads. Their close knowledge of a district full of hiding places kept them free. The entry follows the gang to its end.
britannica-1911-kempenfelt-richard:
Richard Kempenfelt (1718–1782) was a British rear admiral, born at Westminster in 1718. His father, a Swede, is said to have served James II and then to have entered the British army. Richard went into the navy and first served in the West Indies, taking part in the capture of Portobello.

In 1746 he came back to England. From then until 1780, when he was made rear admiral, he saw active service in the East Indies with Sir George Pocock and in many other quarters of the world. In 1781, with a far weaker force, he won a bright victory fifty leagues southwest of Ushant over the French fleet under De Guichen, taking twenty prizes. In 1782 he raised his flag on the Royal George, in the fleet under Lord Howe.
britannica-1911-keyboard:
Keyboard, meaning the row of keys on an organ, piano, or like instrument, is the subject of this 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. The piece gives the word in French, German, and Italian, then defines it plainly. A keyboard is a set of keys that unlock sound in stringed, wind, or struck instruments. The keys sit on a case or board made to hold them.

The article contrasts the organ and the piano, the two main keyboard instruments. On the organ, the keys work valves that open and close the pipes, so touch cannot change the tone. On the piano, touch does matter, and the keys pass the player's feel and rhythm to the sound. The piece then traces the keyboard back to the early organ, its first known use.
britannica-1911-kilmaine-charles-edward:
Charles Edward Kilmaine, an Irish French general, is followed in a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Dublin in 1751, his birth name was Jennings there. At eleven he crossed to France with his father for a new life. He took the name Kilmaine from a Mayo village of his kin. In 1774 he joined a French dragoon band as an officer.

Sea service in Senegal and war in America filled his young years. He fought under Rochambeau in the American war for freedom's cause. Back in France he swore the civic oath in the revolt year 1791. Rank rose fast for him in the wars of 1793 on all fronts. Doubt for his foreign birth cast him down, then raised him back. Lombardy was his charge in the Italian wars that won fame.
britannica-1911-kipling-rudyard:
Rudyard Kipling, born in Bombay in 1865, was a British author raised between India and England. The 1911 Britannica entry gives his father as curator of the Lahore museum and an artist. His mother came from Birmingham, with sisters wed to famed painters of the age. School at the United Services College in Devon left a mark told in Stalky stories.

Back in India at seventeen he became sub editor of a Lahore gazette. Departmental Ditties, light satirical verse, came out in 1886 to first notice. Plain Tales from the Hills followed in 1887 from tales in his own journal. The entry opens the rise of a writer shaped by India at every turn.
britannica-1911-kirwan-richard:
Richard Kirwan (1733–1812) was an Irish scientist, born at Cloughballymore in County Galway in 1733. Part of his early life was spent abroad. In 1754 he entered the Jesuit novitiate, at St Omer or at Hesdin. He came back to Ireland the next year, when he succeeded to the family estates through his brother's death in a duel.

In 1766, having conformed to the established religion two years before, he was called to the Irish bar. In 1768 he gave up practice for scientific work. For the next nineteen years he lived chiefly in London, in the society of the scientific men of the city. He wrote to many scholars on the continent of Europe, as his wide knowledge of languages let him do with ease. His trials on saline substances were a solid help to analytical chemistry.
britannica-1911-knolles-richard:
Richard Knolles (c. 1545–1610) was an English historian, a native of Northamptonshire who was educated at Lincoln College, Oxford, and became a fellow of his college. Some time after 1571 he left Oxford to become master of a school at Sandwich in Kent, where he died in 1610. His name rests on one large book and one translation.

In 1603 Knolles published his Generall Historie of the Turkes, dedicated to King James I and drawn in part on Boissard's lives of the Turkish sultans. New editions followed, the best edited by Sir Paul Rycaut in 1700, who carried the history down to 1699. Though later works replaced it, the book is credited here with real merit in style and arrangement. Knolles also published a translation of Bodin's De Republica in 1606. A Latin grammar long linked to his name is in fact the work of the Baptist minister Hanserd Knollys.
britannica-1911-knot-bird:
The knot is a shore bird found in large numbers at some seasons on the coasts of Britain and other lands of the northern hemisphere. Camden, in his Britannia of 1607, linked the name with King Canute, and later writers repeated him, so Linnaeus called the species Tringa canutus. More weight is given to Sir Thomas Browne, who wrote the name "Gnatts or Knots" about 1672.

Rather larger than a snipe, but with a shorter bill and legs, the knot reaches England in flocks about the middle of May. After a few days it passes north. The young return in autumn in still greater numbers. Its winter plumage is ashy-grey above and white below. In summer the back turns black edged with orange-red, and the under parts a deep chestnut. The knot's egg was a long puzzle, which no zoologist could surely name.
britannica-1911-kynaston-edward:
Edward Kynaston (c. 1640–1706) was an English actor, born in London. He first played in Rhodes's company, having been, like Betterton, a clerk in Rhodes's book-shop before Rhodes set up a company at the Cockpit in Drury Lane. Kynaston was probably the last, and certainly the best, of the men who played women's parts, and his beauty fitted him well for them.

His last female part was Evadne in The Maid's Tragedy, in 1661, with Killigrew's company. By 1665 he was playing leading male parts at Covent Garden. In 1695 he joined Betterton at Lincoln's Inn Fields, but was given smaller roles, and he retired in 1699. He died in 1706 and was buried on the 18th of January.
britannica-1911-lard:
Lard is a substance article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about the melted and strained fat of the hog. The word runs back through French to the Latin laridum, bacon fat. True lard comes from the leaf, the fat of the bowel and kidneys, but trade lard often mixes fat from other parts, and some holds no leaf at all.

Neutral lard is made from fresh killed hogs at a low heat. The finest grade, drawn from the leaf, goes to make oleomargarine, while a second grade serves bakers of biscuits and pastry. The article gives the fat's marks: pure white, of a butter like body, melting between 35 and 45 degrees, with about sixty per cent olein. In medicine lard serves as a base for ointments, and pressure on it yields lard oil for burning and oiling machines.
britannica-1911-le-gallienne-richard:
Richard Le Gallienne (born 1866) is an English poet and critic, and a short life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica lists his early books. He was born in Liverpool on the twentieth of January 1866. He started life in a business office in that city. He soon gave that up to turn author for his living.

His first book, My Lady’s Sonnets, appeared at Liverpool in 1887. In 1889 he served for a short time as literary secretary to Wilson Barrett. That year he published three more works, including a study of George Meredith. In 1891 he joined the staff of the Star newspaper. He wrote for many papers under the signature of Logroller. His verse books include English Poems of 1892 and a volume on Stevenson of 1895. He also made a paraphrase of the Rubáiyát of Omar Khayyám in 1897.
britannica-1911-lebrun-ponce-denis-ecouc:
Ponce Denis Écouchard Lebrun, French lyric poet born in Paris on 11 August 1729, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born in the house of the prince de Conti, where his father served as valet. At school he fell in with a son of Louis Racine and became his disciple in verse.

In 1755 he published an ode on the disasters of Lisbon. He wed Marie Anne de Surcourt in 1759, the Fanny of his elegies. To the early years of that marriage belongs his poem Nature. His fierce temper made his wife suffer much in the home. In 1774 she sued for a separation, backed by his own mother and sister. Loss of his post at the death of his patron and loss of his funds in a bank failure deepened his woes.
britannica-1911-lee-robert-edward:
Robert Edward Lee, an American soldier who lived from 1807 to 1870, is profiled at length in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was the youngest son of Henry Lee, known as Light Horse Harry. Born in Virginia, he entered West Point in 1825. He left four years later, second in his class, as an engineer officer.

Lee won praise for bravery in the Mexican War and rose by brevet steps. He later ran West Point for three years and made key changes there. In 1859 he led the troops sent to stop the John Brown raid at Harpers Ferry. He was against secession but felt bound to follow his own state. When Virginia left the Union, he gave up his United States post. He refused command of the Union field army and joined the Confederate service in Richmond.
britannica-1911-lepsius-karl-richard:
Karl Richard Lepsius (1810-1884) was a German student of ancient Egypt. He was born at Naumburg on 23 December 1810. School at Schulpforta came in 1823. Leipzig, Göttingen, and Berlin followed. A thesis on the Eugubine tables won his degree in 1833. A prize essay on language study came in 1834.

Friendship with Bunsen and Humboldt turned him to Egypt. Four years went to the great stores of Italy, Holland, and England. Royal backing then sent him up the Nile. For three years his party ranged from the Sudan to the Syrian coast. Casts, drawings, maps, and finds passed all hope. Twelve volumes of results were done by 1859. A Berlin chair came in 1847. A second Egypt trip in 1866 found the Decree of Tanis.
britannica-1911-limousin-leonard:
Léonard Limousin (about 1505 to about 1577) was a French enamel painter of Limoges. An innkeeper's son, he led a family of seven enamel workers. Study under Nardon Pénicaud is held likely. German craft shaped his first known work, eighteen plaques of the Passion dated 1532, drawn from Dürer.

Italian masters of Fontainebleau then fed his taste for scroll work and myth tales. French habit kept his own hand clear through it all. Francis I took him into royal service in 1530 as painter and valet. Henry II kept him on. Portraits in enamel, plates, vases, and cups poured from his shop. Near two thousand enamels bear his name in the count kept here. Rich colour and fine grisaille on black or blue ground mark his fame. The Louvre holds his two votive tablets of 1553.
britannica-1911-livingston-edward:
Edward Livingston (1764–1836) was an American jurist and statesman. He was born in Clermont, New York, on 26 May 1764. He was a great-grandson of Robert Livingston, the first of the family to settle in America. He took his degree at Princeton in 1781 and joined the bar in 1785. He set up as a lawyer in New York City and rose fast to high place in his trade.

From 1795 to 1801 Livingston sat in Congress as a Republican. He was a head of the fight against Jay's treaty and moved that the president hand over all the papers on it. At the close of Washington's term he voted with Andrew Jackson against the address to the president. He fought the Alien and Sedition Laws and brought in bills on behalf of American seamen.
britannica-1911-local-government-board:
Local Government Board was a department of the government of the United Kingdom, set up in 1871, and the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica sets out its history in a law and government entry. It followed the General Board of Health, which had been formed in 1848 under the Public Health Act of that year.

That health board was remade in 1854 and kept alive from year to year till 1858, when it was let lapse. Its powers over disease went to the privy council, and its control of local authorities went to the home secretary, with its staff as well. That state of things lasted till 1871, when the Local Government Board Act created the new board. On paper it held many great officers of state, with a president named by the sovereign. In practice the board seldom met, and the president ran the department with his secretaries and staff.
britannica-1911-lockroy-edouard:
Édouard Lockroy (born 1838) was a French man of politics from the far left. Paris was his birthplace on 18 July 1838. His father was an actor and playwright who took the name Lockroy. Art study came first for the son. In 1860 he marched as a volunteer with Garibaldi.

Three years in Syria as Renan's secretary followed. Back in Paris he wrote fierce pieces against the empire. Figaro and Rappel both bore his name. A battalion was his in the siege of Paris. The National Assembly took him in February 1871. He backed the Commune call in March and gave up his seat. Prison at Versailles and Chartres held him till June. No trial came. Seats for Bouches-du-Rhône and Paris followed from 1873. Trade and industry were his in the Freycinet cabinet of 1886.
britannica-1911-lord:
Lord is the subject of a word study in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. The Old English form breaks down into loaf and keeper. In its first sense a lord was the head of a household. He was the master of those who relied on him for their daily bread.

That bread link survives in terms such as lord of the manor and landlord, the entry notes. Most later uses come from its role as the match for Latin and Greek words for master. In the Old Testament it stands for the divine name. The entry traces those layers of sense from the household to church and state use.
britannica-1911-lovelace-richard:
Richard Lovelace (1618-1658), an English poet, is the subject of an article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Woolwich, he came from a Kentish family with a long line of soldiers. His father had served in the Low Countries, was knighted by James the First, and was killed at Grolle in 1628. His brother Francis served Charles the First in the Civil War and held Caermarthen in 1644.

The article says he was schooled at the Charterhouse and at Oxford, where he took a degree in his second year at the queen's wish. His fame rests on a few songs and on the romance of his life. Men often call his poems mere pastimes of a busy soldier. The entry argues the sad course of his life in fact gave him more time for verse than for war.
britannica-1911-lydford:
Lydford, a village in Devonshire, England, once an important town, is described in this 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. It stands near the western edge of Dartmoor, 27 miles north of Plymouth by rail. From its Perpendicular church of St Petrock, fine views of the Dartmoor tors are seen. The village stands on the small river Lyd. That stream runs through a deep, narrow chasm crossed by a single-span bridge.

Lydford was one of the four Saxon boroughs of Devon and held a mint under Æthelred the Unready. It first appears in record in 997, when Danes raided up the Tamar to reach it. Under Edward the Confessor it was Devon's most populous centre after Exeter. Domesday tells that forty houses had been laid waste since the Conquest, and the town never recovered. Its later history centres on its castle.
britannica-1911-macnally-leonard:
Leonard MacNally, an Irish informer who lived from 1752 to 1820, is profiled in this 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. Born in Dublin, the son of a merchant, he was called to the Irish bar in 1776 and to the English bar in 1783. He supported himself in London for a time by writing plays. He also edited the Public Ledger.

Back in Dublin, MacNally set on a course of informing against the revolutionary party, whose resort his house had become. He betrayed political clients whom he defended in court with fine speeches. He made a strong defence for Robert Emmet and cheered him in his last hours. Yet before the trial he had sold the contents of his brief to the Crown lawyers for 200 pounds. Though a professed Protestant all his life, he took absolution from a Catholic priest on his deathbed.
britannica-1911-maitland-edward:
Edward Maitland, an English writer on humane causes who lived from 1824 to 1897, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born at Ipswich in October 1824 and educated at Caius College in Cambridge. He was the son of a clergyman of Brighton and was meant for the Church. His views on faith would not let him take orders.

For some years he lived abroad, first in California and then in Australia as a commissioner of crown lands. Back in England in 1857 he took up a strong humane stand. He held that he had gained a new sense by which he could read the inner state of other folk. He joined with Anna Kingsford, a woman doctor who backed the rights of beasts and the high schooling of women. With her he wrote books on the creeds and founded the Hermetic Society in 1884.
britannica-1911-maitland-sir-richard:
Sir Richard Maitland, Lord Lethington, who lived from 1496 to 1586, was a Scottish lawyer, poet, and keeper of old Scots verse. The 1911 Britannica article says his father fell at Flodden. Maitland read law at Saint Andrews and then in Paris. The English burned his castle at Lethington in 1549. He helped settle border terms with England in 1552.

Though he lost his sight about 1561, Maitland stayed in public life for years. He sat as a lord of session and joined the privy council. In 1562 he became keeper of the Great Seal, a post he gave up in 1567. He sat on the bench until he was eighty-eight. His own poems are short works of satire on the faults of his age. He is best known for the two large books of old Scots poems he saved.
britannica-1911-mansfield-richard:
Richard Mansfield, an American actor who lived from 1857 to 1907, is profiled in this 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. Born in Berlin in May 1857, he was the son of the singer Madame Rudersdorff and a London wine merchant. He first acted at St George's Hall in London. He then drifted into light opera, playing comic leads in The Pirates of Penzance and The Mikado. He played those parts in England and in America.

In 1883 Mansfield joined a New York theatre company and scored a hit in A Parisian Romance. His double role in Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde in 1887 made a deep impression. With that play he won his London fame at the Lyceum in 1888. He produced Richard the Third the next year. He was among the first to stage Shaw's plays in America. As a manager he was noted for lavish staging.
britannica-1911-mant-richard:
Richard Mant (1776-1848), an English churchman, is the subject of an article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Southampton, he was educated at Winchester and at Trinity College in Oxford. He was elected a fellow of Oriel in 1798. After taking orders he held a curacy at Southampton and then a vicarage in Essex.

The article lists his rise and his books. He gave the Bampton lectures in 1811 and became a rector in London five years later. In 1820 he was made an Irish bishop, and in 1823 he moved to a greater see, with a third joined to it in 1842. With a partner he wrote a commentary on the whole Bible. His other works were the Psalms in English verse and a history of the Church of Ireland in two books.
britannica-1911-maret-hugues-bernard:
Hugues Bernard Maret, duke of Bassano, was a French statesman and writer. He lived from seventeen sixty three to eighteen thirty nine. His life entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Dijon and well schooled, he trained in law at Paris.

Debates of the first National Assembly drew Maret to print their record. With Mejean he issued the Bulletin, then merged it into the Moniteur. That paper won wide fame for care and fair dealing under him. After the monarchy fell in seventeen ninety two, he joined the foreign office. He went on a mission to London and met Pitt that December. War in seventeen ninety three ended all hope of a calm accord.
britannica-1911-martha-s-vineyard:
Martha's Vineyard is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article on an island off the southern coast of Massachusetts. The island makes up most of Dukes county and lies about three miles off the mainland. Its greatest length, east to west, is about twenty miles. Its greatest width, north to south, is about nine and a half miles.

Along its north western shore lies Vineyard Sound, the entry notes. Its chief bays include a deep harbour at the northern angle and two harbours on the eastern coast. The surface is mainly flat, save for a hilly strip in the west. There the highest ground rises a little over three hundred feet. Along the south coast lie many ponds, shut off from the ocean by narrow strips of land.
britannica-1911-massey-sir-edward:
Sir Edward Massey is the subject of a life entry in the 1911 Britannica. He was an English soldier in the Great Rebellion. He lived from about 1619 to about 1674. He was the son of a man of Coddington in Cheshire. Little is known of his early life and years. He is said to have served in Dutch ranks in youth. In 1639 he stood as a captain of pioneers.

At the war start he was with the king at York. He soon joined the army of parliament instead. He became deputy head of Gloucester town and fort. In 1643 he rose to be governor of that town. He held it against the king main army that year. Skill and calm in that siege won him thanks. A grant of gold came to him from parliament. In 1644 he beat local royalist bands in the field.
britannica-1911-mccullough-john-edward:
McCullough, John Edward is a life article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about an American actor. Born in Coleraine, Ireland, on the second of November 1837, he went to America at sixteen. He first appeared on stage at the Arch Street Theatre in Philadelphia in 1857. Playing second roles, he supported Edwin Forrest and Edwin Booth.

The article weighs his powers and his end. Virginius was his greatest success, though he was coldly received in England in 1881. In 1884 he broke down in body and mind. He died in an asylum at Philadelphia on the eighth of November 1885. The entry is short, and its picture is of a tragedian formed in Forrest's shadow, whose promise was cut short by collapse.
britannica-1911-meek-fielding-bradford:
Fielding Bradford Meek is the subject of a life entry in the 1911 Britannica. He was an American geologist who lived from 1817 to 1876. He was born at Madison, Indiana, in December 1817. His father was a lawyer in that town. In early life Meek worked as a merchant. His free hours went to fossils and rocks near home. When trade failed he turned his whole mind to science.

In 1848 he won work on a survey in Iowa. Work in two more states followed that first post. In 1852 he became aide to James Hall at Albany. He worked with Hall on old life forms till 1858. A trip to the Bad Lands brought back rich fossils. From 1858 he worked for surveys at Washington. His work bore the stamp of faith and care, the entry says. Books on fossils of California and Missouri close the list.
britannica-1911-monboddo-james-burnett-l:
James Burnett, Lord Monboddo (1714-1799), was a Scottish judge and student of man, born at Monboddo in Kincardineshire. This 1911 Britannica article notes that he studied at Aberdeen, passed his law tests at Edinburgh, and rose fast at the Scottish bar. In 1767 he became a Lord of Session with the title of Lord Monboddo.

He is remembered chiefly for his writings on human origins, and for odd habits that his own age found strange. In his Antient Metaphysics he pictured man rising by degrees from an animal state to one where mind acts free of body. In his work on the origin and progress of language he placed man in the same species as the orang-outang. The article sees points in his thought that touch later views on the descent of man.
britannica-1911-montagu-richard:
Richard Montagu, who lived from 1577 to 1641, was an English churchman. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica opens with his birth at Dorney in Buckinghamshire. He was schooled at Eton and Cambridge, and made a fellow of Eton in 1613. He became dean of Hereford in 1616, then a canon of Windsor. He also served as chaplain to James the First. Like Laud, he disliked the extremes of both Calvinism and Rome.

That middle stance kept him in trouble all his life. A clash with Catholics in his parish brought a pamphlet attack in 1623. His reply coined the phrase of a new gagg for an old goose. Puritans then attacked his own book and appealed to the Commons. The king shielded him, and court favour kept his ground safe. He became bishop of Chichester in 1628, then of Norwich in 1638.
britannica-1911-montbeliard:
Montbeliard is a town of eastern France, in the department of Doubs, and an entry from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica describes its strong frontier place. It stands 1,050 feet above the sea, on the right bank of the river Allaine where it meets the Luzine. Its commune held 10,455 people in 1906.

The entry stresses its weight in the frontier defenses of France since 1871, with forts on nearby hills linking it to Belfort and Besancon. It notes the old castle of the counts, now used as barracks, and the church of Saint Martin, serving a mostly Protestant people. A bronze statue honors George Cuvier, the town's most famous native son.
britannica-1911-moran-edward:
Edward Moran, an American painter of the sea, is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born at Bolton in England in 1829. He crossed to America at the age of fifteen and settled in Philadelphia. There he left his father's trade of weaving and learned to paint.

The entry follows his study in London and his years in New York and Paris. It singles out a set of thirteen large works on the sea history of America. The set runs from the voyage of Leif Ericsson to the return of Admiral Dewey's fleet in 1899. His sons and brothers, also painters, are named at the close.
britannica-1911-morel-ladeuil-leonard:
Léonard Morel-Ladeuil, who lived from 1820 to 1888, was a French goldsmith and sculptor born at Clermont-Ferrand. The 1911 Britannica article says he was apprenticed to a maker of bronzes. Under him he grew into one of the finest chasers in France. He then learned the art of repoussé, work raised in relief from the back. A set shield for the French state won him the praise of Napoleon the Third. The trade then shut him out, vexed that a craftsman had won work direct.

In 1859 the firm of Elkington took him to Birmingham for work in repoussé. His silver pieces Night and Day raised him at once to the top of his trade. The Dreams plateau was bought by Birmingham as a wedding gift for the prince of Wales. He stayed with the firm for twenty-three years in London. His chief work there was the Milton Shield.
britannica-1911-morris-richard:
Richard Morris, who lived from 1833 to 1894, was an English scholar of language. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica lists his editions and school books. He was born in London in September 1833. He took church orders in 1871 and later ran a boys school near London.

Morris prepared twelve volumes of old texts for the Early English Text Society. He edited Chaucer and Spenser from the first hand copies. His books on English word growth and grammar sold widely in schools. They shaped how grammar was taught in his day. Late in life he turned to Pali, the tongue of old Buddhist texts. He became a known expert in that field before his death in 1894.
britannica-1911-moxon-edward:
Edward Moxon is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Moxon was a British poet and publisher who lived from 1801 to 1858. He was born at Wakefield. In 1826 he published a volume of verse that was received with some favour. In 1830 Samuel Rogers set him up as a London publisher in New Bond Street. The first volume he issued was a book of verses by Charles Lamb.

The article tells how he spent a large sum on pictures for an edition of Rogers's Italy. Wordsworth trusted him with his works from 1835 onward. In 1839 he issued the first complete edition of Shelley's poems. Passages in one poem brought a charge of blasphemy against him in 1841. A jury found him guilty, and the passages were cut for a time. He later published works by Browning and Tennyson.
britannica-1911-nithard:
Nithard, who died in 844, was a Frankish writer of history. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica gives his life and his one great work. He was a grandson of Charlemagne through his mother Bertha. He learned at the royal court and held an abbey post.

Nithard served his cousin Charles the Bald in peace and in war. He fought for Charles at Fontenoy in 841. Three years later he died of wounds won against the Northmen. At the king request he wrote four books of history. They cover the strife among the sons of Louis the First. The entry calls the work rough and one sided at times. Yet its author knew the events at first hand.
britannica-1911-nonpareil-bird:
Nonpareil is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article about a small cage bird long sold by English dealers. The bird was brought in chiefly from New Orleans and prized for what the entry calls its matchless beauty. In science it was placed with the buntings and finches, though some writers had classed it as a tanager.

The entry describes the male in bright blue, yellow, green, and scarlet, with purple on the rump. That full colour comes only when the bird is at least two years old. The female is green above and yellow below, and young males fall between the two. Also called the painted bunting, the bird winters in Central America or Mexico and reaches the southern states in April.
britannica-1911-noodt-gerhard:
Gerhard Noodt, a Dutch jurist who lived from 1647 to 1725, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born at Nijmwegen in 1647. He studied law at Leiden, Utrecht, and Franeker, and in time became a professor of law at Leiden. As a writer on law he won a wide name across Europe.

His Latin prose was shaped on the best old models, and his many works soon ranked as standard texts. Two of his tracts were put into French by Jean Barbeyrac and printed at Amsterdam in 1707 and 1714. One dealt with the power of rulers, and one with freedom of conscience. His full works came out at Leiden in 1724. The last edition was in 1767, and later ones hold a life of him by Barbeyrac.
britannica-1911-nord:
Nord is the most northern department of France. It was made chiefly out of Flanders, French Hainault, and the district of Cambrai. It covers 2,229 square miles. Its people numbered 1,895,861 in 1906, a count second only to that of Seine. Many of its people are Belgians. The department runs 112 miles from south-east to north-west. Its width is never more than forty miles.

The North Sea bounds Nord for twenty-one miles in the north-west. Belgium lies to the north-east and east. West of the Scheldt the Flanders part is very flat. The lone hill at Cassel, just 535 feet high, looks north to Dunkirk over rich lowlands. Canals cross land that the sea once covered. Work to drain and claim that land began as early as the twelfth century.
britannica-1911-oglethorpe-james-edward:
James Edward Oglethorpe, an English general and philanthropist who lived from 1696 to 1785, is the subject of a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He is known as the founder of Georgia in America. Born in London, the son of Sir Theophilus Oglethorpe, he entered Corpus Christi College at Oxford in 1714, then left that year to join the army of Prince Eugene.

On the word of the Duke of Marlborough, Oglethorpe became aide de camp to the prince and served with honour against the Turks, above all at the siege and capture of Belgrade. Back in England, he was sent to Parliament for Haslemere in 1722. He gave much care to the plight of poor debtors in London prisons. To give refuge to the insolvent, and to Protestants pressed abroad, he planned a colony in America between Carolina and Florida. That plan became Georgia.
britannica-1911-olgierd:
Olgierd, grand-duke of Lithuania, who died in 1377, is profiled in a 1911 Britannica article. He was one of seven sons of Gedymin, grand-duke of Lithuania. On Gedymin's death in 1341, the domains were divided among the sons. The youngest, Yavnuty, held the capital, Wilna, with a nominal priority.

With the aid of his brother Kiejstut, Olgierd drove out the weak Yavnuty in 1345. He then declared himself grand-duke. The thirty-two years of his reign went to building up Lithuania. He lived to make it one of the greatest states in Europe. Two things, the text says, produced that result. One was the rare political wisdom of Olgierd. The other was the lifelong devotion of his brother Kiejstut. Foes pressed in from two sides. The Teutonic knights lay to the north, and the Tatar hordes to the south.
britannica-1911-osborn-sherard:
Sherard Osborn lived from 1822 to 1875 and was an English admiral and explorer. The 1911 Britannica life adds that he won note in the Arctic seas. He was the son of an officer of the Indian army. Born in April 1822, he joined the navy as a youth in 1837. In 1838 he led a gunboat at the attack on Kedah.

He was present at the fall of Canton in 1841 in China. He also fought at the storming of the forts of Woosung in 1842. From 1844 he served in the Pacific in the flagship of Sir George Seymour. In 1849 he pressed hard for a new search for Franklin. In 1850 he led the steam tender Pioneer in that search.
britannica-1911-owen-sir-richard:
Sir Richard Owen (1804-1892) was an English biologist born at Lancaster. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica follows his path from surgeon training to museum work. Study at Edinburgh and in London brought him under John Abernethy. That link led him to help care for the Hunterian collection instead.

Catalog work there gave him unmatched knowledge of body structure across species. He wrote a classic memoir on the pearly nautilus in 1832. In 1856 he took charge of natural history at the British Museum. He then drove the plan for a new museum at South Kensington. He held office until that move was complete in 1884.
britannica-1911-pace-richard:
Richard Pace (about 1482-1536) was an English diplomat in the reign of Henry VIII. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica traces his schooling at Winchester, Padua, and Bologna. He went to Rome in 1509 with Archbishop Bainbridge of York. Pope Leo X praised him and urged the king to employ him.

He became a royal secretary and then a secretary of state. Wolsey sent him to press the Swiss to attack France in 1515. Later trips took him to Germany and to Venice on church matters. He held three dean posts at once and was at the Field of the Cloth of Gold.
britannica-1911-paisley-claud-hamilton-l:
Claud Hamilton, Lord Paisley, a Scottish man of state born about fifteen forty three, is profiled in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was a younger son of the second earl of Arran. In fifteen fifty three he took the lands of the abbey of Paisley. In fifteen sixty eight he helped Mary, queen of Scots, flee her isle jail.

He fought for her at the battle of Langside past that flight. His lands were seized for those acts. He was then tied to the slaying of two regents in two years in a row. In fifteen seventy three he won his lands back once more. Years later the council chose to seize him and his brother for their past deeds. The brothers fled to England, where the queen used them as pawns in her state game.
britannica-1911-palissy-bernard:
Bernard Palissy, a French potter who lived from about 1510 to 1589, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He is said to have been born at Saintes or at Agen, but both the date and the place are unsure. It is told, on weak grounds, that his father painted glass. Palissy himself says he was bound to a glass painter and learned the first steps of land measure as a boy.

When his time was out he took to the road as a workman, as was the custom. He picked up new skills in France, the Low Countries, and perhaps in Germany and Italy. About 1539 he came home, wed, and settled at Saintes. There he lived by painting portraits and glass and by survey work. The article tells how the sight of a white glazed cup set him on a life-long hunt for the secret of its making.
britannica-1911-parry-sir-william-edward:
William Edward Parry was an English rear admiral and Arctic explorer, born at Bath as the son of a doctor. At age thirteen he joined the flag ship of a fleet in the Channel as a boy volunteer. He rose by steps to midshipman, then to lieutenant in a frigate set to guard the whale fleets of the far north.

That post gave him the chance to learn the craft of star sights in high north seas, the 1911 Britannica entry says. He put his results in a small book on the art of such sights by night. He served on the North American station for some years, then took command of a brig in an Arctic trip under a famed captain. That trip came home with no new finds. Parry, sure in his own mind that more could be done, pressed on.
britannica-1911-partridge-john-bernard:
John Bernard Partridge, a Punch artist, is sketched in a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born in London in 1861, he was a surgeon's son of note. His uncle had painted portraits for Queen Victoria by royal call. School at Stonyhurst and London study set his path toward art. He first trained in an architect's office for a time.

Partridge then learned stained glass work with a London firm. Church ornament held him for four years under Philip Westlake. Press drawing and water-colour work came next in his growth. Book drawing brought him his chief success as an artist. In 1892 he joined the staff of Punch, the famed comic paper. For some years he also acted on stage as Bernard Gould.
britannica-1911-payson-edward: Edward Payson (1783-1827) was an American Congregational preacher, covered in a short entry from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Rindge, New Hampshire, where his father was pastor, he graduated at Harvard in 1803. He then ran a school at Portland, Maine, and in 1807 became junior pastor of the Congregational Church there. From 1811 he was its senior pastor, a post he held until his death in 1827. The entry points readers to the fullest set of his sermons, printed with a memoir by Asa Cummings.
britannica-1911-pease-edward:
Edward Pease, founder of a famed Quaker industrial family in the north of England, who lived from 1767 to 1858, is the subject of a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born at Darlington, son of a woollen maker there. After he left that trade, he met George Stephenson. With Stephenson he took a lead part in building the railway between Stockton and Darlington.

The entry then follows his sons in public life. His second son Joseph helped in the railway work and sat in Parliament for South Durham from 1832 to 1841. He was the first Quaker to sit in Parliament, with interests in collieries, quarries, and ironstone mines. Another son, Henry, also sat for South Durham and worked for the Peace Society. A grandson was made a baronet in 1882.
britannica-1911-petard: Petard names a small blast tool once used by army engineers to break a gate or wall. The 1911 Britannica note gives the French root in a word for a slight blast. The tool was a case of metal or wood shaped like a sugar loaf. A charge of powder filled the case. A fuse set it off at the barrier. The whole note is brief and sticks to form and use.
britannica-1911-peter-lombard:
Peter Lombard (about 1100 to about 1160) was bishop of Paris, better known as Master of the Sentences, and an entry from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica tells his story. Born of obscure parents at Novara, he studied at Bologna, then moved to France with a letter to Bernard of Clairvaux. He soon won a chair of theology in the cathedral school at Paris.

The entry centers on his famous handbook, the Sentences, written between 1145 and 1150. It gathers the views of the church fathers into four books, the first on God. In 1159 Peter became bishop of Paris, though a charge of buying the office clouds the record of his last years.
britannica-1911-petre-sir-edward:
Sir Edward Petre, Jesuit confessor to King James the Second, is the subject of a life story in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born in Paris in sixteen thirty one, he came from a strongly Catholic family. His father headed a junior branch of the Barons Petre. In sixteen forty nine he was sent to a Jesuit college for his schooling.

He entered the order in sixteen fifty two under another name, but took full orders only much later. In sixteen seventy nine he succeeded his elder brother in title and estates. On James's accession he was chosen as the king's confessor. The entry follows the influence that role gave him at court.
britannica-1911-phillips-edward:
English author Edward Phillips, born in London in sixteen thirty, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was nephew of the poet John Milton, his mother being Milton's only sister. His father died in sixteen thirty one. Edward and his younger brother were educated by Milton himself.

He entered Oxford in sixteen fifty, but left the next year to be a bookseller's clerk. Though he differed from Milton in religion and politics, he stayed on warm terms with his uncle to the end. He tutored the son of the diarist John Evelyn for nine years. His most important work is a list of the chief poets of all ages and lands, with short critical notes. It came out in sixteen seventy five. He also wrote a general dictionary.
britannica-1911-pilchard:
Pilchard is an animal article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a fish of the herring family that fills the seas off south west Europe. The pilchard, Clupea pilchardus, abounds in the Mediterranean and on the Atlantic coasts of Europe up to the English Channel. Sardine is another name for the same fish, and on the coasts of Brittany and Normandy it is called celan. The article tells it from other herrings by the ridged gill cover, the large loose scales, and a dark spot at the shoulder.

The pilchard ranks among the most valued fishes of the English Channel. It spawns far from shore in summer, and its eggs float, unlike the herring's, which stick and sink. The sardines of the west coast of France, tinned in oil for export, are young fish of the same stock as the Cornish catch.
britannica-1911-pococke-edward:
Edward Pococke, who lived from 1604 to 1691, was an English scholar of eastern tongues. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica traces his path from Oxford to the Levant. He won a fellowship at Corpus Christi College in 1628. His first work set out four short New Testament letters from a Syriac text. In 1630 he sailed to Aleppo as chaplain to English merchants. There he made himself a deep Arabic scholar.

He also gathered a rich store of hand written books. Archbishop Laud then set up an Arabic chair at Oxford for him. Pococke took it up in 1636, then sailed again to Constantinople. He spent about three years there buying more books. On his return he gained friends on both sides of the civil wars. In 1648 he rose to the chair of Hebrew as well. The entry paints a scholar kept safe by sheer skill and good will.
britannica-1911-poniard: Poniard is a short arms entry in the 1911 Britannica. A poniard is a dagger of a small size. It is used for stabbing at close range in a fight. The English word is an adaptation from French. That French word was taken up in the 1500s. It is formed from a word for the fist or hand. That root points to the clenched hand that grips it. The entry sends readers to the Dagger article for more.
britannica-1911-poynings-sir-edward:
Sir Edward Poynings, who lived from 1459 to 1521, was an English soldier and lord deputy of Ireland. The 1911 Britannica article says he was the only son of Robert Poynings. His mother was a daughter of Sir William Paston, of the famed Paston Letters. Edward joined a Kentish rising against Richard the Third and had to flee abroad. He then attached himself to Henry, earl of Richmond.

Poynings came back with Henry in 1485 and served the new king in war abroad. In 1493 he was made governor of Calais. The next year he went to Ireland as lord deputy. There he beat the clans that backed the pretender Perkin Warbeck. His parliament at Drogheda in 1494 passed the laws named for him. Those laws bound the Irish parliament to the English one until their repeal in 1782.
britannica-1911-ravenscroft-edward:
Edward Ravenscroft, an English dramatist who flourished from 1671 to 1697, is profiled in this 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. He came of an ancient Flintshire family. He was entered at the Middle Temple but gave his attention chiefly to literature. His first piece, Mamamouchi, was staged at Dorset Garden in 1671. The Careless Lovers, a comedy of intrigue, followed in 1673.

Ravenscroft wrote twelve plays in all. Among them are an English Lawyer adapted from a Latin play, and The London Cuckold of 1683. That piece became a stock play until Garrick struck it from the repertory in 1751. He adapted freely from Molière and others. He once confessed that he but winnowed Shakespeare's corn. He dared to decry the heroic drama, and Dryden hit back. Dryden satirized his Mamamouchi in a prologue, calling it a foolish adaptation from Molière.
britannica-1911-record:
Record is the subject of an archives article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The word comes from a Latin verb meaning to recall to mind. In a strict sense a record is a paper drawn up for a legal or office purpose. It is kept in proper custody to preserve the memory of the act it describes. Such a paper often forms one link in a long process.

The article says the keeper's first care is to preserve that link where it exists. Few lands have escaped a period of neglect, when each office kept or neglected its own papers. Two systems followed that stage. One gathers records and staff into a central office. The other leaves records in local stores but centralizes the staff. England chose the first system.
britannica-1911-redgrave-richard:
Richard Redgrave, who lived from 1804 to 1888, was an English artist born at Pimlico in London. The 1911 Britannica entry follows him from design work to the Royal Academy schools in 1826. His Gulliver on the Farmer Table in 1837 made his name as a painter. Academy ranks rose until he became a full Academician in 1851.

From 1847 he gave long service to the government art schools of the day. Posts made him inspector general of art and art head at South Kensington Museum. He helped found that museum and won great picture gifts for the nation. In 1869 he declined a knighthood, a rare turn the entry records.
britannica-1911-retford:
Retford is the subject of a town entry in the 1911 Britannica. The town lies in Nottinghamshire in England. Its full name in state use is East Retford. It stands where two rail lines cross on the way north. Its count in 1901 was just over twelve thousand souls. A church from the 1200s stands in the town. It was rebuilt in 1658 after a grant of funds.

Trade in corn and cheese was large in the town. Iron works, paper mills, and rubber works gave jobs. The site lay near a Roman road on a river. A ford there may explain the town name root. Old charters from kings span the entry past notes. The town sent two men to the law house for years. It lost that right in the year 1885. Grants for fairs at set feasts are listed at length.
britannica-1911-reward:
Reward, a gift or payment in return for services, is the subject of an entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Reward and regard are forms of the same word, the entry shows. Both came into English from Old French forms built on a root meaning to watch or guard. Ward and guard are kin to them as well.

In early English the two words could stand for each other without change of sense. In use they have since split apart, and regard now means attention, respect, or esteem. The entry then turns to reward in English law, which has two sides. One side asks what act or information a reward is offered for. The other asks what bond is made between the person who offers and the person who claims. Courts may order rewards for help in catching persons charged with set crimes against person and property.
britannica-1911-riemann-georg-friedrich-:
Bernhard Riemann is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Riemann was a German mathematician who lived from 1826 to 1866. He was born near Dannenberg in Hanover. His father was a pastor who had settled at Quickborn. The boy learned at home with his five brothers and sisters. He showed strong gifts in number work at an early age.

The article tells how he soon passed his father and his school master in maths. At school in Luneburg the head lent him great books, which he read and mastered in days. In 1846 he went to Gottingen to study language and church subjects, as his father wished. Maths soon became his chief work there. He moved to Berlin in 1847 to hear its famed teachers. In that time he first formed his deep ideas on the theory of functions.
britannica-1911-rifleman-bird:
Rifleman-bird, or rifle-bird, is the name the English in Australia gave to a fine bird of that land. The name may come from its colours, which matched the well known dress of the rifle regiments of the British army. Its long, hanging side plumes and short tail also recalled the pelisse and jacket those troops once wore. The male is clad in velvet black, glossed with rich purple.

Each feather of the male's belly is tipped with a chevron of green bronze. Scale-like feathers of bright green cap his head, and a patch of blue-green shines on his throat. The same hue marks the top of the mid pair of tail quills. The hen is grey-brown above, with a crown streaked in dull white. Her chin and throat are pale, and her lower parts are deep buff with black marks.
britannica-1911-rigby-richard:
Richard Rigby was an English politician who lived from seventeen twenty two to seventeen eighty eight. His life entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was the only son of Richard Rigby of Mistley Hall in Essex. His father, a merchant, made a fortune through the South Sea Company.

Young Rigby joined the circle of Frederick, prince of Wales, in youth. He entered parliament in seventeen forty five and tied his fate to Bedford. Men called him the brazen boatswain of the Bloomsbury gang crew. In seventeen sixty eight he gained the rich post of paymaster general. He left a great fortune when he died at Bath in seventeen eighty eight.
britannica-1911-rigord:
