Rigord was a French chronicler who lived from about eleven fifty to twelve o nine. His life entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was likely born near Alais in Languedoc and trained as a physician. Later he became a monk at Argenteuil and then at Saint Denis.

Rigord styled himself as chronicler to the king of the Franks in Latin. His chief work tells the life of Philip Augustus, king of France. It runs from the coronation in eleven seventy nine to twelve o six. Early parts praise the king, but later parts judge him more harshly. William the Breton cut and carried on the work after Rigord.
britannica-1911-robert-guiscard:
Robert Guiscard, a Norman leader who lived from about 1015 to 1085, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. His surname means the resourceful one. He was the most famed of the Norman freebooters who took south Italy. The Normans first came as hired swords for Greeks and Lombards.

In 1030 a leader of theirs got the fort of Aversa as a base. Robert, a son of Tancred of Hauteville, reached Italy in 1046. He rose fast and in 1057 took the rule of Apulia from his brother. The pope then made peace with the Normans and granted Robert his lands as a fief. With his brother Roger he went on to seize Messina and Palermo in Sicily. Bari fell to him in 1071.
britannica-1911-robinson-edward:
Edward Robinson (1794-1863) was an American scholar of the Bible, and this 1911 Britannica entry traces his career. He was born in Southington, Connecticut, the son of a Congregational minister, and finished at Hamilton College in 1816. At Andover he fell under the teaching of Moses Stuart, helped prepare a Hebrew grammar for the press, and became an instructor in Hebrew himself.

From 1826 to 1830 he studied in Germany, at Halle and Berlin, and later held posts at Andover, where he founded the Biblical Repository. In 1837 he took a chair at Union Theological Seminary and left for three years of study in Palestine and Germany. The fruit was his Biblical Researches of 1841, which won him a gold medal from the Royal Geographical Society. A second volume came in 1856, though failing sight cut short his larger plans.
britannica-1911-rochford:
Rochford, a town in Essex, England, is set out in a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry. It lies on the small river Roach, near the head of a long estuary. It stands east of London on a branch rail line. In nineteen oh one it had just over eighteen hundred folk.

Its church is a late Gothic building, and a corn exchange stands in the town. Some farm trade is carried on. Rochford Hall is a fine gabled mansion of mixed dates, once held by the Boleyns. A claim that Anne Boleyn was born there is in no way proved, the entry warns. Near the town a strange court is held by an old tenure. It meets at midnight, with no light allowed and voices kept to a whisper.
britannica-1911-rockford:
The 1911 Britannica article on Rockford describes a city in northern Illinois. It is the county seat of Winnebago county. It stands on the Rock river, about 85 miles north-west of Chicago. Its population rose from 23,584 in 1890 to 45,401 in 1910. Many of its people were Swedish immigrants.

The article covers the city's railways and its Carnegie library. It notes the hospitals and Rockford College. That school for women first opened in 1849. Water power from a dam on the river drives the factories. They make furniture, knit goods, and farm tools. The city was first settled in 1834. It was chartered as a city in 1852.
britannica-1911-rolle-de-hampole-richard:
Rolle de Hampole, Richard, is the subject of a 1911 Britannica life of an English hermit. He died in 1349, having been born near Pickering in Yorkshire. His father may have served the Neville house as a dependant. Thomas de Neville paid for the boy's studies at Oxford.

At Oxford he gave himself to faith, not to school logic. He had a strong distaste for the fine points of that learning. At age nineteen he came home and made a hermit's dress. He sewed it from his sister's skirts and his father's hood. Then he ran off to live the hermit life in full. At Dalton a friend's father gave him food, shelter, and garb. He then passed three years in the first stages of the inner life.
britannica-1911-ros-sir-richard:
Sir Richard Ros, an English poet born in fourteen twenty nine, is profiled in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was the son of Sir Thomas Ros, lord of two great seats in Yorkshire and in a mid shire. He was born in March of that year. His fame in the text rests on one long poem in his name.

That poem is a French work turned into English speech. It was first put in print in a Chaucer book of fifteen thirty two. A hand book in a great store ascribes the turned form to Ros by name. The poem dates from about the mid part of its age. It is writ in the tongue of the mid lands. Its speech is, to a marked degree, close to the speech of a late day.
britannica-1911-rowlands-richard:
Richard Rowlands, whose real name was Verstegen, was an Anglo-Dutch student of antiquities who lived from about 1560 to past 1620, says an entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He studied early English history and Anglo-Saxon at Christ Church, Oxford, from 1565. He left without a degree.

The entry tells how he moved to Antwerp, took back his family name, and worked as a printer and engraver. A firm Roman Catholic, he wrote sharply against the treatment of Catholics in England under Elizabeth, which landed him in prison in Paris. His works ranged over old English history, dying well, and the faith he defended.
britannica-1911-rush-richard:
Rush, Richard is a life article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about an American statesman and diplomat. The son of Doctor Benjamin Rush, he was born in Philadelphia on the twenty-ninth of August 1780. He graduated at Princeton in 1797 and was called to the bar in 1800, and high office then came to him in quick order. He served as attorney general of Pennsylvania, then in the same post in the cabinet of President Madison.

For a few months in 1817 he acted as secretary of state. As minister to Great Britain he helped settle the boundary with Canada and arranged the joint occupation of Oregon. He later served as secretary of the treasury under Adams and stood as the vice-presidential candidate on the Adams ticket in 1828. His last post was as minister to France, and he died at Philadelphia in 1859.
britannica-1911-russell-sir-william-howa:
William Howard Russell, who lived from 1821 to 1907, was an English war correspondent born near Tallaght in Ireland. The 1911 Britannica entry follows him from Trinity College to lean years on his own. A Times man in Ireland handed him the Longford election reports to cover. Success there turned his mind to journalism for good as a life path.

London and a spell at Cambridge followed, then Times work back in Ireland in 1843. Reports on the O Connell meetings and on Irish railways built his name. Plain speech on a land inspection drew a sharp reply from O Connell himself. The entry opens the rise of the first great modern war reporter.
britannica-1911-sabine-sir-edward:
Edward Sabine is the subject of a life entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was an English star watcher and earth measurer born in Dublin in seventeen eighty eight. He was trained at a royal army school and took a post in the guns at age fifteen. His one taste of war came at a siege in Canada.

The entry follows his posts as star man on bold trips to the far north. He sailed with two famed hunts for a north west sea route. His best work fixed the length of a key swing tool used in earth science. He also mapped the pull of earth magnetism across the globe. He led the top science body of his land for ten years.
britannica-1911-said-pasha-kurd: Said Pasha Kurd, a Turkish statesman born at Suleimanié in 1834, is noted in brief in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was a son of Hussein Pasha. After varied posts in office work, he became governor general of the Archipelago in 1881. He served as minister for foreign affairs in 1882. Berlin then took him as ambassador in 1883. He held the foreign post again in 1885. Later he led the Council of State, a post he kept till his death on 29 October 1907.
britannica-1911-saint-priest-francois-em:
Francois Emmanuel Guignard, comte de Saint Priest, lived from 1735 to 1821 and served France as a statesman. The 1911 Britannica entry notes he was made a knight of Malta at age five. Army service began at fifteen and ended in 1763 with colonel rank. He then spoke for the French court at Lisbon for four years.

From 1768 to 1785 he held the embassy at Constantinople for France. His memoir on that post and on French trade in the Levant came out in 1877. Later he joined the ministry of Necker with no set portfolio in charge. In 1789 he took charge of the royal household under Necker.
britannica-1911-scabbard: Scabbard, the sheath of a sword, is a word traced in a short entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Early forms include scauberk and scaubert. The ending surely comes from a Teutonic root meaning to protect, seen also in hauberk, a guard for the neck. The first part is less certain. Skeat links it to an Old French word for a shell. On that reading the word means an outer shell that covers and protects.
britannica-1911-secretary-bird:
Secretary bird is a strange African bird of prey with long legs. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica opens with the hunt for its name. A Dutch writer first described it well in 1769. His bird lived in the menagerie of the prince of Orange.

At the Cape the bird was called the Archer for its stride. That word was bent in speech into the name Secretary. An English writer in 1770 drew it as a new genus unknowing. Later authors piled wrong names and poor drawings on it. One plate of 1779 gave it its first science name. Cuvier in 1798 set the genus that still holds it alone. The bird stands nearly four feet high, the entry notes. Its odd crest and gait struck every early observer.
britannica-1911-shuffle-board:
Shuffle-board, first called shove board, is a game in which disks are pushed by hand or with a tool, and the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica explains it in a games entry. The aim is to stop the disks on or inside set lines or boxes marked on a board, a table or a floor. The game was once much played in England.

Under names like shove groat and shovel penny, it was a favourite at great country houses from the fourteen hundreds. One board at Chartley Hall ran over thirty feet long and was made of 260 pieces. In the United States the game had a wide vogue. Boards there ran near thirty feet, with a gutter all round and a deuce line near each end. Each side used four disks of polished brass or iron.
britannica-1911-sideboard:
Sideboard, the tall dining room table with drawers and shelves, is traced as a craft form in the 1911 Britannica. At first it was just a side table, true to its name. Tiered forms stood in Tudor homes, kin to the court cupboard. In the early part of the seventeen hundreds plain side tables took their place. New use of fine dark wood drove much of that shift in form.

Stone tops then called for a more stout build than slight wood tops. Fine legs, carved leaves, and mask drops mark the best of the age. Chippendale shops made fine ones, but the text gives him no role in the form shift. Home needs did that work, as wine stores and plate warmers were joined to the table.
britannica-1911-simon-richard:
Richard Simon is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Simon was a French biblical critic, born at Dieppe in 1638. He studied at the college of the Oratory in his home city. A friend's kindness then let him study theology at Paris.

At Paris he showed an early taste for Hebrew and other Eastern tongues. After teaching philosophy at Juilly, he was recalled to a task he loved. He made a catalogue of the Eastern books in the Oratory's library. His first book appeared in 1671, with Latin renderings and notes. Its aim was to show that Greek and Roman teaching on the Eucharist agreed. The entry opens the career of a scholar who brought hard questions to the study of the Bible.
britannica-1911-sleaford:
Sleaford is a market town in Lincolnshire in England, as the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica sets out. It stands in a fertile, partly fenny district on the river Slea in the east. Its count in 1901 was 5,468 for the urban district. It lies 112 miles north of London by the Great Northern railway. 

The church of Saint Denis is one of the finest in the county, the text says. It shows Norman work in the base of its west tower and an Early English spire above. Its nave is of fine late Decorated work with an ornate south porch. A splendid carved rood screen of oak stands inside the church. The trade of Sleaford is principally agricultural, as befits its rich district, and malting is also carried on there.
britannica-1911-smith-richard-baird:
Richard Baird Smith, a British engineer officer who lived from 1818 to 1861, is covered in a 1911 Britannica life story. He was the son of a navy surgeon and was born on December 31, 1818. He was schooled at Lasswade and Addiscombe and joined the Madras Engineers in 1838. He later moved to the Bengal Engineers.

Smith fought through the second Sikh war and then worked on canals for some years. When the Mutiny broke out he held Roorkee and kept its people safe. At the siege of Delhi he served as chief engineer of the works. He urged an early assault on the city, but the chance was let slip. He held the siege firm till fresh troops came, and the attack won in September.
britannica-1911-snow-leopard:
Snow-Leopard is an animal article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a large cat of the high hills of Central Asia. The beast is also called the Ounce. It is built much like the leopard but wears longer fur. The coat is grey, marked with large dark rosettes.

The article gives the size of the beast at about four feet for head and body. The tail runs three feet more, and the height is two feet. It lives among rocks and hunts wild sheep and goats. It also takes sheep, goats, and dogs from villages, and even kills ponies. The text says it has never been known to attack a man. London zoo beasts of this kind proved tame and playful.
britannica-1911-spikenard:
Spikenard is a plant entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It tells of a famed scent used in rich salves of the old world. Roman and eastern courts prized the scent for its lasting power. The New Testament names a salve of pure nard as a gift of great price.

The entry gives old price lists that show how dear the best nard ran. Fake blends cut the pure stuff and made prices swing wide by grade. The true salve mixed nard with roots, fruits, gum, and myrrh. Old Roman books set down each part of that rich mix by name. The hunt for the true plant source of nard fills the rest of the piece.
britannica-1911-spinal-cord:
Spinal cord is an anatomy article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The cord is the part of the central nervous system that lies in the canal of the spine. It runs from the base of the skull to the first lumbar vertebra. It is about eighteen inches long and fills only the upper two-thirds of the canal.

Three membranes wrap the cord, the same three that wrap the brain. The outer is the dura mater, the middle the thin arachnoid, and the inner the pia mater. Between the inner two lies a space filled with cerebro-spinal fluid. A row of saw-tooth ligaments runs down each side of the cord. These tie the pia mater to the dura and hold the cord in place. The piece, drawn from Gray's Anatomy, treats the coverings in close detail.
britannica-1911-stafford:
Stafford is a town article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Stafford is the county town of Staffordshire, England. It stands on the River Sow, a western branch of the Trent. The entry calls it an important railway junction north-west of London.

Lines ran from Stafford to Wolverhampton, Birmingham, and Walsall. Other lines served Shrewsbury, the eastern counties, and the Potteries district. The town kept a number of quaint half-timbered houses amid much new building. Its church of St Mary is a fine cross-shaped building. Parts of it show Norman, Early English, and Decorated work in turn. The church had once been collegiate, and its canons are named in Domesday Book. The entry suits readers who want the frame of an old county town: its river, rails, streets, and church.
britannica-1911-stanley-edward:
Edward Stanley, bishop of Norwich who lived from 1770 to 1849, has a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was the younger brother of the first Baron Stanley of Alderley. Born in London, he was educated at Saint John College, Cambridge. He was ordained in 1802 and became rector of Alderley in Cheshire three years later.

At Alderley Stanley took a great interest in education in his parish. He encouraged in special the teaching of secular subjects at his school there. In 1837 he was consecrated bishop of Norwich in succession. The diocese at that time was conspicuous for laxity and want of discipline in its clergy. He set out to remedy that state, though at first he met much opposition. Ordinations and confirmations were held more regularly, schools were inspected, and unfit clergy were removed under his rule.
britannica-1911-stanyhurst-richard:
Richard Stanyhurst (1547-1618) was an English translator of Virgil, and this 1911 Britannica entry follows his life between Ireland, Oxford, and Spain. He was born in Dublin, where his father was recorder of the city and speaker of the Irish House of Commons. Richard went to University College, Oxford, in 1563 and took his degree five years later. There he grew close to Edmund Campian, then read law in London.

He wrote for Holinshed's Chronicles a description of Ireland and a history of the country under Henry the Eighth. A later writer attacked both as a warped account of Irish affairs seen through English eyes. After his first wife died in 1579 he went to the Netherlands and grew active in the Catholic cause. He spent time in Spain, posing as a physician while reporting on Catholic interests in England.
britannica-1911-starboard-and-larboard:
Starboard and larboard are sea terms for the sides of a ship. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica traces both words to old steering. Starboard is the right side, faced toward the bows. Larboard named the left side in older use.

Both words end in bord, the Old English word for a ship side. Starboard joins that to steer, the steering side. Ships were once steered by a sweep worked from the right. The left side first bore a name meaning back board. Later forms bent toward the sound of starboard itself. That likeness caused mix ups at sea in bad weather. So navies ordered port for the left side, Britain in 1844 and America in 1896.
britannica-1911-stargard:
Stargard, a town of Germany in the Prussian province of Pomerania, is described in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands on the left bank of the Ihna, east of Stettin. Rail lines meet here for more than one route. Its count in nineteen hundred and five was near twenty seven thousand.

The town once sat in the Hanseatic League, and signs of that early weight remain. A large church from the thirteen hundreds stands out. A town hall from the next age and old gates and towers add to the stock. The old walls have in the main been turned into shore walks and drives. New court halls and three large barracks mark the modern town. Trade deals in stock, grain, and raw goods. Mills make cigars, cloth, and knit goods, and iron works add weight.
britannica-1911-steele-sir-richard:
Sir Richard Steele, an English man of letters who lived from 1672 to 1729, is treated in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. His name is bound up for all time with that of his close friend Addison. Steele was the lesser of the two in pure literary gift, the text grants. Yet the gain from their joint work was not all on his side, since Addison has taken more than his share of the credit.

Steele himself joked that he fared like a prince who calls in a strong neighbour and then cannot stand without him. The text holds that quip to be too hard on its maker. In truth the two men were the complement of each other in their work. The balance of mutual gain between them was far more even than Steele claimed.
britannica-1911-sterne-richard:
Richard Sterne, an English churchman who rose to Archbishop of York, gets a life in the 1911 Britannica. Born at Mansfield near the year fifteen hundred, he learned at its free school and at Cambridge. He held posts at Corpus Christi and Jesus Colleges. As aide to Archbishop Laud he backed the royal cause with college plate. Parliament jailed him for that zeal and stripped his posts.

He stood by Laud at his death and taught school while the king was gone. At the return of the king he got his posts back and rose fast. He helped check the Prayer Book text and took the see of York in sixteen sixty four. Blame in the text falls on his love of gain for his kin. He died in sixteen eighty three.
britannica-1911-stillingfleet-edward:
Edward Stillingfleet was an English divine who lived from sixteen thirty five to sixteen ninety. His life entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Cranborne in Dorset, he entered Saint John College, Cambridge, at age thirteen. He took his first degree in sixteen fifty two and a fellowship next year.

Stillingfleet served as tutor in great homes before a post at Sutton. There he published Irenicum in sixteen fifty nine, his early key work. That book sought a truce between Episcopal and Presbyterian church rule camps. He held church form was not vital, yet he condemned Nonconformity then. He aided more than one minister cast out for faith views later.
britannica-1911-stockton-francis-richard:
Francis Richard Stockton, who lived from 1834 to 1902, was an American novelist born in Philadelphia. The 1911 Britannica article says he was born on the fifth of April 1834. He had a high school schooling and became a skilled wood engraver. He wrote for papers and magazines in Philadelphia and New York. In 1873 he became assistant editor of Saint Nicholas. About 1880 he gave up desk work to write full time.

His tales of fancy for children made him widely loved. Books such as Ting-a-Ling and The Floating Prince are named in the entry. His Rudder Grange of 1879, a chain of sketches, won grown readers. The article rates his true gift as the short tale. Best known is The Lady or the Tiger, from 1884, one of the most famed of American stories. He died in Washington on the twentieth of April 1902.
britannica-1911-stratford: Stratford, a city and port of entry in Ontario, Canada, is the subject of a brief entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It is the capital of Perth county, on the Avon river, eighty three miles west south west of Toronto by rail. The entry gives it 9,959 people in 1901. Its chief trades are railway repair and machine shops, flour mills, saw mills, wool mills, and works for engines and farm tools. It also ships out much cheese and other dairy and farm produce.
britannica-1911-strauss-richard:
Richard Strauss (born 1864) was a German composer, born at Munich, the son of Franz Strauss, a famed horn player. This 1911 Britannica article calls him something of a prodigy: a pianist at four, a composer at six, and in earnest study by ten under the Munich court conductor Meyer. Singers took up his songs, and Bülow championed his early works.

Strauss at first wrote under the sway of older masters, Liszt in one work and Mendelssohn in another. Bülow, and still more Alexander Ritter, woke his interest in the modern growth of music. In 1885 he followed Bülow as conductor of the Meiningen orchestra for a few months. After travel in Italy he became a conductor at the Munich Opera under Hermann Levi.
britannica-1911-studer-bernhard:
Bernhard Studer, a Swiss scholar of rocks, gets a life in the 1911 Britannica. Born near Berne in seventeen ninety four, he was trained for the church at first. At Gottingen the lore of rocks won him from that path for life. More study at Freiburg, Berlin, and Paris deepened that new bent. In eighteen sixteen he took a post to teach math and heat lore at Berne.

His first book on a rock bed came out in eighteen twenty five. Deep probes of the west Alps filled his next great work in print. He helped found the college of Berne and took its first rock chair. Maps of all Swiss rocks came from his hand with a peer aide. He ran the state rock probe of his land till his death in eighteen eighty seven.
britannica-1911-sugar-bird:
Sugar-bird is the West Indian name for the small birds of the genus Certhiola, told here in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. They haunt the curing-houses where sugar is kept, drawn by the swarms of flies. They also slip into dwelling houses, hopping over the furniture in search of spiders and insects.

In shape and motion they put a northern watcher in mind of a nuthatch, and their black, yellow, and olive dress recalls a titmouse. They keep in pairs and build a domed, untidy nest holding three white eggs blotched with rusty red. Many kinds are known, some chained to a single island, three ranging the mainland from Mexico to Brazil. The article calls the genus a fine case of how being cut off splits one stock into many forms.
britannica-1911-sumner-charles-richard:
Charles Richard Sumner is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Sumner was an English bishop, born at Kenilworth in 1790. He was educated at Eton and at Trinity College, Cambridge. After his degrees he was ordained deacon and priest.

He ministered to the English congregation at Geneva for two winters. Then came a curacy at Highclere in Hampshire, held for five years. King George the Fourth wished to make him a canon of Windsor in 1820. The prime minister objected, so Sumner took a royal chaplaincy instead. Other posts followed quickly in the king's gift. In 1826 he was consecrated bishop of Llandaff, and in 1827 bishop of Winchester. The entry praises his long rule at Winchester as energetic, tactful, and generous. Though evangelical in his views, he did not limit his patronage to one party.
britannica-1911-sutton-sir-richard:
Sir Richard Sutton (d. c. 1524) founded Brasenose College, Oxford, with William Smyth, bishop of Lincoln. He was the first layman to found a college. He is said to have come of a good north-country family near Macclesfield in Cheshire. Little is known of his life, but he was a barrister. In 1497 he sat on the privy council, and in 1513 he became steward of the nunnery of Sion at Isleworth.

How Smyth and Sutton came to plan a college is not known. In 1508 a will left money for a college of Brasenose if their plan went ahead in a set time. That same year Sutton took a long lease of Brasenose Hall and Little University Hall. From then till his death he bought estates to endow the new college. He is also thought to have given funds to Corpus Christi College, Oxford.
britannica-1911-taft-william-howard:
William Howard Taft, born in 1857, was the twenty seventh president of the United States. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica opens his life at his birth in Cincinnati, Ohio. His father Alphonso had been a judge and a cabinet member. He also served as envoy to Austria and Russia. The son went to public schools in Cincinnati. He shone at Yale in class work, sports, and social life.

He left Yale second in his class in 1878. Law study at Cincinnati brought him a degree and a top prize in 1880. Brief news work for his brother's papers came next. Posts as a county prosecutor and tax chief followed. He gave up the tax post in 1883 to go back to law. In 1887 he was named a judge of the Ohio superior court. The head of the entry stops there, before his rise to the White House.
britannica-1911-taylor-bayard:
Taylor, Bayard is a life story from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about an American author and traveller. He was born at Kennett Square in Pennsylvania on the eleventh of January 1825 and died in 1878. He was the son of a well-to-do farmer. At seventeen he was apprenticed to a printer in West Chester.

A small book of poems, printed at Philadelphia in 1844, brought him a little cash. It also brought him to the notice of the New York Tribune. With that money, and an advance for work to be done in Europe, he sailed east. He roamed on foot through parts of England, France, Germany, and Italy. The article stresses that he was a born traveller. That walking tour of near two years set the course of his life.
britannica-1911-teach-edward:
Edward Teach (died 1718) was an English pirate known far and wide as Blackbeard, and a short life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica sketches his career. He is believed to have been born at Bristol. He is said to have gone to the West Indies in the War of the Spanish Succession. There he worked as a privateer before the peace of 1713.

Teach is first heard of as a pirate at the end of 1716. The next year he seized a large French merchant ship. He renamed her Queen Anne’s Revenge and fitted her as a warship of forty guns. His robberies in the Spanish Main, the West Indies, and off Carolina and Virginia won him an infamous name. He made his winter quarters in a handy inlet in North Carolina.
britannica-1911-temple-sir-richard:
Temple, Sir Richard is a life story from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about an English officer in India. He was born on the eighth of March 1826 and died in 1902. He was schooled at Rugby and Haileybury, then joined the Bengal Civil Service. His hard work and ready pen soon won him notice.

He served for years as private secretary to John Lawrence in the Punjab. He gained skill in finance under James Wilson, then became Resident at Hyderabad. In 1868 he joined the supreme government, first as foreign secretary and then in finance. His work in the famine of 1874 won praise, and he was made lieutenant-governor of Bengal. A baronetcy followed in 1876, and in 1877 he became governor of Bombay.
britannica-1911-thetford:
Thetford, a market town mainly in Norfolk, England, is set out in a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry. Part of the town lies in Suffolk. It stands where the river Thet joins the Little Ouse, in level fertile country. In nineteen oh one it had over four thousand folk.

In the time of Edward the Third the town had twenty churches and eight monasteries. Now three churches stand, mostly of flint work in a late Gothic style. Two gatehouses are the chief remains of the old houses of monks. A vast mound called Castle Hill is the main relic of old times. A grammar school dates from sixteen ten. Brewing and tanning are carried on, with flour mills, brick kilns, and iron foundries. The Little Ouse can be sailed by barges.
britannica-1911-time-standard:
Standard time is the subject of an entry in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Local time is set by the relation of a place's meridian to the sun. Noon at any place is the moment when the sun passes that meridian. In practice mean time is now used everywhere, the entry explains.

As the earth turns, all its meridians are brought under the sun in turn. Noon thus travels around the earth and makes the circuit in twenty four hours. It follows that any hour is later by four minutes for each degree westward. That steady shift is the problem that a standard system of time zones was built to solve.
britannica-1911-trevithick-richard:
Richard Trevithick is the subject of a life entry in the 1911 Britannica. He was an English engineer and inventor from 1771 to 1833. He was born in Cornwall in April of that first year. His father ran key mines in that county. He went to one school only, at Camborne town. He was slow at books but quick with figures. Great strength and skill at wrestling marked the man.

At eighteen he began to help his father at work. Rich ideas for machines came from him in flow. He soon stood as the great rival of James Watt. A better pump for deep mines came in 1797. Two years later he built a strong steam engine. That engine used high pressure with no condenser. On Christmas Eve 1801 his road engine bore riders. Those riders were the first borne by steam power.
britannica-1911-turkey-bird:
Turkey, short for turkey cock or turkey hen, is treated in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica as a word puzzle as much as a bird. The entry calls it a well known large tame bird of the fowl kind. Yet the bird came to Europe from the New World. It had nothing to do with Turkey or with Turks at all.

The text argues the name first fit a different bird, the guinea fowl. Some writers in the fifteen and sixteen hundreds mixed the two birds up. As both grew more common and better known, the mix up cleared. The name turkey then stuck to the New World bird alone. One guess ties it to the bird call note, which can be spelled as turk. The entry is a neat lesson in how names drift.
britannica-1911-turpin-richard:
Richard Turpin (1706–1739) was an English robber, known as Dick Turpin, and a short life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica gives his crimes. He was born in 1706 at Hempstead in Essex. His father kept an alehouse in that village. Turpin was apprenticed to a butcher as a boy.

He was caught at cattle stealing and left that trade. He joined a gang of deer stealers and smugglers in Essex. That gang also robbed farmhouses as a practice. They terrorized the women of the houses while the men were away. Turpin took the lead in that class of outrage, the entry says. When the gang was broken up, he went into partnership with Tom King, a noted highwayman. At last he fled to Yorkshire and set up as a horse dealer. He was convicted of horse stealing at York and hanged.
britannica-1911-wagner-wilhelm-richard:
Wilhelm Richard Wagner (1813-1883) was a German composer of opera, poet, and essay writer. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica begins with his school years at Dresden and Leipzig. He turned a hand to translating Homer books for fun as a boy. Early conducting posts at Magdeburg and elsewhere paid poorly and felt unsettled.

Two early operas gained little or no staging in that lean time. He wed actress Wilhelmina Planer and moved through Königsberg to Riga. A trip to Paris in 1839 brought rejection and hardship instead of fame. Rienzi then won a strong success at Dresden in 1842. The Flying Dutchman followed the next year to a cooler welcome.
britannica-1911-weaver-bird:
Weaver-bird is the shared name for a large group of small birds. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica puts the group at two to three hundred kinds. The name comes from the woven nests that many of them build. Some nests rank among the most skilled work in the bird world. Early writers had spread these birds across four bird groups. Cuvier first drew them into one genus in 1817.

Later writers raised the group to a family of its own, the Ploceidae. The entry splits it into two subfamilies. One lives chiefly in Africa and its islands. The other ranges over parts of Africa, Asia, and Australia. The birds are near kin to finches and sparrow like in build. Males of some kinds glow crimson, scarlet, or gold against black. Females stay dull in tone. Most nests are domed, and some hang in odd shapes.
britannica-1911-weber-wilhelm-eduard:
Wilhelm Eduard Weber, who lived from 1804 to 1891, was a German physicist. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica opens with his birth at Wittenberg. He took his degree at Halle in 1826 and taught there. In 1831 he moved to Göttingen as professor of physics. In 1837 he was one of seven professors expelled for protest. They had objected to the king's scrapping of the constitution. After years away he returned to Göttingen in 1849.

His name rests on his work in measuring electric force. Before him no fixed system for such measures existed. He showed that electric amounts could be defined in pure terms. Length, time, and mass alone fix those units, as Gauss did for magnetism. About 1833 he also built an early electric telegraph. It worked over a span of some 9,000 feet. With his brothers he wrote a famed treatise on waves.
britannica-1911-weiss-bernhard:
Bernhard Weiss, a German Protestant scholar of the New Testament, born in 1827, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born at Königsberg on the twentieth of June. He studied theology at Königsberg, Halle, and Berlin. In 1852 he became a professor at Königsberg, and later a full professor at Berlin.

Weiss stood against the Tübingen school of criticism. In 1880 he was made a superior consistorial councillor. The article lists his many books, well known to students in Britain and America. He edited and revised comments on most of the Gospels and Epistles, through many editions. His own works include a textbook of biblical theology and a life of Jesus. A book on the sources of Luke's Gospel appeared in 1907. He also revised the great comment series begun by Meyer.
britannica-1911-westmacott-sir-richard:
Sir Richard Westmacott, who lived from 1775 to 1856, was a British sculptor. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica opens with his birth in London. His father, a sculptor of some name, taught him the craft as a boy. At eighteen he went to Rome to study under Canova. Classical work held his heart all his life. Within a year he won first prizes at Florence and Rome.

Home in London, he showed work at the Royal Academy each year. He became a full member in 1811. In 1827 he took Flaxman's chair as professor of sculpture there. A knighthood followed in 1837. Public statues and monuments poured from his studio. The entry is cool toward many of them. His monuments in St Paul's and Westminster Abbey won more praise at the time.
britannica-1911-whalley-edward:
Edward Whalley, who lived from about 1615 to about 1675, is the subject of a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was a son of Richard Whalley, once sheriff of Nottinghamshire, and a kin of Oliver Cromwell. He is said to have worked first as a wool draper. When civil war broke out, he took arms for Parliament and rose in Cromwell's horse troops.

The life gives his war record in some detail, from Gainsborough in 1643 to Marston Moor and Naseby. He later held King Charles as a captive at Hampton Court, and treated him with care and courtesy. Whalley sat on the court that tried the king and signed his death warrant. He then served in Scotland, where he was wounded at Dunbar.
britannica-1911-whittington-richard:
Richard Whittington, a mayor of London who died in 1423, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was the third son of Sir William Whittington of Pauntley in Gloucestershire. A mercer by trade, he began in trade with good backing and wed Alice, daughter of a Dorset knight with much land. He sat on the city council and became an alderman in March 1393.

When the mayor died in June 1397, the king named Whittington to fill the post, and the city chose him that autumn. He grew very rich and lent large sums to both Henry the Fourth and Henry the Fifth. Tale has it that at a feast for Henry the Fifth he burnt bonds worth 60,000 pounds that he had paid off. He also oversaw work and funds for the finishing of Westminster Abbey.
britannica-1911-wingfield-sir-richard:
Sir Richard Wingfield, an English envoy who lived from about 1469 to 1525, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was one of a dozen or more sons of a Suffolk knight. He rose as a courtier under Henry the Seventh. In 1511 he was made marshal of Calais.

His errands took him to the pope's court, to the Netherlands, and to France. In 1520 he served as envoy at the French court. He helped plan the great meet of Henry and Francis at the Field of the Cloth of Gold. Twice in 1521 he went to Charles the Fifth to keep him from war on France. He died at Toledo in 1525 while on a mission to Spain. Lands in many parts of England were his reward.
britannica-1911-winkelmann-eduard:
Eduard Winkelmann is the subject of a life entry in the 1911 Britannica. He was a German writer on the past from 1838 to 1896. He was born at Danzig in June 1838. He studied at schools in Berlin and Gottingen. He worked on a great set of German past texts. In 1869 he became a teacher of past at Bern. Four years later he took the same post at Heidelberg.

He also spent time teaching in Russia for a span. He died at Heidelberg in February 1896. One book of his dealt with the Anglo Saxons. A stay in Russia led to a list of Livonian sources. His chief works deal with the empire in later middle ages. Books on two rival kings of that age are named. Long works on Emperor Frederick the Second fill the list. He also edited sets of state acts and rolls.
britannica-1911-yates-richard:
Richard Yates is the subject of a life entry in the 1911 Britannica. He was an American leader in politics from 1818 to 1873. He was born at Warsaw, Kentucky, in January 1818. He took his degree at a college in Illinois in 1838. He was called to the bar and joined the Whig party. He served in the state house in two spans of years. He sat in Congress from 1851 to 1855.

He lost a bid for a third term as a Republican. From 1861 to 1865 he was governor of Illinois. He did well in raising troops for the war. He checked strong pro Southern feeling in the state. He sat in the Senate from 1865 to 1871. There he stood out in the laws of Reconstruction. He died at Saint Louis in November 1873. His son later held the same governor post.
british-highways-and-byways-from-a-motor:
Thos. D. Murphy wrote a tour record of motoring through Britain, printed at Boston in 1908. Five thousand miles of road in England, Wales, and Scotland form the run. Sixteen colour plates, thirty-two duogravures from photos, and two maps dress the book. A half-timbered row at Ledbury fronts the text.

No guide-book aim is claimed in the foreword. Maps and road notes may still serve that use, Murphy grants. Off-beat places fill the route, reached best by car yet open by rail or cycle. Home readers who never cross the sea are kept in mind as well. Good and bad highways, towns great and small, and country folk met on the way give the chronicle its bulk. The car is a means, not the hero: Britain seen slow from its byways is the point.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alexis-xyste-:
Alexis-Xyste Bernard was Bishop of St. Hyacinth in Quebec, Canada, born at Beloeil in December 1847. He studied classics and theology under the Sulpician Fathers in Montreal and was ordained a priest in October 1871. After a year as curate he rose through Sorel College, the cathedral chapter, and diocesan offices, becoming president, canon, archdeacon, diocesan secretary, vicar-general, provost, and prothonotary apostolic.

After Bishop Moreau's death in 1901, Bernard stayed on as vicar-general under Bishop Decelles, and on Decelles's death in 1905 he was elected vicar-capitular. The Sisters of St. Joseph owe him their organization as a teaching body. He also edited nine volumes of the diocese's pastoral letters, plus synodal decrees and a clerical-conference summary. He refused the see of St. Hyacinth for reasons of health until Pius X ordered him to accept, and he was consecrated in February 1906.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ancient-dioce:
Putta, the exiled Bishop of Rochester, is named first Bishop of Hereford, in 676, though Bede says only that he received a church and land in Mercia from Sexulf of Lichfield. That grant likely formed the diocese's nucleus. Its bounds were unfixed at the end of the eighth century. In 793 the body of Ethelbert, martyred king of the East Saxons, was buried at Hereford, and his shrine drew pilgrims seeking miracles.

The cathedral, served by secular canons, took Saint Mary and Saint Ethelbert as its titulars. The Welsh destroyed the shrine in 1055 and badly damaged the rebuilt cathedral. Bishop Robert de Losinga restored it after the Norman Conquest. Successors added the central tower about 1200, with choir, Lady Chapel, and north transept work in the thirteenth century. Later unskilful restoration replaced medieval work with eighteenth-century building. The Hereford Use and the Mappa Mundi close the article.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-antoine-simon:
Antoine-Simon Maillard, a French missionary sent to Acadia in 1735, became the apostle of the Micmac people. After Louisbourg fell in 1745, he hid in the woods and served scattered Acadians and native peoples across Cape Breton and Nova Scotia. Over eight years he mastered the Micmac tongue, a language of great difficulty.

For the Micmacs he made a picture alphabet, a grammar, a dictionary, a prayer book, a catechism, and sermons. The English, who tolerated no other Catholic priest in Acadia, later built him a church at Halifax and paid him a pension. His people kept the faith he taught, and the entry honours a missionary of patience and deep influence.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-asgaard:
Asgaard, from As, plural Aesir, Norse for the gods, and gaard, yard or enclosure, the Garden of the Gods, was the place where gods and goddesses dwelt apart and ruled. A bridge called Bilrast ran to it. In its middle stood a great castle with Odavold, where gods held their assemblies. It held two magnificent halls: Gladsheim, with Odin's throne Hlidskjalf and seats for gods, and Vingolf, with a seat for Frigg and seats for goddesses.

From that heavenly country the gods govern the world and humanity. Odin reigns as father and head, penetrating all, animating all, giving people intelligence and enthusiasm and breathing into them desire for combat and war. Beside him stands his wife Frigg, the all-nourishing earth, dwelling at Fensal, with other gods' homes such as Thrudvang scattered through Asgaard. The entry maps Norse heaven as a walled estate of halls.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-baron-louis-j:
Baron Louis Jacques Thénard was a chemist born at Louptière in France in 1777, who died at Paris in 1857. Too poor to pay Vauquelin's twenty-franc monthly fee, he entered the laboratory only through the chemist's sisters' intercession. After three years he lectured despite a provincial accent, saving theater money to study actors' speech. His first original memoir appeared in 1799, beginning half a century of chemical contributions.

In a single month he invented Thénard blue, a cobalt pigment for the Sèvres factory. His 1813 Treatise on Chemistry held vogue for twenty-five years, so that nearly all Europe learned chemistry from Thénard. Working with Gay-Lussac, he discovered boron, studied hydrogen dioxide, and nearly beat Davy to isolating chlorine. Made a baron by Charles X in 1825, he served in the legislature, and his village later took his name.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-beard:
Among Jews and most Eastern peoples, the beard was cherished as a symbol of virility. Cutting another man's beard was an outrage, shaving one's own marked mourning, and a defiled beard suggested madness. Ceremonial beard cuttings smacking of pagan superstition were strictly forbidden, and monuments show Jews invariably bearded. Egyptians, by contrast, commonly shaved: Joseph was made to shave before meeting Pharaoh.

Greece and Rome also shaved shortly before Christ, until Hadrian's accession restored beards, as imperial statues show. For early Christian clergy evidence is unclear, though ancient monuments mostly show bearded Apostles. Jerome seems to censure long beards, but no firm conclusion follows from him or Augustine. Capuchins and Camaldolese Hermits wear beards by rule as austerity and penance, while other priests need their bishop's leave for exemption.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bl-theophane-:
Blessed Théophane Vénard, a French missionary martyred in Tonkin, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born at St-Loup in the diocese of Poitiers in 1829, he died in Tonkin in 1861. Schooled at Doué-la-Fontaine, Montmorillon, and Poitiers, he entered the Paris Foreign Missions seminary and was ordained in 1852.

After fifteen months at Hong Kong he reached West Tonkin, where Christians suffered under Minh-Menh's persecutions. A new royal edict drove bishops and priests into hiding, and Vénard, captured after years of secret ministry, was beheaded. Letters home, full of joy and wit, made him beloved in France. The entry presents a young martyr of Vietnam.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bl-thomas-for: Blessed Thomas Ford, a martyr, was born in Devonshire and died at Tyburn on 28 May 1582. He took his M.A. at Trinity College, Oxford, in 1567, went to Douai in 1570, and was among the first three students ordained there, receiving all orders at Brussels in March 1573. After a divinity degree he returned to England in 1576 as chaplain at Lyford, was arrested with Edmund Campion in 1581, thrice tortured in the Tower, and executed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bonaventure-g:
Bonaventure Giffard, vicar apostolic of the Midlands, kept English Catholic life alive through prison and decades of hiding. Born at Wolverhampton in 1642, he was schooled at Douai and Paris, earned a Sorbonne doctorate, and became preacher to James II. In 1688 he was consecrated bishop at Whitehall and put in charge of the Midlands vicariate.

James made him president of Magdalen College, Oxford, over the electors' Protestant choice, but he was ejected within five months. After the Revolution he spent nearly two years in Newgate prison, then lived in peril from pursuivants for over twenty-four years. From 1703 he also covered Leyburn's district, and from 1708 to 1713 the Western vicariate, aided by his brother Andrew until 1714.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-charles-louis:
A life of Charles Louis Richard, a Dominican theologian and publicist from Lorraine who died by firing squad during the French Revolution. Born at Blainville-sur-l'Eau in 1711 to a poor family of noble descent, he entered the Order of St. Dominic at sixteen, studied theology in Paris, and took his doctorate at the Sorbonne. He then preached and defended religion against the philosophes, the Enlightenment writers Voltaire and d'Alembert among them.

Driven into exile at Mons in Belgium by the Revolution, Richard was caught during the second French invasion of 1794. Too old to flee, he was tried by court martial and shot for his pamphlet comparing the French who executed their king with the Jews who crucified Christ. His works include a vast sacred encyclopedia, the Bibliothèque sacrée, in five volumes, with a supplement, and a five-volume analysis of Church councils printed at Paris between 1772 and 1777.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-charles-mauri:
An entry on Charles Maurice de Talleyrand-Périgord, Prince of Benevento, Bishop of Autun, and a slippery diplomat of revolutionary France. Born in Paris in 1754, the eldest son of an old family, he was steered into holy orders because a childhood accident left him lame. Ordained in 1779, he became agent-general of the clergy, then bishop in 1789, and was elected to the Estates General, the assembly that opened the Revolution.

Talleyrand backed the Declaration of the Rights of Man, praised the seizure of Church property, swore the Civil Constitution, and was excommunicated in 1791 after consecrating bishops for the new regime. Sent to London in 1792, banished by the Convention, and exiled in America, he returned to Paris in 1796. He rose again as foreign minister, serving successive regimes with the same cool skill. The entry follows his career through empire and restoration.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-charles-warre:
An entry on Charles Warren Stoddard, an American author whose South Sea writings won praise from leading critics. Born at Rochester, New York, in 1843, he moved with his family to San Francisco in 1855, gave up college plans through poor health, and tried the stage before turning to verse. His anonymous poems found success. His first South Sea Islands visit in 1864 produced the Idyls, letters praised by Howells as the lightest and freshest writing on that summer ocean.

Stoddard made four more South Sea trips, visited Molokai often, and knew Father Damien, the leper priest. His book on the Lepers of Molokai helped fix Damien's standing in public esteem. Received into the Catholic Church in 1867, he told his conversion story in A Troubled Heart and How it was Comforted. Later books ranged from Hawaii to Egypt and Alaska. He died at Monterey in 1909.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-claude-bernar:
Claude Bernard, a French physiologist born on 12 July 1813 at Saint Julien near Villefranche and dead at Paris on 10 February 1878, grew up the son of a vineyard owner. The village cure began his schooling, continued at the Jesuit college in Villefranche. In Lyons he became a pharmacist's assistant, and his literary hopes produced a staged comedy and then a five-act drama. Critic Saint Marc Girardin praised the drama in 1834 but advised medicine as a surer living.

In 1839 he became interne to Magendie at the College de France and then his lecture assistant, despite a retiring manner that had hidden his power. His first important work studied the pancreas and its functions. Then came his most noteworthy discovery, the sugar-forming function of the liver. Biologists had supposed animals could only use compounds furnished by plants, but Bernard showed the animal body building complex compounds within itself.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-claude-ferdin:
Claude-Ferdinand Gaillard, a French engraver and painter, was born at Paris on 7 January 1834 and died there on 27 January 1887. He studied chiefly with Cogniet, beginning engraving in 1850. At first he engraved fashion-plates to live, but steady application won the Prix de Rome in 1856. Critics at his first showing in 1860 called his prints laboured, soft, and flaccid, more like drypoint than burin work.

Gaillard had already chosen a new manner, and in 1863 he stood among the refuses, though Burty hailed his Bellini portrait as a master's work, engraved with religious care. His method used soft, delicate lines drawn closely together but never crossing, rendering every fold and wrinkle with vaporous delicacy. His best-known plate, L'Homme a l'Oeillet, brought only a hundred dollars and took eight days. Portraits of Pius the Ninth and Leo the Thirteenth made him the most celebrated engraver of his day.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-commander-jam:
Thomas Meehan's entry follows Commander James Harman Ward, born at Hartford, Connecticut, in 1806. He died in the attack on Matthias Point, Virginia, on 27 June 1861. He was the first Union naval officer to fall in the Civil War. A founder of the Naval Academy under its present system, he shaped the modern service through his books on naval science. A Catholic convert, he was buried from Saint Patrick's church, Hartford, amid a memorable war-time demonstration.

Ward entered the navy as a midshipman on 4 March 1823 and made lieutenant in 1831. Service off Africa yielded his Manual of Naval Tactics of 1858. He lectured on gunnery at Philadelphia in 1842, urged a naval school, and taught there from 1845 to 1847. His lectures on ordnance and his book Steam for the Million drew wide notice. Made commander in 1853, he organized the Potomac flotilla in May 1861 and died directing it against Confederate river batteries.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-confraterniti:
Ferdinand Heckmann's entry explains confraternities of the Cord, pious associations whose members wear a cord honoring a saint, seeking grace through his intercession. Belt wearing runs ancient, above all among Jews, whose priests and prophets wore them. Christ bade his Apostles gird their loins. Early Church virgins wore the cincture as purity's sign, and it marked chastity, mortification, and humility. A saint's cord first appears in Saint Monica's life. Medieval faithful wore cinctures for saints before formal confraternities arose.

Chief groups follow. Our Lady of Consolation, or the Black Leathern Belt of Saint Augustine, leads. The Cord of Saint Francis follows his conversion. The Cord of Saint Thomas ties to a 1657 cure of an Augustinian nun at Antwerp. The Cord of Saint Joseph and others from saints' lives complete the list. Each archconfraternity carries indulgences, rules, and a patron's story, binding a worn cord to prayer and penance.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-constant-foua:
John Francis Fenlon's entry follows Constant Fouard, ecclesiastical writer born at Elbeuf near Rouen on 6 August 1837, whose early life prepared his fame. He studied classics at Boisguillaume, philosophy at Issy from 1855 to 1857, and theology at Saint-Sulpice from 1857 to 1861. Paris professors John Logan, lifelong mentor, and Le Hir, who with Vigouroux drew him into Biblical science, shaped a life's devotion. Ordained in 1861, he entered the Sulpician novitiate, leaving after months through illness without joining.

He taught at Boisguillaume, then studied classics at Saint Barbara college, Paris, winning the Licentiate in Letters in 1867. Honors followed: theology doctor in 1877, Rouen canon in 1884, and Biblical Commission member in 1903. His work wins esteem for narrative interest, pure diction, doctrinal correctness, and a conservative, not reactionary, view. As a whole it pictures early Christianity faithfully. Two books on Saint Paul rank most esteemed, and the English translation earns praise as well done.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-einhard:
Einhard, less correctly Eginhard, was the historian of Charlemagne's court, born about 770 near the Main and dead at Seligenstadt in 840. Trained at Fulda, he was sent by Abbot Baugulf to Charlemagne's court and finished his schooling at the Palace School under Alcuin, who praised his skill in mathematics and building. Though small and plain, he became one of the emperor's most trusted advisers.

Charlemagne put him in charge of great buildings, including Aachen Cathedral and the palaces of Aachen and Ingelheim, earning him the court nickname Beseleel, after the builder of the tabernacle. He also carried out embassies, treating for Saxon hostages in 802 and seeking papal approval for the partition of the empire at Rome in 806. In 830 he withdrew to Mulheim, brought the relics of Marcellinus and Peter there, and founded the abbey where he spent his last years as abbot.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ekkehard:
Ekkehard is the name of five monks of Saint Gall in Switzerland, from the tenth to the thirteenth century, and this entry sorts them out one by one. The first, Ekkehard the Elder, dead in 973, ran the inner school and served as dean. He refused the abbacy after a broken leg left him lame. He built a hospice for the sick and for strangers. He also wrote the Latin epic Waltharius, on Walter of Aquitaine and Hildegunde, plus hymns and sequences.

The second, Ekkehard the Courtier, dead in 990, taught in the monastery school, while later namesakes carried on the house's learning in music and chronicle writing. The last, Ekkehard the Least, dead about 1220, was dean under Innocent III and wrote a life of Saint Notker the Stammerer about 1214. Together the five show Saint Gall as a home of teaching, song, and history across three centuries.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ernest-franco:
Ernest-Francois Mallard was a French mineralogist, born on 4 February 1833 at Châteauneuf-sur-Cher and dead on 6 July 1894 in Paris. From 1872 he was professor of mineralogy at the Ecole des Mines, and from 1890 a member of the Academy of Science. Many reports appeared year after year in the Bulletin de la Société minéralogique de France and in the Annales des Mines.

The optical anomalies of some crystals he tried to grasp clearly in their actual relationship and then to explain by a hypothesis. It supposes that the highly symmetrical form of these crystals is caused by many smaller crystals with fewer symmetrical planes, arranged in a certain manner. His best general explanation came in his lecture Crystallic Groupings, which appeared in the Revue Scientifique in 1887. His hypothesis found many defenders and many dissenters, especially among his German colleagues.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ethelhard:
Ethelhard was the fourteenth Archbishop of Canterbury, England, date of birth unknown, dead on 12 May 805. Much obscurity surrounds his life before his election. Symeon of Durham calls him Abbas Hludensis Monasterii, but the monastery is uncertain. It has been located at Louth in Lincolnshire, most probably, and also at Lydd, Luddersdown, and Malmesbury.

Offa, King of the Mercians from 757 to 796, had divided England into Northumbria, Mercia, and Wessex. Offa sought an independent ecclesiastical organization for his kingdom, for Mercia, after conquering Kent, was still subject to Canterbury, ruled by Jaenbert from 766 to 791. Offa's scheme was to weaken Canterbury by dividing the southern province and creating a Mercian archbishopric at Lichfield. This he accomplished when Higbert received the pallium as Archbishop of Lichfield during the Legatine visit of George and Theophylact, sent by Pope Hadrian I in 786 to 788.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-flodoard:
Flodoard was a French historian and chronicler born at Epernay in 894 and dead in 966. Educated at Reims, he became a cathedral canon and keeper of its archives. He visited Rome under Leo VII and wrote a long Latin poem on Christ and the early saints. Loyal to Archbishop Artold when deposed, he became his trusted adviser on restoration.

At Rotbert's instance he wrote the History of the Church of Reims from archives and Hincmar. The work is prized for full material and truthful narration. His Annals, covering 919 to 966, record events in plain, simple language year by year. The chronicle is a prime source for France, Lorraine, and the East Frankish realm.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francis-mario:
Francis Marion Crawford, born of American parents at Bagni di Lucca in Italy on 2 August 1854 and dead near Sorrento on 9 April 1909. He was a novelist who made Italian life his true field. His father Thomas Crawford was a distinguished sculptor, his mother Louisa Ward a sister of Julia Ward Howe, and his youth passed largely at Rome. After colleges in America, England, and Germany he finished at the Roman University, studying Sanskrit and comparative philology under Professor Lignana while already writing English literature.

Four and a half years in the East Indies and America as journalist and critic led to his first novel, Mr. Isaacs, in 1882, which leaped into fame, followed by Dr. Claudius in 1883 and A Roman Singer in 1884. That third book opened his lasting subject, Italian character and society, which he explored from the villa he bought near Sorrento after his marriage in 1884.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francois-just:
Francois-Juste-Marie Raynouard, born at Brignoles on 8 September 1761 and dead at Passy on 27 October 1836. He was a French poet, dramatist, and philologist who pioneered the study of Romance languages. He studied law at Aix and practised at the bar. When revolution broke out he embraced liberty at first, sat in the Legislative Assembly with the Girondins, then gave up the new ideas. During the Terror he was seized and held at the Abbaye, freed after the ninth Thermidor, and returned home to great success as an attorney.

In leisure he wrote poems and tragedies, including Socrate au temple d'Aglaure, Eleonore de Baviere, and Les Templiers, played in 1805 by Napoleon's command. Their success won him the French Academy in 1807.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francois-mans:
Francois Mansard, also spelled Mansart, was a French architect born at Paris, probably of Italian stock, in 1598 and dead there in 1666. His influence on architecture lasted through his final thirty years. Among contemporaries only Salomon de Brosse matched him in ability, yet defects and oddities so glaring they drew published satires long kept commissions from him. He held architecture so highly that he rarely settled a plan at the outset, expecting improvements to suggest themselves later, and so lost the Louvre commission, refusing to hand in detailed plans.

Having built one wing of the chateau of Maisons-Lafitte in 1642, he tore it down to rebuild on a better plan, producing his finest non-church work. Beginning the abbey church of Val-de-Grace in 1645, his fastidious self-criticism made him abandon it at ground plan for others to finish, though he is said to have built his design elsewhere.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-franz-burkard:
Franz Burkard is the name of two celebrated German jurists of the Reformation age, easily confused. One died suddenly at Rain on 9 December 1539. He began teaching canon law at Ingolstadt in 1519, stoutly opposing Lutheranism. With his brother Peter, a professor there, he led the prosecution of Andreas Seehofer, who had taught the new doctrine and was sentenced to retire to a monastery.

The other Burkard died at Bonn on 6 August 1584. To quell religious war over tolerance for Protestant worship, a volume under his name, De Autonomia, appeared at Munich in 1586. Its real author was the king's secretary Andreas Erstenberger, hidden behind the dead Burkard's name at William V's urging, since Rudolf II would brook no opposition to Protestants.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gilbert-geneb:
Gilbert Génébrard was a learned Benedictine scholar of Scripture and Eastern languages, born at Riom in 1535 and dead at Semur in 1597. He entered the Cluniac monastery of Mausac, studied at Clermont and Paris, and took his doctorate in theology in 1562. A year later he became professor of Hebrew and exegesis at the Collège Royal. A Catholic Encyclopedia article counts him among the most learned teachers of his university.

His many learned commentaries made him famous across Europe. St. Francis de Sales counted it an honor to have studied under him. He translated rabbinic writings into Latin, edited Origen in 1574, and published a noted commentary on the Psalms in 1577. Named Archbishop of Aix in 1591, he backed the Catholic League against Henry IV, submitted in 1593, and was banished by the Provençal Parliament in 1596.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-godfrey-giffa:
Godfrey Giffard was Bishop of Worcester, born about 1235, who died on 26 January 1301. Son of Hugh Giffard of Boyton and Sybil de Cormeilles, he rose with his elder brother Walter, Archbishop of York. He became canon and archdeacon of Wells, then Chancellor of the Exchequer in 1266 and Chancellor of England later that year. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows a bishop who ruled his diocese nearly thirty-four years.

Elected by the monks of Worcester, he received the temporalities in June 1268. He was consecrated at Canterbury that September and enthroned at Christmas. During his chancellorship a parliament at Marlborough passed useful laws restraining abuses of distress, regulating tenure, and improving civil and criminal procedure. As bishop he finished and fortified Hartlebury Castle, ever since the bishops' principal palace, and wrestled with long feuds with the cathedral monks and Malvern Priory.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gunning-s-bed:
Baltimore physician Gunning S. Bedford, born in 1806 and named for his uncle, a framer of the American Constitution, became a leading teacher of obstetrics in the United States. After Mount St. Mary's College and a medical degree from Rutgers, plus two years of study abroad, he held chairs at Charleston at twenty-six and then at Albany.

Moving to New York in 1836, he founded the University Medical College four years later. Beside it he opened the country's first obstetrical clinic for women too poor to pay a doctor, a boon for the poor and for medicine alike. He taught until illness stopped him in 1862. His Diseases of Women and Practice of Obstetrics ran through many editions in French and German as American textbooks.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hartford:
Connecticut's Diocese of Hartford, erected by Gregory XVI in September 1843, first covered Connecticut and Rhode Island, with its bishop living at Providence until a new see rose there in 1872. Now matching Connecticut alone, it holds 375,000 Catholics, a third of the state's people, across about five thousand square miles.

Colonial Catholics were few and often priestless, from Irish soldiers of the Pequot war to 400 Acadians scattered in 1756 who lost the faith without clergy. Bernard O'Cavanaugh became the first resident priest in 1828, and at the diocese's birth only three priests served Connecticut. William Tyler, its first bishop, lived in a shanty at Providence, begged priests from Dublin, and died of consumption in 1849 after five years.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-henry-bard:
Henry Bard, a soldier and diplomat born in 1604, travelled through France, Italy, Turkey, Palestine, and Egypt before taking a fellowship at King's College, Cambridge. A favourite of Charles I, he took up arms in the Civil War and was wounded and lost an arm at Cheriton Down. He later burned Camden House rather than surrender it to Parliament. He governed Worcester, scaled the ramparts at Naseby, and became Baron Bard and Viscount Bellamont in Ireland in 1646.

While travelling to Ireland, Bard was captured and freed on promising to go overseas. The court at The Hague became his refuge. Arrested in 1649 on a murder charge that came to nothing, he was sent by Charles II in 1656 as ambassador to the Shah of Persia. He sought funds for recovering the throne. The mission failed, since Persia owed England aid given at Ormuz. Bard died in a windstorm in Arabia about 1660.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-henry-bedford:
Henry Bedford, born in London in 1816, entered Cambridge intending to become an Anglican clergyman and became a popular High Church writer and preacher. A strongly Tractarian sermon set him against the Bishop of London, and he converted to Catholicism in 1851. A defect in his right hand barred him canonically from ordination, so he turned instead to education, joining the staff of All Hallows Missionary College near Dublin in 1852.

At All Hallows, Bedford spent half a century as professor of natural science, treasurer, and director, while writing constantly for Catholic periodicals and lecturing on Catholic subjects. His essays ranged across travel, archaeology, art, science, music, and English literature, appearing chiefly in The Month, The Irish Monthly, and The Irish Ecclesiastical Record. His Vacation Rambles, issued in a series through the 1870s, gathered some of the best of that periodical work.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-henry-of-herf:
Henry of Herford, a Dominican friar and chronicler who died at Minden on 9 October 1370, was a native of Herford in Westphalia and professed in the Dominican friary at Minden. He compiled his chronicle Liber de Rebus Memorabilioribus there, summarizing older historians from Eusebius down to writers of his own age. It continues to the coronation of Emperor Charles IV in 1355. It became a chief source of historical knowledge for the fourteenth century and was printed under Potthast's editorship at Göttingen in 1859.

Henry also composed the Catena Aurea, a summary of theology in ten parts, and a still unpublished treatise on the conception of the glorious Virgin. The entry thus preserves a monastic compiler whose value lay less in originality than in gathering and ordering the historical knowledge available to his century.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hugh-ward:
Hugh Ward, in Irish Aedh Buidh Mac-an-Bhaird, was an Irish hagiographer, born in Donegal about 1590 and dead in 1635. His father Geoffrey, chief of Lettermacward, led the Tirconnell branch of the Mac-an-Bhaird, who from remote times cultivated literature and served as chief historians to the O'Donnells. In 1607 Ward left Ireland for Spain and entered Salamanca University.

There Luke Wadding met him and guided him into the Franciscans in 1616. After degrees and ordination he lectured on philosophy at Paris and became Louvain's St. Anthony's College professor of divinity, elected its rector in 1626. Wadding praised his intellect and Irish learning, and Ponce ranked his scholastic lectures second to none. Ward's chief passion, though, was Irish saints' lives and ancient records, a publishing plan he pioneered.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-humphrey-beri:
Humphrey Berisford was an English confessor of about 1588. He is known only from a seventeenth-century manuscript compiled by Father Christopher Grene, now at the English College in Rome and partly printed in Foley's Records. The account calls him a Derbyshire gentleman whose father, an esquire, was Protestant.

Berisford studied at Douay about two years. Returning home, his father set him to a lawsuit, and an opponent, fearing defeat, accused him before the judge as a recusant. Examined, he constantly professed his faith. The judge offered favour to his suit and liberty if he would only promise to attend the established church, which he utterly refused. He was therefore imprisoned, where he remained seven years, the account's blank plausibly filled, and died a prisoner at Derby Gaol.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jacques-echar:
Jacques Echard, a Dominican historian, was born at Rouen on 22 September 1644 and died at Paris on 15 March 1724. As the son of a wealthy royal official, he got a thorough grounding in classical and secular learning. He joined the Dominican order at Paris and stood out for hard study, and when Jacques Quétif died in 1698, Echard picked up his unfinished project.

Quétif had mapped out a literary history of the Dominican order and had pulled together close to a fourth of its material; Echard was charged with finishing the work. After long labor and research in most of Europe's libraries, the history came out in 1721, filling two quarto volumes under the title Scriptores ordinis praedicatorum. Each writer's sketch sets out a list of works, with dates and edition details, and Echard likewise lists unpublished, spurious, and doubtful works.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-james-ambrose:
James Ambrose Dominic Aylward, theologian and poet, was born at Leeds on 4 April 1813 and died at Hinckley in England on 5 October 1872. He was schooled at Hinckley's Dominican priory. He joined the Dominican order and took priestly orders in 1836. He rose to provincial in 1850, to first prior of Woodchester in 1854, and to provincial once more in 1866. He wrote several devout manuals for his community.

His Novena for the Holy Season of Advent, drawn from missal and breviary prophecies and anthems, came out at Derby in 1849. In 1867 he re-edited a life of St Catherine of Siena, rendered from Italian by John Fen in 1609. That same year he issued an English version of Chocarne's Inner Life of Lacordaire. Essays dealing with mystical elements in religion, and with spiritism old and modern, appeared after his death under Cardinal Manning's editorship in 1874.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-baptiste:
Jean-Baptiste Blanchard, born Duchesne at Tourteron in 1731 and dead in 1797, was a French Jesuit educator who wrote under a changed name. He joined the Society in 1746, taught at Metz, Verdun, and Pont-à-Mousson, and left the order in 1762, settling near Namur to study teaching.

Blanchard's books on fables and morals led to his chief work, a guide to Christian education of both sexes, printed after his death in 1803. Borrowing Rousseau's Emile yet judging it keenly, he split schooling into body, morals, and girls' training, stressing health and hygiene. Though little in it was new, teachers prized its sound picks and plain advice.

Père Girard, born Jean-Baptiste Girard at Fribourg in 1765 and dead there in 1850, was a Swiss Franciscan who remade his canton's schools. He entered the order at sixteen, taught in its colleges, studied at Würzburg, and returned to Fribourg in 1789 for mission and teaching work.

As director of Fribourg's schools from 1807 to 1823, Girard made schooling compulsory, set up sound administration and textbooks, and used pupil monitors while fighting rote memory drill. Every subject, he held, should serve the child's whole growth. His reforms drew bitter foes wedded to old routine, yet they crowned his life's work and outlasted the quarrels.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-louis-bo:
Jean-Louis Bonnard, a French missionary and martyr born in 1824 at Saint-Christôt-en-Jarret and beheaded in 1852, studied at Saint-Jodard and the Lyons seminary before finishing at Paris's foreign missions seminary. Ordained at Nantes, he sailed for western Tonkin and arrived in May 1850.

Put in charge of two parishes in 1851, Bonnard was seized on 21 March 1852 and jailed. Sentence of death, once confirmed by the king, was carried out at once on 30 April. His body, cast into a river, was recovered by Christians and sent to the foreign missions seminary. The Church has declared him Venerable, a witness honoured for dying on mission ground.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-nicolas-:
Jean-Nicolas Beauregard, a French Jesuit preacher born at Metz in 1733 and dead in Germany in 1804, joined the Society at Nancy in 1749. After teaching classics and rhetoric for six years at Nancy, Verdun, Strasbourg, and Pont-à-Mousson, he turned to preaching in 1767, the work of his life.

Beauregard won fame in smaller French towns, then still greater success in Paris. His Lent sermons before the court in 1789 were said to foretell the evils about to engulf France. Fleeing revolution in 1794, he lived in London, Maastricht, and Cologne, ending his days at a princess's castle, his sermons mostly still in manuscript.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-picard:
Jean Picard, a French astronomer born at La Flèche in 1620 and dead in Paris in 1682. A priest and prior of Rillé, he studied under Gassendi and watched the 1645 solar eclipse with him. In 1655 he succeeded his master as astronomy professor at the Collège de France.

Picard's chief feat was measuring a meridian arc from Sourdon to Malvoisine in 1669 and 1670, fixing a degree at 57,060 toises, only fourteen too small. He fitted telescopes and micrometers to instruments from 1667, read angles to a quarter minute, and tied his standard rod to a seconds pendulum so it could be remade. Newton used his figures to revise his own reckoning.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-bromyard:
John Bromyard was a Dominican theologian and a leading opponent of John Wyclif. Named for his birthplace in Herefordshire, he entered the Dominican order, distinguished himself at Oxford in theology and jurisprudence, and labored in the theology faculty at Cambridge. He died about 1390.

His name does not appear in the acts of the London Synod of 1382, where Archbishop Courtenay condemned Wyclif's doctrines as heretical. Yet all agree he led in drafting the decree of condemnation. His Summa for Preachers, prized enough to run through many editions, was excerpted into pamphlets widely circulated among the people. His Opus Trivium arranged topics from theology and civil and canon law for preachers' convenience.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-gerard:
John Gerard was an English Jesuit whose autobiography is a classic record of the underground priesthood under Elizabeth. Born in 1564, second son of Sir Thomas Gerard of Bryn, he left home at thirteen for Douai. He studied at Oxford and the Jesuit college at Paris. After two years in the Marshalsea prison he reached Rome in 1586 and entered the Jesuit novitiate in 1588.

Sent back to England within a year, he landed alone on the Norfolk coast amid the Armada panic. Feeling against Catholics then ran so high that priests were being butchered in London. An accomplished horseman and sportsman, he traveled disguised as huntsman or lost rider.
